  • Complete equilibrium requires both conditions together: the sum of forces is zero for translational equilibrium and the sum of torques is zero for rotational equilibrium.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Q1. How are vectors added and subtracted geometrically?

Ans: Geometrically, vectors are added by the head-to-tail rule: the second vector is drawn with its tail at the head of the first, keeping its magnitude and direction unchanged, and the resultant is drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the last; for more vectors the process is repeated, forming a polygon. Two vectors can also be added by the parallelogram law: drawn from a common tail, the diagonal of the parallelogram built on them is the resultant. Subtraction A - B is done by adding the negative of B: reverse the direction of B and then add it to A head-to-tail; geometrically the difference vector joins the head of B to the head of A when both are drawn from the same point.

Q: Q2. If a vector is multiplied by a positive scalar, how is the result related to the original vector? What if the scalar is zero? Negative?

Ans: Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar k gives a new vector k times as long, in exactly the same direction as the original vector; only its magnitude is scaled. If the scalar is zero, the result is the null (zero) vector: it has zero magnitude and no direction. If the scalar is negative, the magnitude is scaled by the absolute value of the scalar and the direction is reversed, i.e. the product points exactly opposite to the original vector.

Q: Q3. What are rectangular components of a vector? How rectangular components are used to represent a vector?

Ans: The rectangular components of a vector are its projections on the mutually perpendicular coordinate axes. For a vector A making angle theta with the x-axis in a plane, A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta; in three dimensions there is also A_z along the z-axis. They are used to represent the vector completely as A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k, where i, j, k are unit vectors along the axes. From the components, the magnitude A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2) and the direction (for example tan theta = A_y / A_x in the plane) can be recovered, and addition, subtraction and products become simple algebraic operations on components.

Q: Q4. Explain addition of vectors by rectangular components.

Ans: To add vectors by rectangular components: (1) resolve every vector into its x, y (and z) components using A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta, with signs according to the quadrant; (2) add all the x-components algebraically to get R_x, and all the y-components to get R_y; (3) the resultant magnitude is R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2) and its direction is given by theta_R = tan^-1(R_y / R_x), corrected for the quadrant from the signs of R_x and R_y. For example, in Example 2.2 the components of 15 N at 70 degrees and 25 N at 220 degrees add to R_x = -14.02 N and R_y = -1.98 N, giving F_R = 14.16 N at theta_R = 187.97 degrees.

Q: Q5. Define the dot product (scalar product) of two vectors. What geometric interpretation does the dot product have? Give examples.

Ans: The dot (scalar) product of two vectors A and B is the scalar quantity A . B = A B cos theta, where theta is the smaller angle between them; it can also be computed from components as A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z. Geometric interpretation: it is the magnitude of one vector multiplied by the component (projection) of the other vector along the first, A . B = A (B cos theta); it is also related to the angle between the vectors, and it vanishes when they are perpendicular. Examples: work W = F . d, power P = F . v, and the flux of a field through a surface.

Q: Q6. Define the cross product (vector product) of two vectors. What geometric interpretation does the cross product have? Give examples.

Ans: The cross (vector) product of two vectors A and B is a new vector A cross B whose magnitude is A B sin theta, where theta is the smaller angle between them, and whose direction is perpendicular to the plane of A and B, given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand from A towards B and the thumb gives the direction (the direction of advance of a right-handed screw turned from A to B). Geometric interpretation: its magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram having A and B as adjacent sides (and twice the area of the triangle they form). Examples: torque tau = r cross F, angular momentum L = r cross p, and the magnetic force on a moving charge, F = q v cross B.

Q: Q7. Define torque. Show that torque is the vector product of force and position vector.

Ans: Torque is the turning effect of a force about an axis; its magnitude is the product of the force and the perpendicular distance (moment arm) from the axis to the line of action of the force, tau = F d = F r sin theta, where r is the position vector from the axis (point) to the point of application of F and theta is the angle between r and F. This is exactly the magnitude of the vector product r cross F, and the direction of r cross F, given by the right-hand rule, is along the axis of rotation. Hence torque is the vector product of the position vector and the force: tau = r cross F, which proves the statement.

Q: Q8. What is mechanical equilibrium? Explain different types of equilibrium.

Ans: Mechanical equilibrium is the state of a body in which the net force and the net torque on it are both zero, so it has no tendency to accelerate as a whole or to start rotating; a body at rest in this state is in static equilibrium. Types: stable equilibrium, in which a slightly displaced body returns to its original position (its centre of gravity is raised on displacement, e.g. a ball in a bowl); unstable equilibrium, in which a displaced body moves further away (centre of gravity is lowered, e.g. a ball on top of a dome); and neutral equilibrium, in which a displaced body stays in its new position (centre of gravity stays at the same height, e.g. a ball on a flat surface).

Q: Q9. What type of equilibrium is guaranteed by each condition of equilibrium?

Ans: The first condition of equilibrium, sum of F = 0 (the vector sum of all external forces is zero), guarantees translational equilibrium: the body has no linear acceleration, so a body at rest stays at rest and a moving body keeps constant velocity. The second condition, sum of torque = 0 (the sum of all external torques about any axis is zero), guarantees rotational equilibrium: the body has no angular acceleration, so it does not start rotating. Only when both conditions hold together is complete (static) equilibrium guaranteed.

mcqs.q: How are vectors added geometrically?
options: By multiplying their magnitudes and adding their angles

By the head-to-tail rule, drawing the second vector with its tail at the head of the first, with the resultant drawn from the tail of the first to the head of the last; two vectors can also be added by the parallelogram law
Only by resolving them into components
By placing them tail to tail and joining their heads
mcqs.why: In the head-to-tail rule each following vector is drawn from the head of the previous one with its magnitude and direction unchanged, and the resultant runs from the tail of the first to the head of the last, forming a polygon for many vectors; the parallelogram law gives the same resultant as the diagonal when two vectors share a common tail.

mcqs.q: How is the subtraction A - B performed geometrically?
options: By shortening B by the length of A
By reversing the direction of B and then adding it to A head to tail; with a common origin the difference joins the head of B to the head of A
By drawing B on top of A and measuring the overlap
Subtraction of vectors is not defined geometrically
mcqs.why: Subtraction is addition of the negative vector: B is reversed in direction and then added to A by the head-to-tail rule, and when both vectors are drawn from the same point the difference vector runs from the head of B to the head of A.

mcqs.q: A vector is multiplied by a scalar. What happens for a positive scalar, for zero and for a negative scalar?
options: A positive scalar reverses the direction, zero gives the same vector, and a negative scalar only lengthens it
A positive scalar scales the magnitude keeping the same direction, zero gives the null vector with no direction, and a negative scalar scales the magnitude and reverses the direction
The direction never changes for any scalar
Only the direction changes; the magnitude is never affected
mcqs.why: Multiplying by a positive scalar gives a vector in exactly the same direction with its length scaled; a zero scalar gives the null vector of zero magnitude and no direction; a negative scalar scales the magnitude by its absolute value and points the product exactly opposite to the original vector.

mcqs.q: What are the rectangular components of a vector and how do they represent it?
options: They are the vector's projections on the coordinate axes, A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta, and the vector is written A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k, from which its magnitude and direction can be recovered
They are three vectors each equal to the original vector
They can only be found graphically from a scale drawing
They are the same as the magnitude of the vector in three directions
mcqs.why: The rectangular components are the projections of the vector on the mutually perpendicular axes; writing the vector as the sum of its components with the unit vectors represents it completely, and the magnitude follows from the square root of the sum of squared components while the direction follows from the ratio of the components.

mcqs.q: What are the steps for adding vectors by the method of rectangular components?
options: Add all the magnitudes, then average the angles

Resolve every vector into x and y components, add all x components to get R_x and all y components to get R_y, then take R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2) with direction from tan inverse of R_y over R_x, corrected for the quadrant
Draw the vectors to scale and measure the resultant with a ruler
Multiply the components of one vector by those of the other
mcqs.why: Each vector is first resolved using A_x = A cos theta and A_y = A sin theta with signs from its quadrant; the components are then added algebraically axis by axis, and the resultant magnitude and direction are recovered from R_x and R_y, with the direction corrected for the quadrant shown by their signs.

mcqs.q: What is the dot product of two vectors and what is its geometric meaning?
options: It is a vector of magnitude A B sin theta
It is the scalar A B cos theta, equal to the magnitude of one vector multiplied by the projection of the other along it, as in work W = F . d
It is always equal to the area of the parallelogram on the two vectors
It is zero whenever the vectors are parallel
mcqs.why: The dot product is the scalar quantity A B cos theta, also computed from components as A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z; geometrically it is one vector's magnitude times the component of the other along it, it vanishes for perpendicular vectors, and examples include work and power.

mcqs.q: What is the cross product of two vectors and what is its geometric meaning?
options: It is the scalar A B cos theta
It is a scalar equal to the projection of one vector on the other

It is a vector of magnitude A B sin theta, perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors by the right-hand rule, whose magnitude equals the area of the parallelogram built on them, as in torque tau = r cross F
It is a vector parallel to both of the original vectors
mcqs.why: The cross product is a new vector whose magnitude A B sin theta equals the area of the parallelogram having the two vectors as adjacent sides, and whose direction, perpendicular to their plane, is given by the right-hand rule; torque, angular momentum and the magnetic force on a moving charge are examples.

mcqs.q: How is torque shown to be the vector product of the position vector and the force?
options: Torque equals force divided by distance, which matches a scalar product
Torque has magnitude F r sin theta, exactly the magnitude of r cross F, and its direction by the right-hand rule is along the axis of rotation, so torque equals r cross F
Torque is a scalar, so it cannot be a vector product
Torque equals r dot F because both involve r and F
mcqs.why: Torque is the turning effect of a force, with magnitude equal to the force times the perpendicular distance from the axis, F r sin theta where theta is the angle between r and F; this is exactly the magnitude of the vector product r cross F, and the right-hand rule gives its direction along the axis of rotation.

mcqs.q: What is mechanical equilibrium and what are its three types?
options: Equilibrium means the body is moving at constant speed only

Equilibrium is the state where net force and net torque are both zero; a displaced body returns in stable equilibrium, moves further away in unstable equilibrium, and stays in its new position in neutral equilibrium
The three types are translational, rotational and dynamic equilibrium
Equilibrium requires the centre of gravity to be at the lowest possible point in every type
mcqs.why: A body is in mechanical equilibrium when the net force and the net torque on it are both zero; in stable equilibrium a slightly displaced body returns and its centre of gravity is raised, in unstable equilibrium it moves further away as its centre of gravity is lowered, and in neutral equilibrium it stays put with its centre of gravity at the same height.

mcqs.q: What does each condition of equilibrium guarantee?
options: The first condition guarantees rotational equilibrium and the second guarantees translational equilibrium
Both conditions together are needed, but neither guarantees anything on its own
The first condition, sum of F = 0, guarantees translational equilibrium with no linear acceleration, and the second, sum of torque = 0, guarantees rotational equilibrium with no angular acceleration
The second condition alone guarantees complete static equilibrium
mcqs.why: The first condition, that the vector sum of all external forces is zero, ensures the body has no linear acceleration, while the second condition, that the sum of all external torques about any axis is zero, ensures it has no angular acceleration and does not start rotating; only both together give complete equilibrium.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The resultant velocity of a 120 m/s airplane in a 30 m/s cross wind is about 113 m/s at 4.4 degrees below the positive x-axis.
  • Reversing a vector subtraction negates both components, keeping the same magnitude and turning the direction by 180 degrees.
  • The resultant of 20 N at 30 degrees and 30 N at 150 degrees is 26.46 N at 109.11 degrees, in the second quadrant.
  • The equilibrant of a force system is a single pull equal in magnitude to the resultant and opposite in direction, 180 degrees away.
  • For a diving board in equilibrium the bolt force is 1150 N downward and the fulcrum force is 1750 N upward, whichever point is taken as the axis.
  • A boy of weight 400 N can walk 4.5 m along a 6 m plank before the rope tension reaches its breaking value of 400 N.
  • A small sag angle greatly increases clothesline tension: an 18 N bag at a sag of 3.50 degrees produces a tension of 148 N.
  • The reactions of an 8.0 m I-beam carrying its own 4410 N weight and a 2156 N load are about 2850 N at the left support and 3710 N at the right support.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 2.1 - Airplane Through Wind

Q: Q1. An airplane is moving at 120 m/s at an angle of 10 degrees with x-axis, through a 30 m/s cross wind, blowing at angle of 260 degrees with x-axis. Determine the resultant velocity of the airplane. (20 m)

Ans: Given: Velocity of airplane = 120 m/s at 10 degrees with x-axis; wind velocity = 30 m/s at 260 degrees with x-axis
Formula: Resultant components: R_x = 120 cos 10 degrees + 30 cos 260 degrees; R_y = 120 sin 10 degrees + 30 sin 260 degrees; R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2)
Substitution: R_x = 120 x 0.985 + 30 x (-0.174) = 118.2 - 5.2 = 113.0 m/s
R_y = 120 x 0.174 + 30 x (-0.985) = 20.8 - 29.5 = -8.7 m/s
R = sqrt(113.0^2 + 8.7^2) = sqrt(12769 + 76) = 113.3 m/s
Direction: theta = tan^-1(8.7 / 113.0) = 4.4 degrees below the x-axis, i.e. 355.6 degrees with the positive x-axis
Answer: About 113 m/s at 4.4 degrees below the positive x-axis
Note: The book's printed answer (20 m) is incorrect because it is incomplete and dimensionally wrong for a resultant velocity of 120 m/s and 30 m/s vectors; the correct resultant magnitude is about 113 m/s.

Extension Exercise

Q: Q1. In example 2.2 also calculate the resultant force for F_R = F_1 - F_2 and F_R = F_2 - F_1.

Ans: Data from Example 2.2: F_1 = 15 N at theta_1 = 70 degrees, F_1x = 5.13 N, F_1y = 14.09 N; F_2 = 25 N at theta_2 = 220 degrees, F_2x = -19.15 N, F_2y = -16.07 N.
For F_R = F_1 - F_2:
Formula: R_x = F_1x - F_2x, R_y = F_1y - F_2y, R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2)
Substitution: R_x = 5.13 - (-19.15) = 24.28 N
R_y = 14.09 - (-16.07) = 30.16 N
R = sqrt(24.28^2 + 30.16^2) = sqrt(589.5 + 909.6) = sqrt(1499.1) = 38.7 N
Direction: theta_R = tan^-1(30.16 / 24.28) = 51.2 degrees with the positive x-axis (first quadrant)
Answer: F_R = F_1 - F_2 = 38.7 N at 51.2 degrees
For F_R = F_2 - F_1: this is the negative of the above vector, so R_x = -24.28 N, R_y = -30.16 N, magnitude is again 38.7 N, and the direction is 180 + 51.2 = 231.2 degrees with the positive x-axis (third quadrant)
Answer: F_R = F_2 - F_1 = 38.7 N at 231.2 degrees

Assignment 2.2 - Vector Addition

Q: Q1. A Force F_1 = 20 N making an angle theta_1 = 30 degrees with positive x-axis and Force F_2 = 30 N making an angle theta_2 = 150 degrees with positive x-axis, acts at a point, calculate the resultant force. (F_R = 26.46 N, theta_R = 109.11 degrees)

Ans: Given: F_1 = 20 N at theta_1 = 30 degrees, F_2 = 30 N at theta_2 = 150 degrees
Formula: R_x = F_1 cos theta_1 + F_2 cos theta_2; R_y = F_1 sin theta_1 + F_2 sin theta_2; F_R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2)
Substitution: R_x = 20 cos 30 degrees + 30 cos 150 degrees = 17.32 - 25.98 = -8.66 N
R_y = 20 sin 30 degrees + 30 sin 150 degrees = 10.0 + 15.0 = 25.0 N
F_R = sqrt(8.66^2 + 25.0^2) = sqrt(75 + 625) = sqrt(700) = 26.46 N
Direction: reference angle = tan^-1(25.0 / 8.66) = 70.89 degrees; R_x is negative and R_y positive, so the resultant is in the second quadrant: theta_R = 180 - 70.89 = 109.11 degrees
Answer: F_R = 26.46 N, theta_R = 109.11 degrees

Assignment 2.3 - Resultant Vector

Q: Q1. Two forces of 20 N and 10 N are making an angle of 120 degrees with each other. Find a single pull that would (a) replace the given forces system (b) balance the given forces system. ((a) F_R = 17.32 N, theta_R = 30 degrees, (b) F_R = 17.32 N, theta_R = 210 degrees)

Ans: Given: F_1 = 20 N, F_2 = 10 N, angle between them theta = 120 degrees
Formula: Resultant F_R = sqrt(F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 cos theta); direction tan phi = F_2 sin theta / (F_1 + F_2 cos theta), phi measured from F_1
Substitution: F_R = sqrt(400 + 100 + 2 x 20 x 10 x cos 120 degrees) = sqrt(500 - 200) = sqrt(300) = 17.32 N
tan phi = (10 x sin 120 degrees) / (20 + 10 x cos 120 degrees) = 8.66 / 15 = 0.577, so phi = 30 degrees from the 20 N force
(a) The single pull that replaces the system is the resultant itself: 17.32 N at 30 degrees to the 20 N force
(b) The single pull that balances the system is the equilibrant: equal and opposite to the resultant, 17.32 N at 30 + 180 = 210 degrees
Answer: (a) F_R = 17.32 N, theta_R = 30 degrees; (b) F_R = 17.32 N, theta_R = 210 degrees

Assignment 2.4 - Vector Multiplication

Q: Q1. Show that (A . B)^2 + (A x B)^2 = A^2 B^2

Ans: Let theta be the angle between vectors A and B.
Given: A dot B = A B cos theta, and the magnitude of A cross B = A B sin theta
Formula: (A dot B)^2 + (magnitude of A cross B)^2 = (A B cos theta)^2 + (A B sin theta)^2
Substitution: = A^2 B^2 cos^2 theta + A^2 B^2 sin^2 theta
= A^2 B^2 (cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta)
Since cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1, the right side becomes A^2 B^2
Answer: (A dot B)^2 + (A cross B)^2 = A^2 B^2, proved. Note: in the second term it is the squared magnitude of the vector product that is meant.

Extension Exercise

Q: Q1. Solve example 2.6 by taking fulcrum as the axis of rotation.

Ans: This is the diving board problem of the text (printed as Example 2.5 in the book, Figure 2.35): Hina's weight F_H = 450 N at the end of the 5 m board, board weight F_C = 150 N at its centre C, 2.5 m from the bolt; the fulcrum is 1.5 m from the bolt. In the book's solution the axis is taken at the bolt, giving F_F = 1750 N and F_B = 1150 N. Taking the fulcrum as the axis instead:
Given: Distances from fulcrum: bolt 1.5 m (left), centre C 2.5 - 1.5 = 1.0 m (right), Hina 5 - 1.5 = 3.5 m (right)
Formula: Second condition of equilibrium about the fulcrum: sum of torques = 0; the fulcrum force itself has zero torque about its own point
Substitution: F_B x 1.5 m = F_C x 1.0 m + F_H x 3.5 m
F_B x 1.5 = 150 x 1.0 + 450 x 3.5 = 150 + 1575 = 1725 N m
F_B = 1725 / 1.5 = 1150 N (bolt pulls down on the board)
First condition of equilibrium (vertical forces): F_F = F_B + F_C + F_H = 1150 + 150 + 450 = 1750 N (fulcrum pushes up)
Answer: Bolt force F_B = 1150 N downward, fulcrum force F_F = 1750 N upward, the same results as obtained with the bolt as axis, as they must be for a body in equilibrium.

Assignment 2.5 - Breaking Tension

Q: Q1. A uniform plank of weight 200 N and length 6 m is supported by a rope as shown in the figure. If the breaking tension in the rope is 400 N. How far can a boy of weight 400 N walk towards the support? (4.5 m)

Ans: Diagram (in words): A horizontal uniform plank is hinged (supported) at its left end against a wall; a vertical rope attached at the right (far) end holds it up, labelled F_T = 400 N upward. The plank length l_T = 6 m is marked from the hinge to the rope; the plank's own weight F_P = 200 N acts downward at its centre, l_P = 3 m from the hinge; a boy of weight F_M = 400 N stands on the plank with his weight arrow pointing down, walking from the hinge towards the rope.
Given: Plank weight = 200 N at 3 m from the hinge, rope at 6 m from the hinge, maximum (breaking) tension = 400 N, boy's weight = 400 N at unknown distance x from the hinge
Formula: Second condition of equilibrium, torques about the hinge = 0: T x 6 = 200 x 3 + 400 x x
Substitution: 400 x 6 = 600 + 400 x
2400 - 600 = 400 x
x = 1800 / 400 = 4.5 m
Answer: The boy can walk 4.5 m from the hinge towards the support (rope) before the tension reaches its breaking value of 400 N

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: Q1. A person throws a ball straight up with a speed of 12 m/s. If the bus is moving at 25 m/s, what is the velocity of the ball to an observer on ground? (v_R = 28 m/s, theta_R = 26 degrees)

Ans: Given: Ball velocity relative to bus = 12 m/s vertically up; bus velocity = 25 m/s horizontal; the person is in the moving bus (as read with the printed answer)
Formula: v_R = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2); theta_R = tan^-1(v_y / v_x)
Substitution: v_R = sqrt(25^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(625 + 144) = sqrt(769) = 27.7 m/s, about 28 m/s
theta_R = tan^-1(12 / 25) = tan^-1(0.48) = 25.6 degrees, about 26 degrees above the horizontal
Answer: v_R = 28 m/s, theta_R = 26 degrees

Q: Q2. A football leaves the foot of a punter at an angle of 54 degrees (positive x-direction) at a speed of 21 m/s. Determine the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity. (12 m/s and 17 m/s)

Ans: Given: Speed v = 21 m/s at 54 degrees above the positive x-direction
Formula: v_x = v cos theta; v_y = v sin theta
Substitution: v_x = 21 x cos 54 degrees = 21 x 0.588 = 12.3 m/s, about 12 m/s
v_y = 21 x sin 54 degrees = 21 x 0.809 = 17.0 m/s, about 17 m/s
Answer: Horizontal component = 12 m/s and vertical component = 17 m/s

Q: Q3. A 1.84-kg school bag hangs in the middle of a clothesline, causing it to sag by an angle theta = 3.50 degrees. Find the tension T in the clothesline. (148 N)

Ans: Given: Mass of bag m = 1.84 kg, weight W = m g = 1.84 x 9.8 = 18.0 N, sag angle theta = 3.50 degrees on each side
Formula: For equilibrium, 2 T sin theta = W, so T = W / (2 sin theta)
Substitution: T = 18.0 / (2 x sin 3.50 degrees) = 18.0 / (2 x 0.0611) = 18.0 / 0.122 = 147.7 N
Answer: T = 148 N

Q: Q4. Find the magnitude and direction of vector represented by the following pair of components (a) A_x = -2.3 cm, A_y = +4.1 cm (b) A_x = +3.9 m, A_y = -1.8 m ((a) A = 4.7 and theta_A = 119.3 degrees (b) A = 4.3 and theta_A = 335.2 degrees)

Ans: (a) Given: A_x = -2.3 cm, A_y = +4.1 cm
Formula: A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2); theta_A = tan^-1(A_y / A_x), corrected for the quadrant
Substitution: A = sqrt(2.3^2 + 4.1^2) = sqrt(5.29 + 16.81) = sqrt(22.10) = 4.7 cm
Reference angle = tan^-1(4.1 / 2.3) = 60.7 degrees; A_x is negative and A_y positive (second quadrant), so theta_A = 180 - 60.7 = 119.3 degrees
Answer (a): A = 4.7 cm and theta_A = 119.3 degrees
(b) Given: A_x = +3.9 m, A_y = -1.8 m
Substitution: A = sqrt(3.9^2 + 1.8^2) = sqrt(15.21 + 3.24) = sqrt(18.45) = 4.3 m
Reference angle = tan^-1(1.8 / 3.9) = 24.8 degrees; A_x is positive and A_y negative (fourth quadrant), so theta_A = 360 - 24.8 = 335.2 degrees
Answer (b): A = 4.3 m and theta_A = 335.2 degrees

Q: Q5. Vector F having magnitude 5.5 N makes 10 degrees with x-axis and vector r with magnitude 4.3 m makes 80 degrees with x-axis. What is the magnitude of their dot and cross products? (8.1 N m and 22.2 N m)

Ans: Given: F = 5.5 N at 10 degrees with x-axis; r = 4.3 m at 80 degrees with x-axis; angle between F and r = 80 - 10 = 70 degrees
Formula: Dot product magnitude = F r cos theta; cross product magnitude = F r sin theta
Substitution: F . r = 5.5 x 4.3 x cos 70 degrees = 23.65 x 0.342 = 8.09, about 8.1 N m
Magnitude of F cross r (equal to r cross F in magnitude) = 5.5 x 4.3 x sin 70 degrees = 23.65 x 0.940 = 22.2 N m
Answer: Dot product = 8.1 N m and cross product magnitude = 22.2 N m

Q: Q6. The magnitude of dot and cross product of two vectors 6 sqrt(3) and 6 respectively. Find the angle between the vectors. (30 degrees)

Ans: Given: A . B = 6 sqrt(3), magnitude of A cross B = 6
Formula: A . B = A B cos theta and A cross B magnitude = A B sin theta; dividing, tan theta = (A B sin theta) / (A B cos theta)
Substitution: tan theta = 6 / (6 sqrt(3)) = 1 / sqrt(3) = 0.577
theta = tan^-1(0.577) = 30 degrees
Answer: The angle between the vectors is 30 degrees

Q: Q7. A uniform rod 1 m long with weight 6 N can be supported in a horizontal position on a sharp edge with weights of 10 N and 15 N suspended from its ends. What is the position of point of balance? (0.41 m)

Ans: Given: Uniform rod length 1 m, weight 6 N acting at its centre (0.5 m); weights 10 N and 15 N suspended from its two ends
Formula: Taking torques about the balance point (or finding the centre of gravity of the loaded rod): position of balance from the 10 N end, x = (10 x 0 + 6 x 0.5 + 15 x 1) / (10 + 6 + 15)
Substitution: x = (0 + 3 + 15) / 31 = 18 / 31 = 0.58 m from the 10 N end
Distance from the 15 N end = 1 - 0.58 = 0.42 m
Answer: The point of balance is 0.58 m from the 10 N end, i.e. about 0.42 m from the 15 N end (book prints 0.41 m)

Q: Q8. A 4.0-m-long uniform ladder with weight of 120 N leans against a wall making 70 degrees above a cement floor as shown in Figure. Assuming the wall is frictionless, but the floor is not, determine the forces exerted on the ladder by the floor and by the wall. (122 N)

Ans: Diagram (in words): A uniform ladder of length l = 4 m leans with its foot on a horizontal floor (labelled Floor) and its top against a vertical wall (labelled Wall) on the right; the ladder makes 70 degrees with the floor at its foot; the ladder's weight W = 120 N acts vertically down (green arrow) from its midpoint; F_W is the horizontal push of the wall on the top of the ladder, pointing away from the wall; F_G is the force of the floor at the foot, shown as a red arrow directed up along the ladder.
Given: Ladder length 4.0 m, weight W = 120 N at its midpoint (2.0 m from the foot), angle with floor = 70 degrees; wall frictionless, so the wall exerts only a horizontal force F_W
Formula: Torque about the foot = 0: F_W x (4 sin 70 degrees) = W x (2 cos 70 degrees); then floor force = sqrt(F_W^2 + W^2)
Substitution: F_W = (120 x 2 x cos 70 degrees) / (4 x sin 70 degrees) = 120 x 0.5 x cot 70 degrees = 60 x 0.364 = 21.8 N
Force by the wall = 21.8 N horizontally
Vertical force by floor = W = 120 N; horizontal force by floor (friction) = F_W = 21.8 N
Resultant force by floor = sqrt(120^2 + 21.8^2) = sqrt(14400 + 475) = 122 N
Answer: Force by the wall = about 22 N; resultant force by the floor = 122 N, at tan^-1(120 / 21.8) = about 80 degrees to the floor

Q: Q9. The 450-kg uniform I-beam supports the load of 220 kg as shown. Determine the reactions at the supports. (2850 N)

Ans: Diagram (in words): A horizontal I-beam rests on two supports, one under each end; a red upward arrow at the left support is labelled R_A = ? and a red upward arrow at the right support is labelled R_B = ?; a load of 220 kg hangs from the beam at a point 5.6 m from the left support (R_A) and 2.4 m from the right support (R_B), so the span is 8.0 m.
Given: Beam mass 450 kg, weight = 450 x 9.8 = 4410 N acting at its centre, 4.0 m from each support; load mass 220 kg, weight = 220 x 9.8 = 2156 N at 5.6 m from R_A; span = 5.6 + 2.4 = 8.0 m
Formula: R_A + R_B = total weight; torques about A: R_B x 8.0 = 4410 x 4.0 + 2156 x 5.6
Substitution: R_B x 8.0 = 17640 + 12074 = 29714
R_B = 29714 / 8.0 = 3714 N, about 3710 N
R_A = (4410 + 2156) - 3714 = 6566 - 3714 = 2852 N, about 2850 N
Answer: R_A = 2850 N and R_B = about 3710 N
Note: The book's printed answer (2850 N) gives only R_A; the reaction at the other support, R_B = about 3710 N, is also required and is supplied here.

mcqs.q: An airplane is moving at 120 m/s at an angle of 10 degrees with x-axis, through a 30 m/s cross wind, blowing at angle of 260 degrees with x-axis. Determine the resultant velocity of the airplane.
options: 113 m/s at 4.4 degrees below the positive x-axis
150 m/s at 10 degrees with the x-axis
90 m/s at 4.4 degrees below the positive x-axis
mcqs.why: Formula: R_x = 120 cos 10 degrees + 30 cos 260 degrees; R_y = 120 sin 10 degrees + 30 sin 260 degrees; R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2). Substitution: R_x = 118.2 - 5.2 = 113.0 m/s and R_y = 20.8 - 29.5 = -8.7 m/s. Step: R = sqrt(113.0^2 + 8.7^2) = sqrt(12845) = 113.3 m/s, and the direction is tan inverse of 8.7/113.0 = 4.4 degrees below the x-axis. Result: About 113 m/s at 4.4 degrees below the positive x-axis. Note: The book's printed answer of 20 m is incorrect and incomplete for a resultant of 120 m/s and 30 m/s vectors; the corrected resultant of about 113 m/s is used here.

mcqs.q: In example 2.2 also calculate the resultant force for F_R = F_1 - F_2 and F_R = F_2 - F_1, where F_1 = 15 N at 70 degrees and F_2 = 25 N at 220 degrees.
options: F_1 - F_2 = 14.16 N at 187.97 degrees; F_2 - F_1 is the same vector
F_1 - F_2 = 38.7 N at 51.2 degrees; F_2 - F_1 = 38.7 N at 231.2 degrees
F_1 - F_2 = 38.7 N at 231.2 degrees; F_2 - F_1 = 38.7 N at 51.2 degrees
F_1 - F_2 = 10 N at 51.2 degrees; F_2 - F_1 = 10 N at 231.2 degrees
mcqs.why: Formula: R_x = F_1x - F_2x and R_y = F_1y - F_2y, with R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2), using F_1x = 5.13 N, F_1y = 14.09 N, F_2x = -19.15 N and F_2y = -16.07 N. Substitution: R_x = 5.13 - (-19.15) = 24.28 N and R_y = 14.09 - (-16.07) = 30.16 N. Step: R = sqrt(589.5 + 909.6) = sqrt(1499.1) = 38.7 N at tan inverse of 30.16/24.28 = 51.2 degrees; reversing the subtraction negates both components, keeping the magnitude and adding 180 degrees to the direction. Result: F_1 - F_2 = 38.7 N at 51.2 degrees and F_2 - F_1 = 38.7 N at 231.2 degrees.

mcqs.q: A Force F_1 = 20 N making an angle of 30 degrees with positive x-axis and Force F_2 = 30 N making an angle of 150 degrees with positive x-axis, acts at a point, calculate the resultant force.
mcqs.why: Formula: R_x = F_1 cos theta_1 + F_2 cos theta_2; R_y = F_1 sin theta_1 + F_2 sin theta_2; F_R = sqrt(R_x^2 + R_y^2). Substitution: R_x = 20 cos 30 degrees + 30 cos 150 degrees = 17.32 - 25.98 = -8.66 N and R_y = 10.0 + 15.0 = 25.0 N. Step: F_R = sqrt(75 + 625) = sqrt(700) = 26.46 N; the reference angle is tan inverse of 25.0/8.66 = 70.89 degrees, and with R_x negative and R_y positive the resultant lies in the second quadrant. Result: F_R = 26.46 N at 180 - 70.89 = 109.11 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two forces of 20 N and 10 N are making an angle of 120 degrees with each other. Find a single pull that would (a) replace the given forces system (b) balance the given forces system.
options: (a) 17.32 N at 30 degrees to the 20 N force; (b) 17.32 N at 210 degrees
(a) 30 N at 30 degrees; (b) 30 N at 210 degrees
(a) 17.32 N at 60 degrees; (b) 17.32 N at 240 degrees
(a) 26.46 N at 30 degrees; (b) 26.46 N at 210 degrees
mcqs.why: Formula: F_R = sqrt(F_1^2 + F_2^2 + 2 F_1 F_2 cos theta) and tan phi = F_2 sin theta / (F_1 + F_2 cos theta), with phi measured from F_1. Substitution: F_R = sqrt(400 + 100 + 400 x cos 120 degrees) = sqrt(500 - 200) = sqrt(300) = 17.32 N. Step: tan phi = (10 x sin 120 degrees) / (20 + 10 x cos 120 degrees) = 8.66 / 15 = 0.577, so phi = 30 degrees from the 20 N force; the balancing pull, the equilibrant, is equal and opposite, at 30 + 180 = 210 degrees. Result: (a) Replacement pull 17.32 N at 30 degrees; (b) balancing pull 17.32 N at 210 degrees.

mcqs.q: Solve example 2.6 by taking fulcrum as the axis of rotation. Hina's weight is 450 N at the end of the 5 m diving board, the board's weight is 150 N at its centre 2.5 m from the bolt, and the fulcrum is 1.5 m from the bolt.
options: Bolt force 1750 N downward, fulcrum force 1150 N upward
Bolt force 1150 N downward, fulcrum force 1750 N upward
Bolt force 600 N downward, fulcrum force 1200 N upward
Bolt force 1150 N upward, fulcrum force 1750 N downward
mcqs.why: Formula: Second condition of equilibrium about the fulcrum, sum of torques = 0, then the first condition, sum of vertical forces = 0; the fulcrum force has zero torque about its own point. Substitution: Distances from the fulcrum are 1.5 m for the bolt, 1.0 m for the board's centre and 3.5 m for Hina, so F_B x 1.5 = 150 x 1.0 + 450 x 3.5 = 1725 N m. Step: F_B = 1725 / 1.5 = 1150 N, and F_F = F_B + F_C + F_H = 1150 + 150 + 450 = 1750 N. Result: Bolt force 1150 N downward and fulcrum force 1750 N upward, the same as with the bolt as the axis.

mcqs.q: A uniform plank of weight 200 N and length 6 m is supported by a rope at its far end. If the breaking tension in the rope is 400 N, how far can a boy of weight 400 N walk from the hinge towards the support?
mcqs.why: Formula: Second condition of equilibrium about the hinge, sum of torques = 0: T x 6 = 200 x 3 + 400 x x, where the plank's weight acts at its centre 3 m from the hinge and x is the boy's distance. Substitution: 400 x 6 = 600 + 400 x, that is 2400 = 600 + 400 x. Step: 400 x = 2400 - 600 = 1800, so x = 1800 / 400 = 4.5 m. Result: The boy can walk 4.5 m from the hinge before the tension reaches its breaking value of 400 N.

mcqs.q: A person throws a ball straight up with a speed of 12 m/s. If the bus is moving at 25 m/s, what is the velocity of the ball to an observer on ground?
options: 28 m/s at 26 degrees above the horizontal
mcqs.why: Formula: v_R = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2) and theta_R = tan inverse of (v_y / v_x), with v_x = 25 m/s from the bus and v_y = 12 m/s from the throw. Substitution: v_R = sqrt(625 + 144) = sqrt(769) = 27.7 m/s, about 28 m/s. Step: theta_R = tan inverse of 12/25 = tan inverse of 0.48 = 25.6 degrees, about 26 degrees above the horizontal. Result: v_R = 28 m/s at 26 degrees above the horizontal.

mcqs.q: A football leaves the foot of a punter at an angle of 54 degrees (positive x-direction) at a speed of 21 m/s. Determine the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity.
mcqs.why: Formula: v_x = v cos theta and v_y = v sin theta. Substitution: v_x = 21 x cos 54 degrees = 21 x 0.588 = 12.3 m/s, about 12 m/s, and v_y = 21 x sin 54 degrees = 21 x 0.809 = 17.0 m/s, about 17 m/s. Step: The cosine gives the component along the direction of the angle and the sine gives the perpendicular component, and together they satisfy sqrt(12^2 + 17^2) = 21 m/s. Result: Horizontal component 12 m/s and vertical component 17 m/s.

mcqs.q: A 1.84-kg school bag hangs in the middle of a clothesline, causing it to sag by an angle of 3.50 degrees. Find the tension T in the clothesline.
mcqs.why: Formula: For equilibrium of the bag, 2 T sin theta = W, so T = W / (2 sin theta), with W = m g. Substitution: W = 1.84 x 9.8 = 18.0 N, and T = 18.0 / (2 x sin 3.50 degrees) = 18.0 / (2 x 0.0611) = 18.0 / 0.122. Step: Dividing gives T = 147.7 N, because only the small vertical components of the two tensions support the weight. Result: T = 148 N.

mcqs.q: Find the magnitude and direction of vectors represented by the component pairs (a) A_x = -2.3 cm, A_y = +4.1 cm (b) A_x = +3.9 m, A_y = -1.8 m.
options: (a) 4.7 cm at 60.7 degrees; (b) 4.3 m at 24.8 degrees
(a) 4.7 cm at 119.3 degrees; (b) 4.3 m at 335.2 degrees
(a) 6.4 cm at 119.3 degrees; (b) 5.7 m at 335.2 degrees
(a) 4.7 cm at 240.7 degrees; (b) 4.3 m at 155.2 degrees
mcqs.why: Formula: A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2) and the reference angle is tan inverse of (A_y / A_x), corrected for the quadrant from the signs of the components. Substitution: (a) A = sqrt(5.29 + 16.81) = sqrt(22.10) = 4.7 cm with reference angle tan inverse of 4.1/2.3 = 60.7 degrees; (b) A = sqrt(15.21 + 3.24) = sqrt(18.45) = 4.3 m with reference angle tan inverse of 1.8/3.9 = 24.8 degrees. Step: Pair (a) lies in the second quadrant, so its angle is 180 - 60.7 = 119.3 degrees; pair (b) lies in the fourth quadrant, so its angle is 360 - 24.8 = 335.2 degrees. Result: (a) 4.7 cm at 119.3 degrees and (b) 4.3 m at 335.2 degrees.

mcqs.q: Vector F having magnitude 5.5 N makes 10 degrees with x-axis and vector r with magnitude 4.3 m makes 80 degrees with x-axis. What is the magnitude of their dot and cross products?
options: Dot product 22.2 N m and cross product magnitude 8.1 N m
Dot product 8.1 N m and cross product magnitude 22.2 N m
Dot product 23.65 N m and cross product magnitude 23.65 N m
Dot product 8.1 N m and cross product magnitude 8.1 N m
mcqs.why: Formula: Dot product magnitude = F r cos theta and cross product magnitude = F r sin theta, where theta is the angle between the vectors. Substitution: The angle between them is 80 - 10 = 70 degrees, so the dot product is 5.5 x 4.3 x cos 70 degrees = 23.65 x 0.342 = 8.09, about 8.1 N m. Step: The cross product magnitude is 5.5 x 4.3 x sin 70 degrees = 23.65 x 0.940 = 22.2 N m. Result: Dot product 8.1 N m and cross product magnitude 22.2 N m.

mcqs.q: The magnitude of dot and cross product of two vectors is 6 sqrt(3) and 6 respectively. Find the angle between the vectors.
mcqs.why: Formula: A . B = A B cos theta and the cross product magnitude is A B sin theta, so dividing gives tan theta = (A B sin theta) / (A B cos theta). Substitution: tan theta = 6 / (6 sqrt(3)) = 1 / sqrt(3) = 0.577. Step: theta = tan inverse of 0.577, which is the standard angle whose tangent is 1 over root 3. Result: The angle between the vectors is 30 degrees.

mcqs.q: A uniform rod 1 m long with weight 6 N can be supported in a horizontal position on a sharp edge with weights of 10 N and 15 N suspended from its ends. What is the position of point of balance?
options: 0.58 m from the 10 N end, about 0.42 m from the 15 N end
mcqs.why: Formula: The balance point is the centre of gravity of the loaded rod: x = (10 x 0 + 6 x 0.5 + 15 x 1) / (10 + 6 + 15), measured from the 10 N end, with the rod's own 6 N acting at its centre. Substitution: x = (0 + 3 + 15) / 31 = 18 / 31. Step: 18 divided by 31 is 0.58 m from the 10 N end, leaving 1 - 0.58 = 0.42 m from the 15 N end. Result: The point of balance is 0.58 m from the 10 N end, about 0.42 m from the 15 N end.

mcqs.q: A 4.0-m-long uniform ladder with weight of 120 N leans against a wall making 70 degrees above a cement floor. Assuming the wall is frictionless, but the floor is not, determine the forces exerted on the ladder by the floor and by the wall.
options: Force by the wall about 22 N; resultant force by the floor 122 N
Force by the wall 120 N; resultant force by the floor 22 N
Force by the wall about 44 N; resultant force by the floor 128 N
Force by the wall about 22 N; resultant force by the floor 120 N
mcqs.why: Formula: Torque about the foot = 0 gives F_W x (4 sin 70 degrees) = W x (2 cos 70 degrees), and the floor's resultant is sqrt(F_W^2 + W^2) because its vertical part balances W and its horizontal friction balances F_W. Substitution: F_W = (120 x 2 x cos 70 degrees) / (4 x sin 70 degrees) = 60 x cot 70 degrees = 60 x 0.364 = 21.8 N. Step: The floor's resultant is sqrt(14400 + 475) = sqrt(14875) = 122 N, acting at about 80 degrees to the floor. Result: Force by the wall is about 22 N and the resultant force by the floor is 122 N.

mcqs.q: The 450-kg uniform I-beam supports the load of 220 kg. The load hangs 5.6 m from the left support and 2.4 m from the right support. Determine the reactions at the supports.
options: R_A = 2850 N and R_B = about 3710 N
mcqs.why: Formula: R_A + R_B equals the total weight, and torques about A give R_B x 8.0 = 4410 x 4.0 + 2156 x 5.6, with the beam's weight 450 x 9.8 = 4410 N at its centre 4.0 m from A and the load's weight 220 x 9.8 = 2156 N at 5.6 m; the span is 5.6 + 2.4 = 8.0 m. Substitution: R_B x 8.0 = 17640 + 12074 = 29714, so R_B = 3714 N, about 3710 N. Step: R_A = 6566 - 3714 = 2852 N, about 2850 N. Result: R_A = 2850 N and R_B = about 3710 N. Note: The book's printed answer gives only R_A = 2850 N; the reaction at the other support is also required and is supplied here.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • For a ball thrown vertically upward, the acceleration remains 9.8 m/s^2 downward throughout the flight, whatever the direction or speed of the throw.
  • The time rate of change of linear momentum of a body is equal to the net force acting on it.
  • The area under a velocity-time graph is numerically equal to the displacement of the body.
  • The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration, and a slope that gradually decreases means the body is retarding.
  • Impulse is measured in newton seconds (N s), the same unit as momentum.
  • When a ball rebounds elastically from a wall, its momentum changes by twice its original momentum because the direction reverses.
  • During projectile motion the horizontal component of velocity stays constant because no horizontal force acts.
  • The range of a projectile is the same for two complementary projection angles, such as 43 degrees and 47 degrees, and is maximum at 45 degrees.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: Q1. A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 19.6 m/s. For its complete trip (up and back down to the starting position), its average speed is:

Options: (a) 19.6 m/s. (b) 9.8 m/s. (c) 6.5 m/s. (d) 4.9 m/s.

Correct answer: 9.8 m/s.

Q: Q2. If you throw a ball downward, then its acceleration immediately after leaving your hand, assuming no air resistance, is

Options: (a) 9.8 m/s^2. (b) more than 9.8 m/s^2. (c) less than 9.8 m/s^2. (d) Speed of throw is required for answer

Correct answer: 9.8 m/s^2.

Q: Q3. The time rate of change of momentum gives

Options: (a) Force (b) Impulse (c) Acceleration (d) Power

Correct answer: Force

Q: Q4. The area between the velocity-time graph is numerically equal to:

Options: (a) Velocity (b) Displacement (c) Acceleration (d) Time

Correct answer: Displacement

Q: Q5. If the slope of velocity-time graph gradually decreases, then the body is said to be moving with:

Options: (a) Positive acceleration (b) Negative acceleration (c) Uniform velocity (d) ZERO acceleration

Correct answer: Negative acceleration

Q: Q6. A 7.0-kg bowling ball experiences a net force of 5.0 N. What will be its acceleration?

Options: (a) 35 m/s^2. (b) 7.0 m/s^2 (c) 5.0 m/s^2 (d) 0.71 m/s^2

Correct answer: 0.71 m/s^2

Q: Q7. SI unit of impulse is:

Options: (a) kg ms^-2 (b) N s (c) N s^-1 (d) N m

Correct answer: N s

Q: Q8. A ball with original momentum +4.0 kg x m/s hits a wall and bounces straight back without losing any kinetic energy. The change in momentum of the ball is:

Options: (a) +4 N s (b) -4 N s (c) +8 N s^2 (d) -8 N s

Correct answer: -8 N s

Q: Q9. A body is traveling with a constant acceleration of 10 m s^-2. If S_1 is the distance traveled in 1st second and S_2 is the distance traveled in 2nd second, which of the following shows a correct relation between S_1 and S_2?

Options: (a) S_1 = S_2 (b) S_1 = 3 S_2 (c) S_2 = 3 S_1 (d) 2 S_2 = 3 S_1

Correct answer: S_2 = 3 S_1

Q: Q10. During projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity:

Options: (a) Changes with time (b) Becomes zero (c) Remains constant (d) Increases with time

Correct answer: Remains constant

Q: Q11. A projectile is thrown horizontally from a 490m high cliff with a velocity of 100 ms^-1. The time taken by projectile to reach the ground is

Options: (a) 2.5 s (b) 5.0 s (c) 7.5 s (d) 10 s

Correct answer: 10 s

Q: Q12. A projectile is launched at 45 degrees to the horizontal with an initial kinetic energy E. Assuming air resistance to be negligible what will be the kinetic energy of the projectile when it reaches its highest point?

Options: (a) 0.50 E (b) 0.71 E (c) 0.70 E (d) E

Correct answer: 0.50 E

Q: Q13. To improve the jumping record the long jumper should jump at an angle of

Options: (a) 30 degrees (b) 45 degrees (c) 60 degrees (d) 90 degrees

Correct answer: 45 degrees

Q: Q14. Range of a projectile on a horizontal plane is same for the following pair of angles:

Options: (a) 15 degrees and 18 degrees (b) 43 degrees and 47 degrees (c) 20 degrees and 80 degrees (d) 52 degrees and 62 degrees

Correct answer: 43 degrees and 47 degrees

mcqs.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 19.6 m/s. For its complete trip (up and back down to the starting position), its average speed is:
mcqs.why: The ball rises 19.6 m and falls the same distance, covering 39.2 m in 4.0 s in total, so the average speed is 39.2 / 4.0 = 9.8 m/s.

mcqs.q: If you throw a ball downward, then its acceleration immediately after leaving your hand, assuming no air resistance, is
options: Speed of throw is required for answer
mcqs.why: With no air resistance the only force on the ball after it leaves the hand is gravity, so its acceleration is 9.8 m/s^2 downward regardless of how it was thrown.

mcqs.q: The time rate of change of momentum gives
mcqs.why: Newton's second law in momentum form states that force equals the time rate of change of momentum, F = change in momentum divided by time taken.

mcqs.q: The area between the velocity-time graph is numerically equal to:
mcqs.why: The area under a velocity-time graph is velocity multiplied by time, and velocity multiplied by time is exactly the displacement of the body.

mcqs.q: If the slope of velocity-time graph gradually decreases, then the body is said to be moving with:
mcqs.why: The slope of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration; a slope that keeps decreasing passes toward negative values, which means the body is moving with negative acceleration.

mcqs.q: A 7.0-kg bowling ball experiences a net force of 5.0 N. What will be its acceleration?
mcqs.why: Using a = F / m with F = 5.0 N and m = 7.0 kg gives a = 5.0 / 7.0 = 0.71 m/s^2, far smaller than the force or mass values themselves.

mcqs.q: SI unit of impulse is:
mcqs.why: Impulse is force multiplied by time, so its SI unit is the newton multiplied by the second, written N s, which is also the unit of momentum.

mcqs.q: A ball with original momentum +4.0 kg x m/s hits a wall and bounces straight back without losing any kinetic energy. The change in momentum of the ball is:
mcqs.why: The momentum changes from +4.0 to -4.0 kg m/s on rebounding without loss of speed, so the change is -4.0 - 4.0 = -8 N s.

mcqs.q: A body is traveling with a constant acceleration of 10 m s^-2. If S_1 is the distance traveled in 1st second and S_2 is the distance traveled in 2nd second, which of the following shows a correct relation between S_1 and S_2?
mcqs.why: For motion from rest the distances in successive seconds are in the ratio 1 : 3 : 5, so the distance in the second second is three times that in the first second.

mcqs.q: During projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity:
mcqs.why: Gravity acts only vertically during projectile motion, so there is no horizontal acceleration and the horizontal component of velocity remains constant.

mcqs.q: A projectile is thrown horizontally from a 490m high cliff with a velocity of 100 ms^-1. The time taken by projectile to reach the ground is
mcqs.why: The fall time is found from t = square root of (2h / g) = square root of (2 x 490 / 9.8) = square root of 100 = 10 s.

mcqs.q: A projectile is launched at 45 degrees to the horizontal with an initial kinetic energy E. Assuming air resistance to be negligible what will be the kinetic energy of the projectile when it reaches its highest point?
mcqs.why: At the highest point only the horizontal component survives, so the kinetic energy is E cos^2 45 degrees = E x 0.5 = 0.50 E.

mcqs.q: To improve the jumping record the long jumper should jump at an angle of
mcqs.why: Range is proportional to sin 2 times the angle, which is greatest when twice the angle is 90 degrees, that is, at a launch angle of 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: Range of a projectile on a horizontal plane is same for the following pair of angles:
mcqs.why: Angles that add to 90 degrees give the same value of sin 2 times the angle, and 43 degrees plus 47 degrees equals 90 degrees, so their ranges match.

mcqs.q: In a one-dimensional elastic collision, a moving ball strikes an identical stationary ball head-on. What happens to the two balls?
options: Both balls move forward together at half the original speed
The moving ball stops and the stationary ball moves off with the original velocity
The moving ball rebounds with its original speed
Both balls stop dead after the collision
mcqs.why: For equal masses the elastic collision formulas give the bodies exchanged velocities: the first ball gives up all its velocity to the second, a special case derived in the solved comprehensive answer.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Motion is judged relative to the observer, so a slower train seen from a faster train moving the same way appears to move backward.
  • Velocity can reverse direction while acceleration stays constant, as with a ball thrown upward under the constant acceleration of gravity.
  • The ground pushes up on a standing person with a normal reaction equal to the weight, and the two forces balance so there is no rise.
  • Balls thrown upward and downward from a tower with the same speed strike the ground with the same final speed.
  • A follow-through lengthens the contact time between bat and ball, so the impulse and the change in momentum of the ball are larger.
  • Crumple zones lengthen the stopping time in a crash, which reduces the average force on the passengers for the same change in momentum.
  • A bomb released from a moving aeroplane keeps the plane's horizontal velocity, follows a parabolic path and lands beyond the point below the release.
  • The projection angle at which the kinetic energy at the summit is one-fourth of the launch kinetic energy is 60 degrees.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: Q1. If you are riding on a train that speeds past another train moving in the same direction on an adjacent track, it appears that the other train is moving backward. Why?

Ans: Motion is judged relative to the observer. Your train is moving faster, so relative to you the other train's position changes in the backward direction: its velocity relative to you is its own velocity minus your greater velocity, which is negative. The other train is still moving forward relative to the ground, but relative to your faster train it falls behind, so it appears to move backward.

Q: Q2. Can the velocity of a body reverse the direction when acceleration is constant? If you think so, give an example.

Ans: Yes. Acceleration being constant only means velocity changes at a steady rate; it can pass through zero and grow in the opposite direction. Example: a ball thrown vertically upward has the constant acceleration g = 9.8 m/s^2 downward throughout. Its upward velocity decreases to zero at the top and then it moves downward with increasing speed, so the velocity reverses direction while the acceleration never changes.

Q: Q3. When you stand still on the ground, how large a force does the ground exert on you? Why doesn't this force make you rise up into the air?

Ans: The ground exerts an upward normal reaction exactly equal to your weight, F = m g. It does not make you rise because it is balanced by your weight acting downward, so the net force on you is zero and there is no acceleration. You would rise only if the upward force became greater than your weight.

Q: Q4. A man standing on the top of a tower throws a ball vertically up with certain velocity. He also throws another ball vertically down with the same speed. Neglecting air resistance, which ball will hit the ground with higher speed?

Ans: Both balls hit the ground with the same speed. The ball thrown upward rises, stops, and falls back past the top of the tower with exactly the throwing speed, now directed downward. From that point onward it is in exactly the same state as the ball thrown downward, and both gain the same extra speed while falling the height of the tower, as v^2 = u^2 + 2 g h shows.

Q: Q5. The cricket coach explains that the follow-through with the shot will make the ball travel a greater distance. Explain the reasoning in terms of the impulse-momentum theorem.

Ans: The impulse-momentum theorem says impulse J = F x Delta t = change in momentum = m v_f - m v_i. In a follow-through the bat stays in contact with the ball for a longer time Delta t, so for the same average force the impulse is larger. A larger impulse gives the ball a larger change in momentum and hence a larger launch speed, and a faster ball travels a greater distance.

Q: Q6. When you release an inflated but untied balloon, why does it fly across the room?

Ans: This is Newton's third law and conservation of momentum. The stretched balloon forces the air out of the neck in one direction; the air in turn exerts an equal and opposite reaction force on the balloon, pushing it the other way. As air rushes out backward, the balloon gains momentum forward so that the total momentum of balloon plus air stays constant, and it flies across the room until the air runs out.

Q: Q7. Modern cars are not rigid but are designed to have 'crumple zones' (irregular fold) that collapse upon impact. What is the advantage of this new design?

Ans: A crumple zone collapses gradually, so the car and its passengers are brought to rest over a longer time and a longer distance. The change in momentum is the same, but since F_avg = Delta p / Delta t, the longer stopping time greatly reduces the average force on the passengers. The collapsing metal also absorbs much of the kinetic energy, so less of it reaches the passenger compartment, reducing injury.

Q: Q8. Why we can hit a long sixer in a cricket match rather than if we toss a ball for our selves?

Ans: A bowled ball arrives at the bat already carrying a large speed, momentum and kinetic energy supplied by the bowler. At impact the relative speed between bat and ball is large, the ball rebounds with a large speed, and part of the incoming energy is returned to the ball, so it can travel far. A ball we toss up for ourselves is almost at rest when the bat meets it, so all of its outgoing speed must come from the bat alone and it cannot be sent as far.

Q: Q9. An aeroplane while travelling horizontally, dropped a bomb when it was exactly above the target, the bomb missed the target. Explain.

Ans: When released, the bomb keeps the horizontal velocity of the aeroplane (inertia). While gravity pulls it down, it continues moving forward with that horizontal velocity, following a parabolic path. So by the time it reaches the ground it has travelled a considerable horizontal distance beyond the point of release and lands past the target. To hit the target, the bomb must be released before the plane reaches the point above the target.

Q: Q10. Calculate the angle of projection for which kinetic energy at the summit is equal to one-fourth of its kinetic energy at point of projection.

Ans: At the summit only the horizontal component of velocity survives, v = v_o cos theta, so K.E. at summit = (1/2) m v_o^2 cos^2 theta = K.E. at projection x cos^2 theta.
Given: K.E. at summit = (1/4) x K.E. at projection
Formula: cos^2 theta = 1/4
Working: cos theta = 1/2, so theta = 60 degrees
Answer: The angle of projection is 60 degrees.

Q: Q11. For any specific velocity of projection, the maximum range is equal to four times of the corresponding height. Discuss.

Ans: The statement is true for the angle that gives maximum range, theta = 45 degrees. Maximum range R_max = v_o^2 / g (putting sin 2 theta = sin 90 degrees = 1 in R = v_o^2 sin 2 theta / g). The height attained at 45 degrees is H = v_o^2 sin^2 45 degrees / (2 g) = v_o^2 x (1/2) / (2 g) = v_o^2 / (4 g) = R_max / 4. Hence R_max = 4 H: the maximum range is four times the height reached in that same 45 degrees projection. It is not true for other angles, where R and H follow their own formulas.

Q: Q12. What is the angle for which the maximum height reached and corresponding range are equal?

Ans: Given: H = R for the same projection speed v_o
Formula: H = (v_o^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g) and R = (v_o^2 sin 2 theta) / g = (2 v_o^2 sin theta cos theta) / g
Setting H = R: (v_o^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g) = (2 v_o^2 sin theta cos theta) / g
Cancelling v_o^2 sin theta / g from both sides: (sin theta) / 2 = 2 cos theta, so tan theta = 4
Working: theta = tan^-1 (4) = 75.96 degrees
Answer: The angle is about 76 degrees.

mcqs.q: You are on a fast train that overtakes a slower train moving in the same direction on the next track. Why does the slower train appear to move backward?
options: Because the slower train is actually reversing
Because its velocity relative to you is its velocity minus your greater velocity, which is negative
Because of the wind between the two trains
Because your eyes cannot follow fast objects
mcqs.why: Motion is judged relative to the observer: relative to the faster train, the slower train's position changes backward because its velocity minus the observer's greater velocity is negative, even though it still moves forward relative to the ground.

mcqs.q: Can the velocity of a body reverse its direction while its acceleration remains constant?
options: Yes, a ball thrown upward slows, stops and falls back while gravity's acceleration stays constant and downward
No, constant acceleration keeps velocity in one direction
Only if the acceleration also reverses
Only when the body is moving in a circle
mcqs.why: A constant acceleration changes velocity at a steady rate, so the velocity can shrink to zero and then grow in the opposite direction; the thrown ball does exactly this under the unchanging downward acceleration of gravity.

mcqs.q: When you stand still on the ground, why does the upward force from the ground not lift you into the air?
options: Because the ground exerts no force on you
Because the upward normal reaction exactly equals your weight, so the net force is zero
Because your weight is greater than the reaction
mcqs.why: The ground exerts an upward normal reaction equal to mg, and since it is exactly balanced by the downward weight, the net force is zero and there is no acceleration; you would rise only if the upward force exceeded your weight.

mcqs.q: From the top of a tower one ball is thrown vertically up and another vertically down, both with the same speed. Neglecting air resistance, which hits the ground faster?
options: Both hit the ground with the same speed
The upward ball, because it falls from a greater height above the tower
mcqs.why: The upward ball returns past the top of the tower with exactly the throwing speed, now directed downward, so from there both balls are in the identical state and gain the same extra speed over the tower's height.

mcqs.q: Why does a follow-through make a cricket ball travel farther, in terms of the impulse-momentum theorem?
options: It increases the mass of the ball
It keeps the bat in contact with the ball longer, so the impulse and the change in momentum are larger for the same average force
It reduces the effect of gravity on the ball
It makes the ball spin faster
mcqs.why: Impulse equals force multiplied by contact time and equals the change in momentum; a follow-through lengthens the contact time, so the impulse is larger, the ball leaves with a larger speed and travels a greater distance.

mcqs.q: Why does an inflated balloon fly across the room when it is released untied?
options: The escaping air pulls the balloon along with it
The balloon is lighter than air and floats away
The air is forced out one way and exerts an equal and opposite reaction force that pushes the balloon the other way
Static electricity pushes it away from the hand
mcqs.why: By Newton's third law and conservation of momentum, the balloon pushes the air out backward and the air pushes the balloon forward with an equal and opposite force, so the balloon gains forward momentum as the air gains backward momentum.

mcqs.q: What is the advantage of crumple zones in modern cars?
options: They make the car body more rigid in a crash
They collapse gradually, lengthening the stopping time so the average force on the passengers is much smaller
They increase the change in momentum of the passengers
They stop the car in a shorter distance
mcqs.why: The change in momentum in a crash is fixed, and average force equals change in momentum divided by stopping time; by collapsing gradually the crumple zone increases the stopping time and distance, greatly reducing the average force and absorbing kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: An aeroplane flying horizontally drops a bomb exactly above its target, yet the bomb misses. Why?
options: The bomb falls straight down but the target moves
The bomb keeps the aeroplane's horizontal velocity and travels forward while falling, landing beyond the target
Air resistance pushes the bomb backward behind the target
Gravity acts sideways on a falling bomb
mcqs.why: On release the bomb keeps the horizontal velocity of the aeroplane by inertia and follows a parabolic path, so while gravity pulls it down it also travels a considerable horizontal distance and lands past the target; it must be released before the plane is above the target.

mcqs.q: For what angle of projection is the kinetic energy at the summit equal to one-fourth of the kinetic energy at projection?
mcqs.why: At the summit only the horizontal component v cos of the launch angle survives, so the summit kinetic energy is the launch kinetic energy multiplied by cos squared of the angle; setting cos squared equal to one-fourth gives cos equal to one-half, an angle of 60 degrees.

mcqs.q: For a given projection speed, at what angle are the maximum height reached and the corresponding range equal?
mcqs.why: Setting the height formula equal to the range formula and cancelling common factors leaves tan of the angle equal to 4, whose inverse tangent is about 75.96 degrees, so the height and range are equal near 76 degrees.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The slope of a displacement-time graph gives the velocity of the body.
  • The slope of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration, and the area under it gives the displacement.
  • Linear momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = m v, a vector measured in kg m/s.
  • Newton's second law in momentum form states that the net force equals the rate of change of linear momentum.
  • For an isolated system with no external net force, the total linear momentum remains constant.
  • In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.
  • For a projectile the maximum height is (v_o^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g) and the time of flight is (2 v_o sin theta) / g.
  • The range of a projectile is (v_o^2 sin 2 theta) / g, maximum at 45 degrees, and the same for complementary angles theta and 90 degrees minus theta.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Q1. Explain displacement - time graph and velocity - time graph. In each type give brief details along with appropriate diagram for illustration.

Ans: Diagram (in words): A displacement-time graph has displacement on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. A straight line sloping up shows uniform velocity, a horizontal line shows the body at rest, and a curve of increasing steepness shows acceleration. A velocity-time graph has velocity on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. A horizontal line shows uniform velocity, a straight line sloping up shows uniform acceleration, a line sloping down shows retardation, and a curve shows variable acceleration.
In a displacement-time graph the slope at any point, Delta s / Delta t, gives the velocity of the body: a positive slope means motion in the positive direction, a negative slope means motion in the reverse direction, and zero slope means rest.
In a velocity-time graph the slope, Delta v / Delta t, gives the acceleration, and the area under the graph gives the displacement, since area = velocity x time. These two graphs together describe completely how the position and velocity of a body change with time.

Q: Q2. Apply Newton's Laws to explain the motion of objects in a variety of context.

Ans: Newton's first law (inertia) explains why a passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly: the body tends to continue in its state of motion. It also explains why a tablecloth can be pulled out from under dishes without moving them.
Newton's second law, F = m a, explains everyday motion quantitatively: the same push accelerates a light bicycle much more than a loaded truck; a car engine must exert a larger force to accelerate a loaded car; and the recoil of a gun is small because the gun is heavy. In a lift, the apparent weight changes because the normal reaction must provide m g plus or minus m a.
Newton's third law explains walking (we push the ground backward and the ground pushes us forward), swimming, rowing, the flight of a rocket and jet (gases pushed backward, craft pushed forward), and why a balloon flies when its air escapes. In every context the three laws together decide whether an object stays at rest, moves uniformly, accelerates, or interacts with another body.

Q: Q3. What is linear momentum? Derive and state Newton's second law in terms of linear momentum.

Ans: Linear momentum of a body is the product of its mass and velocity, p = m v. It is a vector in the direction of the velocity, with SI unit kg m/s.
Derivation: Let a force F act for time Delta t on a body of mass m, changing its velocity from v_i to v_f. Then a = (v_f - v_i) / Delta t. From F = m a, F = m (v_f - v_i) / Delta t = (m v_f - m v_i) / Delta t = (p_f - p_i) / Delta t = Delta p / Delta t.
Statement: The time rate of change of linear momentum of a body is equal to the net force applied on it, and the change in momentum takes place in the direction of the force. This form, F = Delta p / Delta t, is Newton's second law in terms of momentum and it also leads to the impulse-momentum theorem, F x Delta t = Delta p.

Q: Q4. State and explain law of conservation of linear momentum for an isolated system of bodies.

Ans: Statement: For an isolated system (a system on which no external net force acts), the total linear momentum remains constant; it can neither be created nor destroyed, only transferred between the bodies of the system.
Explanation: Consider two bodies of masses m_1 and m_2 moving with velocities u_1 and u_2 that collide for a time Delta t. By Newton's third law the force on the first body is equal and opposite to the force on the second, F_1 = -F_2. Using F = Delta p / Delta t for each body, Delta p_1 / Delta t = -Delta p_2 / Delta t, so Delta p_1 + Delta p_2 = 0, that is, m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2 = m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2. The total momentum after the collision equals the total momentum before it. The same holds for explosions, recoil of a gun, and rocket propulsion, provided external forces such as friction are absent or negligible during the short interaction.

Q: Q5. Define elastic and inelastic collisions. Give examples in each case. Derive mathematical equations for calculating the final velocities of the elastically colliding bodies in one dimension.

Ans: An elastic collision is one in which both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved, e.g. collisions between atomic particles and between hard ivory or steel balls. An inelastic collision is one in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; the lost kinetic energy changes into heat, sound and deformation, e.g. a bullet embedding itself in a wooden block. If the bodies stick together it is a perfectly inelastic collision.
Derivation for one-dimensional elastic collision: Let masses m_1, m_2 have initial velocities u_1, u_2 and final velocities v_1, v_2.
Conservation of momentum: m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2, so m_1 (u_1 - v_1) = m_2 (v_2 - u_2) ... (i)
Conservation of kinetic energy: (1/2) m_1 u_1^2 + (1/2) m_2 u_2^2 = (1/2) m_1 v_1^2 + (1/2) m_2 v_2^2, so m_1 (u_1^2 - v_1^2) = m_2 (v_2^2 - u_2^2) ... (ii)
Dividing (ii) by (i): u_1 + v_1 = v_2 + u_2, that is, the relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation, u_1 - u_2 = v_2 - v_1.
Solving this together with the momentum equation gives the final velocities:
v_1 = ((m_1 - m_2) / (m_1 + m_2)) u_1 + ((2 m_2) / (m_1 + m_2)) u_2
v_2 = ((2 m_1) / (m_1 + m_2)) u_1 + ((m_2 - m_1) / (m_1 + m_2)) u_2
Special cases: if m_1 = m_2 the bodies exchange velocities; if a light body strikes a heavy stationary body it rebounds with almost its own speed while the heavy body barely moves.

Q: Q6. What is projectile motion? Give examples. Find out the expression of instantaneous velocity for a projectile.

Ans: Projectile motion is the two-dimensional motion of a body thrown into the air with some initial velocity at an angle, moving under gravity alone (air resistance neglected). Examples: a cricket ball hit for a six, a football kicked at an angle, water leaving a hose pipe, and a bomb released from a moving aeroplane.
The motion is treated as a horizontal motion with constant velocity and a vertical motion with constant acceleration g, independent of each other. Let the body be projected with velocity v_o at angle theta. Then v_ox = v_o cos theta and v_oy = v_o sin theta.
At time t: the horizontal component stays v_x = v_o cos theta, and the vertical component becomes v_y = v_o sin theta - g t.
The instantaneous velocity is the vector sum of these components. Its magnitude is v = sqrt(v_x^2 + v_y^2) = sqrt((v_o cos theta)^2 + (v_o sin theta - g t)^2), and its direction phi with the horizontal is given by tan phi = v_y / v_x.
At the highest point v_y = 0, so the instantaneous velocity there is purely horizontal and equal to v_o cos theta, its minimum value during the flight.

Q: Q7. What is maximum height and time of flight for projectile? Derive mathematical equations for Maximum height attained and time of flight.

Ans: Maximum height H is the greatest vertical distance reached by the projectile above the point of projection. Time of flight T is the total time the projectile stays in the air before returning to the level of projection.
Derivation of maximum height: Consider the vertical motion. Initial vertical velocity = v_o sin theta, final vertical velocity at the top = 0, acceleration = -g. Using v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2 a S: 0 = (v_o sin theta)^2 - 2 g H, so H = (v_o^2 sin^2 theta) / (2 g).
Derivation of time of flight: Using v_f = v_i + a t for the upward journey, 0 = v_o sin theta - g t_up, so t_up = (v_o sin theta) / g. The downward journey takes the same time, so the total time of flight is T = 2 t_up = (2 v_o sin theta) / g.
Both H and T depend only on v_o and theta; H is greatest for vertical projection (theta = 90 degrees).

Q: Q8. What is range of a projectile. State in which condition the range will be maximum if speed of projection is kept constant in a uniform gravitational field. Also show that there are two projection angles for the same range.

Ans: The range R is the horizontal distance travelled by the projectile during its time of flight before it returns to the level of projection.
Derivation: Horizontal velocity = v_o cos theta (constant) and time of flight T = (2 v_o sin theta) / g. So R = v_o cos theta x T = (2 v_o^2 sin theta cos theta) / g = (v_o^2 sin 2 theta) / g.
Maximum range: For fixed v_o, R is maximum when sin 2 theta is maximum, i.e. sin 2 theta = 1, so 2 theta = 90 degrees and theta = 45 degrees. The maximum range is R_max = v_o^2 / g.
Two angles for the same range: sin 2 theta has the same value for 2 theta and 180 degrees - 2 theta, that is, for projection angles theta and 90 degrees - theta. For example, 30 degrees and 60 degrees give the same range because sin 60 degrees = sin 120 degrees. Hence, except for the maximum at 45 degrees, every range can be obtained with two complementary projection angles, one low and flat and one high and lobbed.

mcqs.q: What does the slope of a displacement-time graph give?
options: The distance travelled in one second only at the origin
The force acting on the body
mcqs.why: The slope of a displacement-time graph is change in displacement divided by change in time, which is the definition of velocity; a positive slope means motion in the positive direction and zero slope means the body is at rest.

mcqs.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
mcqs.why: The area under a velocity-time graph is velocity multiplied by time, and that product is the displacement of the body, while the slope of the same graph separately gives the acceleration.

mcqs.q: A passenger lurches forward when a bus brakes suddenly. Which law explains this?
options: Newton's first law, the law of inertia
Newton's second law, F = m a
Newton's third law of action and reaction
The law of conservation of energy
mcqs.why: The passenger's body tends to continue in its state of motion when the bus slows, which is inertia, the content of Newton's first law; the same law explains a tablecloth being pulled out from under dishes without moving them.

mcqs.q: Newton's second law stated in terms of linear momentum says that the net force on a body equals:
options: The rate of change of its linear momentum
Its mass multiplied by its momentum
The change in its velocity alone
mcqs.why: Starting from F = m a and writing acceleration as the change in velocity over time gives F = (m v_f - m v_i) / time = change in momentum over time, so force is the time rate of change of linear momentum.

mcqs.q: The law of conservation of linear momentum holds for an isolated system, which means a system where:
options: No forces act between the bodies inside it
No external net force acts on it
The total kinetic energy is also constant
mcqs.why: During a collision the internal forces are equal and opposite by Newton's third law, so the momentum changes of the bodies cancel; provided no external net force acts, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

mcqs.q: How does an elastic collision differ from an inelastic collision?
options: Momentum is conserved only in an elastic collision
Kinetic energy is conserved in an elastic collision but not in an inelastic one, while momentum is conserved in both
Kinetic energy is conserved only in an inelastic collision
Neither quantity is conserved in either type
mcqs.why: In an elastic collision, such as between hard steel balls, both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved; in an inelastic collision momentum is still conserved but part of the kinetic energy changes into heat, sound and deformation.

mcqs.q: Two equal masses collide elastically in one dimension. What special result follows?
options: Both move off at the average of the two speeds in the same direction
The faster body rebounds with its own speed
mcqs.why: Putting equal masses into the elastic collision velocity formulas makes each body's final velocity equal to the other body's initial velocity, so the two bodies simply exchange velocities.

mcqs.q: At the highest point of its flight, the instantaneous velocity of a projectile projected at angle theta with speed v_o is:
options: Equal to the full launch speed v_o
mcqs.why: At the highest point the vertical component of velocity has fallen to zero while the horizontal component never changes, so the instantaneous velocity there is purely horizontal and equal to v_o cos theta, its minimum value during the flight.

mcqs.q: The maximum height attained by a projectile projected with speed v_o at angle theta is:
mcqs.why: Applying v_f squared = v_i squared + 2 a S to the vertical motion, with final vertical velocity zero and acceleration -g, gives 0 = (v_o sin theta) squared - 2 g H, so H = (v_o squared sin squared theta) / (2 g).

mcqs.q: For a fixed projection speed, the range of a projectile is maximum when the projection angle is:
mcqs.why: The range is (v_o squared sin 2 theta) / g, and sin 2 theta reaches its maximum value of 1 when twice the angle is 90 degrees, that is at 45 degrees, giving the maximum range v_o squared / g.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The slope of each segment of a velocity-time graph gives the acceleration on that segment, and the average acceleration uses only the overall change in velocity and total time.
  • For a fast particle crossing a thin sheet, v_f^2 = v_i^2 + 2 a S gives a retardation of 2.4 x 10^17 m/s^2 for the proton in the solved assignment.
  • By Newton's third law an astronaut's 36 N push gives the massive spacecraft only 0.0033 m/s^2 but gives the astronaut -0.39 m/s^2.
  • A girl falling 12.0 m into a net reaches 15.34 m/s, and the net stops her with an average force of about 2.11 x 10^3 N.
  • In an elastic collision with a stationary car, the car's final speed is (2 m_1 / (m_1 + m_2)) times the pickup's initial speed.
  • A cricket ball launched at 28 m/s has range 80 sin 2 theta metres, so only the 45-degree hit clears a 72 m boundary.
  • The distance travelled in the nth second of free fall from rest is (g/2)(2n - 1), giving 15 m in the 2nd second and 25 m in the 3rd second with g = 10 m/s^2.
  • Increasing the stopping time with an air bag cuts the average force on a crashing passenger from 7.0 x 10^5 N to 3.1 x 10^4 N.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 3.1

Q: Q1. The velocity time graph shows the motion of car in a straight line. By reading the scale carefully, calculate (a) the acceleration of the car between segment A and B, B and C, C and D and D and E, from the slope of the graph. Also (b) Calculate the car's average acceleration for the complete journey.

Ans: Diagram (in words): The graph has velocity v (m/s) on the vertical axis, marked 0, 25, 50, 75, and time t (s) on the horizontal axis, marked 0, 5, 10, 15.
