Ans: The weight a body feels is its apparent weight, the normal reaction or tension supporting it, which for a lift moving with downward acceleration a is W_apparent = m (g - a). If the elevator falls freely, its acceleration equals g, so a = g. Then W_apparent = m (g - g) = 0. The floor of the lift falls away under the body as fast as the body itself falls, so the floor pushes up on the body with no force at all. With no supporting force acting, the body feels completely weightless.

Q: Q11. When a tractor moves with uniform velocity, its heavier wheel rotates slowly than its lighter wheel, why? Explain.

Ans: All the wheels of the tractor move forward with the same linear velocity v, because they belong to the same vehicle. For rolling without slipping, v = r omega, so omega = v / r. The heavier rear wheels of a tractor are much bigger in radius than the smaller front wheels. With the same v but a larger r, the angular velocity omega = v / r of the big wheel is smaller. Hence the heavier, larger wheel rotates more slowly than the lighter, smaller wheel.

mcqs.q: Why is the rim of an engine flywheel made heavy?
options: To increase its friction with the axle
To give it a large moment of inertia so the engine runs smoothly
To reduce its moment of inertia
To make it spin faster during the power stroke
mcqs.why: Mass concentrated in the rim lies far from the axis, giving a large moment of inertia that resists sudden changes in angular velocity and smooths the engine motion.

mcqs.q: How does rifling inside a rifle barrel improve accuracy?
options: It increases the bullet's linear speed only
It cools the barrel during firing
It spins the bullet so angular momentum keeps it pointing nose-first
It reduces the mass of the bullet
mcqs.why: The spiral grooves spin the bullet about its long axis; conservation of angular momentum keeps it nose-first and resists tumbling, so it flies straighter to the target.

mcqs.q: How can spinning distinguish a raw egg from a hard-boiled egg?
options: The raw egg spins smoothly for longer
The boiled egg wobbles and stops quickly
The raw egg wobbles and stops quickly because its liquid interior lags and shifts
mcqs.why: A boiled egg is solid and spins steadily like a rigid body, while the liquid inside a raw egg lags behind and shifts about, making it wobble and stop quickly.

mcqs.q: Why is centripetal acceleration directed towards the centre of the circle?
options: Because the speed increases towards the centre
Because the change in velocity between two close positions points towards the centre
Because gravity always points to the centre
Because the radius decreases during motion
mcqs.why: Velocity is tangent and its direction changes continuously; the change in velocity for two close positions points inward, so acceleration, the rate of change of velocity, is centripetal.

mcqs.q: Why does a swinging ball break a string that could just support its weight at rest?
options: The string becomes weaker when moving
The ball becomes heavier while swinging
At the lowest point tension must supply weight plus centripetal force, exceeding the breaking strength
Air resistance adds to the tension
mcqs.why: At rest tension equals weight alone, but at the lowest point of the swing tension equals m g plus m v squared over r, which exceeds what the string can bear.

mcqs.q: What happens to an insect near the axis of a wheel when friction is very small?
options: It is immediately thrown off the wheel
It rotates exactly with the wheel
It gains the full angular velocity at once
It nearly stays in place and appears to rotate backwards relative to the wheel
mcqs.why: Very small friction transfers almost no torque or centripetal force, so the wheel turns underneath the insect, which lags far behind and appears to rotate backwards.

mcqs.q: How many geo-stationary satellites are needed at minimum for global TV coverage?
mcqs.why: One geo-stationary satellite covers about 120 degrees of longitude, so covering the full 360 degrees needs 360 divided by 120, that is three satellites.

mcqs.q: Why does a coasting rotating system slow down as water drops into its beaker?
options: The added water increases moment of inertia while angular momentum stays constant, so angular velocity decreases
The water increases the external torque on the system
The water decreases the moment of inertia
Angular momentum increases while inertia stays fixed
mcqs.why: No external torque acts, so L equals I omega stays constant; collected water raises I, therefore omega must fall and the system slows down.

mcqs.q: When does a body in a lift become completely weightless?
options: When the lift moves up at constant speed
When the lift falls freely with acceleration equal to g, making apparent weight m(g minus g) equal to zero
When the lift is at rest
mcqs.why: Apparent weight is m times g minus a; in free fall a equals g, so the apparent weight becomes zero and the floor exerts no supporting force.

mcqs.q: Why does the larger rear wheel of a tractor rotate more slowly than the smaller front wheel?
options: The rear wheel has a smaller linear velocity
Both wheels share the same linear velocity, and omega equals v over r is smaller for the larger radius
The front wheel slips on the road
The rear wheel carries no load
mcqs.why: All wheels move forward with the same linear velocity v, and for rolling without slipping omega equals v divided by r, so the bigger wheel has the smaller angular velocity.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Centripetal acceleration has magnitude v^2 / r, directed towards the centre, and also equals r omega^2.
  • Centripetal force is F = m v^2 / r = m omega^2 r, directed towards the centre of the circle.
  • Angular momentum magnitude is |L| = |r x p| = m v r = m r^2 omega for circular motion.
  • Moment of inertia plays in rotation the same role that mass plays in linear motion, with tau = I alpha.
  • Orbital velocity is v = sqrt(G M / r), so a satellite nearer the Earth must move faster.
  • Real weight is m g, while apparent weight is the support force and changes when the body accelerates.
  • Artificial gravity in a rotating station comes from the rim's centripetal acceleration, set equal to g by choosing the rotation frequency.
  • If no external torque acts, total angular momentum L = I omega remains constant.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Q1. What are centripetal acceleration and centripetal force? Derive their equations.

Ans: Centripetal acceleration is the acceleration of a body moving in a circle, directed towards the centre of the circle, which arises because the direction of velocity changes continuously. Centripetal force is the resultant force towards the centre that produces this acceleration and keeps the body on the circular path.
Derivation: Consider a body of mass m moving with uniform speed v in a circle of radius r about centre C.
At point A its velocity is v1 and at a nearby point B its velocity is v2, with angle A C B = Delta theta.
Draw the velocity triangle PQR with PQ = v1 and PR = v2; then QR = Delta v, the change in velocity.
Triangles ACB and PQR are similar isosceles triangles, so arc AB / AC = QR / PQ.
For a small time Delta t, arc AB = v Delta t, so v Delta t / r = Delta v / v.
Rearranging: Delta v / Delta t = v^2 / r.
Taking the limit Delta t tends to zero gives the centripetal acceleration: a_c = v^2 / r, directed towards the centre.
Using v = r omega, also a_c = r omega^2, and in vector form a_c = -omega^2 r.
By Newton's second law, F_c = m a_c, so the centripetal force is F_c = m v^2 / r = m r omega^2, directed towards the centre.

Q: Q2. Show that angular momentum in magnitude is given by: |L| = |r x p| = m r^2 omega = m v r

Ans: Angular momentum of a particle is defined as the cross product of its position vector and its linear momentum: L = r x p.
Its magnitude is |L| = r p sin theta, where theta is the angle between r and p.
For a particle moving in a circle, the momentum p is tangent to the circle while r is along the radius, so theta = 90 degrees and sin theta = 1.
Therefore |L| = r p.
Putting p = m v: |L| = m v r.
For circular motion v = r omega, so |L| = m (r omega) r = m r^2 omega.
Hence |L| = |r x p| = m r^2 omega = m v r, and the direction of L is perpendicular to the plane of r and p, given by the right-hand rule.

Q: Q3. Show that role playing by mass in linear motion is playing by moment of inertia in rotatory motion.

Ans: Mass measures inertia in linear motion: it tells how strongly a body resists a change in its linear velocity under a force, F = m a. Moment of inertia plays exactly the same role in rotatory motion: it tells how strongly a body resists a change in its angular velocity under a torque, tau = I alpha.
The parallel can be seen quantity by quantity.
Linear momentum p = m v corresponds to angular momentum L = I omega.
Linear kinetic energy (1/2) m v^2 corresponds to rotational kinetic energy (1/2) I omega^2.
Inertia = m in linear motion corresponds to moment of inertia I = sum of m_i r_i^2 in rotatory motion.
Just as a heavier body needs a larger force for the same linear acceleration, a body with larger moment of inertia needs a larger torque for the same angular acceleration.
The only difference is that moment of inertia depends on the distribution of mass about the axis as well as on the mass itself. Hence moment of inertia is the mass of rotatory motion.

Q: Q4. What do you mean by "INTELSAT". At what frequencies it operates. For how many T.V station this system is used?

Ans: INTELSAT stands for International Telecommunication Satellite (system/organization). It is a system of geo-stationary communication satellites placed in orbit above the equator, through which telephone calls, data and television programmes are relayed between countries around the world. Because the satellites are geo-stationary, ground stations can point fixed dish antennas at them all the time.
The system operates in the microwave region of radio frequencies, working at about 6 GHz for the up-link (Earth to satellite) and about 4 GHz for the down-link (satellite to Earth).
This system is used by T.V. stations all over the world for international transmission of television programmes, so that events in one country can be watched live in many other countries.

Q: Q5. Show that in angular form, centripetal acceleration is: a_c = -omega^2 r

Ans: For a body moving in a circle of radius r with speed v, the centripetal acceleration has magnitude a_c = v^2 / r and is directed towards the centre.
The radius vector r points outward from the centre to the body, so the inward direction is the direction of -r.
Writing the acceleration in vector form: a_c = -(v^2 / r^2) r, where the minus sign shows it is opposite to r.
For circular motion the linear and angular speeds are related by v = r omega, so v^2 / r^2 = omega^2.
Substituting: a_c = -omega^2 r.
This is the angular form of centripetal acceleration; its magnitude is r omega^2 and it always points towards the centre of the circle.

Q: Q6. Show that centripetal force is also shown by F_c = (-m v / r) r-hat = -m omega^2 r = (-m v^2 / r^2) r

Ans: Centripetal force is the mass times the centripetal acceleration: F_c = m a_c.
The centripetal acceleration has magnitude v^2 / r and is directed towards the centre, opposite to the outward unit vector r-hat, so a_c = -(v^2 / r) r-hat.
Therefore F_c = -(m v^2 / r) r-hat, which can also be written as F_c = (-m v / r) (v r-hat) in the book's grouped form, i.e. magnitude m v^2 / r acting along -r-hat.
Since the position vector is r = r r-hat, we can write r-hat = r / r, giving F_c = -(m v^2 / r^2) r.
Using v = r omega, v^2 / r^2 = omega^2, so F_c = -m omega^2 r.
Hence F_c = (-m v / r) r-hat = -m omega^2 r = (-m v^2 / r^2) r, all showing a force of magnitude m v^2 / r directed towards the centre.

Q: Q7. Show that a satellite near the earth will have greater velocity.

Ans: For a satellite of mass m in a circular orbit of radius r about the Earth (mass M_e), gravity provides the centripetal force.
G M_e m / r^2 = m v^2 / r.
Cancelling m and one factor of r: v^2 = G M_e / r.
So the orbital velocity is v = sqrt(G M_e / r).
Since G and M_e are constant, v is proportional to 1 / sqrt(r).
Therefore the smaller the orbital radius r, that is, the nearer the satellite is to the Earth, the greater its orbital velocity must be; a satellite in a low orbit moves faster than one in a high orbit.

Q: Q8. What do you mean by weight of a body? Use examples to distinguish between real weight and the apparent weight of a body.

Ans: The weight of a body is the force with which the Earth attracts it, W = m g, acting towards the centre of the Earth. This is its real weight, and it does not change as long as g is constant.
Apparent weight is the weight a body appears to have, measured by a spring balance or felt as the support force (tension or normal reaction) acting on it. It changes when the body is accelerated.
Example 1: A fish of weight 41.0 N hangs from a spring balance in a lift at rest. The balance reads 41.0 N, so apparent weight = real weight.
Example 2: The lift accelerates upward. The balance reads more than 41.0 N (for example 49.78 N for an acceleration of 2.10 m/s^2 in the book's case), because apparent weight = m (g + a), which is greater than the real weight.
Example 3: The lift accelerates downward. The balance reads less (32.22 N in the book's case), because apparent weight = m (g - a).
Example 4: If the lift falls freely, a = g and the balance reads zero; the body is apparently weightless although its real weight m g still acts on it.

Q: Q9. Explain, how gravity is provided to the occupants of the space ship.

Ans: In an orbiting space ship the occupants are in free fall and feel weightless, which is uncomfortable for long journeys. Gravity is provided artificially by rotating the space ship (or a wheel-shaped space station) about its axis at a chosen frequency.
The occupants stand on the inner surface of the outer rim. As the station rotates, the rim pushes on them with a normal reaction directed towards the centre, providing the centripetal force for their circular motion. They feel this push through their feet exactly as they feel the ground's push under gravity on Earth, so it acts as artificial gravity.
The centripetal acceleration is a_c = r omega^2 = r (2 pi f)^2, where r is the radius of the station and f its frequency of rotation.
Setting a_c = g gives f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(g / r).
Rotating the station at this frequency gives the occupants an artificial gravity equal to Earth's gravity.

Q: Q10. Give different three examples to illustrate the phenomenon of conservation of angular momentum.

Ans: The law states that if no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum L = I omega remains constant.
Example 1: A diver or gymnast leaves the board with arms and legs stretched out, rotating slowly. In the air no external torque acts about the centre of mass. On tucking the body in, the moment of inertia I decreases, so omega increases to keep I omega constant, and the diver completes extra somersaults.
Example 2: An ice skater spinning with arms stretched out pulls her arms in towards her body. Her moment of inertia decreases and, to conserve angular momentum, her spin speed increases greatly.
Example 3: A man standing on a rotating turntable holds heavy weights with arms stretched horizontally and is set rotating slowly. When he draws the weights in to his chest, I decreases and his angular velocity increases considerably; stretching his arms out again slows him down. In each case I omega stays constant.

Q: Q11. Explain why mud guards are used on the wheels of cycles, motor cars and other driving vehicles?

Ans: As a wheel rolls on a wet or muddy road, mud and water stick to the tyre and are carried around with it. A particle on the rim moves in a circle, and if it leaves the tyre it flies off along the tangent to the wheel at that point, because once the grip (centripetal force) is removed it continues in a straight line. Mud leaving the top and back of the wheel is therefore thrown backwards and upwards towards the rider and following vehicles. Mud guards are curved covers fitted close over the wheels. The flying mud strikes the guard instead of the rider, slides down it and drops near the wheel. In this way mud guards protect the rider, passengers and the vehicle itself from tangential spray.

mcqs.q: What is the magnitude of centripetal acceleration for a body moving with speed v in a circle of radius r?
mcqs.why: The similar-triangles derivation gives delta v over delta t equal to v squared over r in the limit, so the centripetal acceleration has magnitude v squared over r towards the centre.

mcqs.q: Which expression gives the centripetal force on a mass m moving in a circle?
options: m v squared divided by r, directed towards the centre
mcqs.why: Centripetal force is mass times centripetal acceleration, F equals m times v squared over r, equivalently m r omega squared, always directed towards the centre.

mcqs.q: For a particle in circular motion, what is the magnitude of angular momentum?
options: m r squared omega, equal to m v r
mcqs.why: L equals r cross p with r perpendicular to p, giving magnitude r p equals m v r, and substituting v equals r omega gives m r squared omega.

mcqs.q: How does moment of inertia in rotation correspond to mass in linear motion?
options: It plays the same role: torque equals I alpha just as force equals m a
It replaces velocity in rotational equations
It depends only on angular velocity
mcqs.why: Moment of inertia measures resistance to change in rotation exactly as mass measures resistance to change in linear motion, with tau equals I alpha paralleling F equals m a.

mcqs.q: At what frequencies does the INTELSAT system operate?
options: About 1 GHz up-link and 2 GHz down-link
About 6 GHz up-link and about 4 GHz down-link
mcqs.why: INTELSAT geo-stationary satellites relay signals in the microwave region at about 6 GHz for the Earth-to-satellite up-link and about 4 GHz for the down-link.

mcqs.q: What is the angular form of centripetal acceleration?
options: a equals omega squared r directed outward
a equals minus omega squared r, pointing towards the centre
a equals omega r directed tangentially
mcqs.why: Writing v squared over r squared as omega squared and noting acceleration is opposite to the outward radius vector gives a sub c equals minus omega squared r.

mcqs.q: How does orbital velocity of a satellite depend on its orbital radius?
options: v is proportional to one over the square root of r, so a nearer satellite moves faster
v is proportional to r squared
mcqs.why: Gravity supplying the centripetal force gives v squared equals G M over r, so v varies as one over root r and a low-orbit satellite must move faster.

mcqs.q: A lift accelerates upward with a body inside. How does its apparent weight compare with its real weight?
options: Apparent weight is less than real weight
Apparent weight m(g plus a) is greater than real weight m g
mcqs.why: Real weight is m g, while the support force in an upward-accelerating lift is m times g plus a, so the body appears heavier than its real weight.

mcqs.q: How is artificial gravity produced in a rotating space station?
options: By the rim's normal reaction providing centripetal acceleration r omega squared, felt through the feet like gravity
By air pressure inside the station
mcqs.why: Occupants stand on the inner rim; its push towards the centre supplies the centripetal force, and setting r omega squared equal to g reproduces Earth-like gravity.

mcqs.q: A diver tucks his body during a somersault. What happens and why?
options: His moment of inertia increases and he spins slower
His moment of inertia decreases and, with angular momentum conserved, his spin rate increases
His angular momentum increases in the air
mcqs.why: No external torque acts in the air, so I omega is constant; tucking reduces I, therefore omega increases and the diver completes extra somersaults.

mcqs.q: Why are mud guards fitted over vehicle wheels?
options: To increase the speed of the wheels
To cool the tyres on wet roads
To add weight over the wheels
Mud leaves the tyre tangentially and the guard intercepts it before it sprays the rider
mcqs.why: Once grip is lost, mud flies off along the tangent to the wheel; the curved guard placed close over the wheel catches this tangential spray and drops it near the wheel.

mcqs.q: Which set correctly pairs linear and rotational kinetic energy?
options: One-half m v squared and one-half I omega squared
One-half I v squared and one-half m omega squared
m v squared and I omega squared
mcqs.why: The rotational analogue of one-half m v squared is one-half I omega squared, just as angular momentum I omega parallels linear momentum m v.

mcqs.q: What is the frequency of rotation needed for artificial gravity equal to g in a station of radius r?
options: f equals 2 pi times root of g over r
f equals one over 2 pi times root of g over r
f equals root of r over g
f equals g divided by r
mcqs.why: Setting r times 2 pi f squared equal to g and solving for f gives f equals one over two pi multiplied by the square root of g over r.

mcqs.q: If a lift falls freely, what does a spring balance inside it read for a hanging body?
options: Zero, because apparent weight is m(g minus g)
mcqs.why: In free fall the acceleration equals g, so apparent weight m times g minus a becomes zero even though the real weight m g still acts on the body.

mcqs.q: What happens to angular velocity when a skater pulls her arms in while spinning?
options: It decreases because moment of inertia increases
It stays the same because mass is unchanged
It decreases because angular momentum is lost
It increases because moment of inertia decreases while angular momentum is conserved
mcqs.why: Pulling the arms in reduces the moment of inertia; with no external torque I omega stays constant, so the angular velocity must increase greatly.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Average angular velocity is total angular displacement divided by time, and 1 rev equals 2 pi radians.
  • Centripetal acceleration a_c = v^2 / R doubles when both v and R are doubled.
  • For a banked turn tan theta = v^2 / (R g), giving the required speed for a given angle and radius.
  • Angular acceleration follows from alpha = tau / I once torque and moment of inertia are known.
  • Angular momentum of a disc is L = I omega with I = (1/2) M R^2 for a solid disc.
  • The total kinetic energy of a rolling solid sphere is (7/10) M v^2, combining translation and rotation.
  • For rolling without slipping v = r omega, so angular speed follows directly from linear speed and radius.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 5.1

Q: Q1. A rotating pulley completes 12 rev in 4 s. Determine the average angular velocity in rev/s, rpm, and in rad/s?

Ans: Given: Number of revolutions = 12 rev
Time taken, t = 4 s
Formula: Average angular velocity = total angular displacement / time taken
In rev/s: omega = 12 rev / 4 s
omega = 3.00 rev/s
In rpm: omega = 3.00 rev/s x 60 s/min
omega = 180 rpm
In rad/s: 1 rev = 2 pi rad, so omega = 3.00 x 2 pi rad/s
omega = 18.8 rad/s
Answer: 3.00 rev/s, 180 rpm, and 18.8 rad/s
Note: The book's printed answer (28.6 rpm) is incorrect because 3.00 rev/s x 60 s/min = 180 rpm, not 28.6 rpm.

Assignment 5.2

Q: Q1. An airplane dives along a curved path of radius R and velocity v. The centripetal acceleration is 10 m s^-2. If both the velocity and the radius are doubled, what will be the new acceleration?

Ans: Given: Initial centripetal acceleration, a_c = 10 m/s^2
Velocity is doubled: v becomes 2v
Radius is doubled: R becomes 2R
Formula: a_c = v^2 / R
Substitution for the new acceleration: a_new = (2v)^2 / (2R)
a_new = 4 v^2 / 2R
a_new = 2 x (v^2 / R)
a_new = 2 x 10 m/s^2
Answer: 20 m/s^2

Assignment 5.3

Q: Q1. At what speed (in km/h) is a bank angle of 45 degrees required for an aeroplane to turn on a radius of 60 m?

Ans: Given: Bank angle, theta = 45 degrees
Radius of turn, R = 60 m
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: tan theta = v^2 / (R g), so v = sqrt(R g tan theta)
Substitution: v = sqrt(60 x 9.8 x tan 45 degrees)
tan 45 degrees = 1
v = sqrt(588)
v = 24.2 m/s
Converting to km/h: v = 24.2 x 3.6
Answer: 87.3 km/h (approx. 87.34 km/h)

Assignment 5.5

Q: Q1. A cord is wrapped around the rim of a cylinder that has a mass of 10 kg and a radius of 30 cm. If the rope is pulled with a force of 60 N, what is the angular acceleration of the cylinder?

Ans: Given: Mass of cylinder, M = 10 kg
Radius, R = 30 cm = 0.30 m
Pulling force, F = 60 N
Formula: Moment of inertia of a solid cylinder, I = (1/2) M R^2
Substitution: I = (1/2) x 10 x (0.30)^2
I = 0.45 kg m^2
Formula: Torque, tau = F x R
Substitution: tau = 60 x 0.30 = 18 N m
Formula: tau = I alpha, so alpha = tau / I
Substitution: alpha = 18 / 0.45
Answer: alpha = 40 rad/s^2

Assignment 5.6

Q: Q1. A belt is wrapped around the edge of a pulley that is 40 cm in diameter. The pulley rotates with a constant angular acceleration of 3.50 rad/s^2. At t = 0, the rotational speed is 2 rad/s. What is the angular displacement and angular velocity of the pulley 2 s later?

Ans: Given: Initial angular velocity, omega_i = 2 rad/s
Angular acceleration, alpha = 3.50 rad/s^2
Time, t = 2 s
Formula: omega_f = omega_i + alpha t
Substitution: omega_f = 2 + 3.50 x 2
omega_f = 9.00 rad/s
Formula: theta = omega_i t + (1/2) alpha t^2
Substitution: theta = 2 x 2 + (1/2) x 3.50 x (2)^2
theta = 4 + 7
theta = 11 rad
Answer: theta = 11 rad, omega_f = 9.00 rad/s
Note: The book's printed answer (theta = 238 rad) is incorrect because theta = omega_i t + (1/2) alpha t^2 = 4 + 7 = 11 rad for the given data.

Assignment 5.7

Q: Q1. A DVD disc has a radius of 0.0600 m, and a mass of 0.0200 kg. The moment of inertia of a solid disc is I = (1/2) M R^2, where M is the mass of the disc, and R is the radius. When a DVD in a certain machine starts playing, it has an angular velocity of 160.0 rad s^-1. What is the angular momentum of this disc?

Ans: Given: Radius of disc, R = 0.0600 m
Mass of disc, M = 0.0200 kg
Angular velocity, omega = 160.0 rad/s
Formula: Moment of inertia of a solid disc, I = (1/2) M R^2
Substitution: I = (1/2) x 0.0200 x (0.0600)^2
I = 3.6 x 10^-5 kg m^2
Formula: Angular momentum, L = I omega
Substitution: L = 3.6 x 10^-5 x 160.0
Answer: L = 0.00576 kg m^2/s

Assignment (unnumbered)

Q: Q1. A spring balance is attached to the ceiling of a lift. A man hangs his bag on the spring and the spring reads 49 N, when the lift is stationary. If the lift moves downward with an acceleration of 5 m/s^2, what will be the reading of the spring balance?

Ans: Given: Reading when the lift is stationary (real weight), W = 49 N
Downward acceleration of lift, a = 5 m/s^2
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: Mass of the bag, m = W / g
Substitution: m = 49 / 9.8 = 5.0 kg
Formula: For a lift accelerating downward, apparent weight = m (g - a)
Substitution: Apparent weight = 5.0 x (9.8 - 5)
Apparent weight = 5.0 x 4.8
Answer: 24 N
Note: The book's printed answer also shows 784 N, which is incorrect for this question because the reading for downward acceleration is m(g - a) = 24 N; 784 N does not follow from the given data.

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: Q1. If the plate microwave oven has a radius of 0.15 m and rotates at 6.0 rev/min, calculate the total distance traveled by the fly during a 2.0 min cooking period.

Ans: Given: Radius of plate, r = 0.15 m
Rotation rate = 6.0 rev/min
Cooking time = 2.0 min
The fly sits at the rim of the plate, so it travels along the circumference.
Formula: Distance in one revolution = 2 pi r
Substitution: 2 x 3.14 x 0.15 = 0.942 m
Number of revolutions in 2.0 min = 6.0 x 2.0 = 12 rev
Formula: Total distance = revolutions x distance per revolution
Substitution: Total distance = 12 x 0.942
Answer: 11.3 m (approx. 11 m)

Q: Q2. A circular drum of radius 40 cm is initially rotating at 400 revolution/min. It is brought to stop after making 50 revolutions. What is the angular acceleration and the stopping time?

Ans: Given: Initial rotation rate = 400 rev/min
Final angular velocity, omega_f = 0
Angular displacement, theta = 50 rev
Formula: Convert omega_i to rad/s: omega_i = 400 x 2 pi / 60
omega_i = 41.9 rad/s
Convert theta to rad: theta = 50 x 2 pi = 314 rad
Formula: omega_f^2 = omega_i^2 + 2 alpha theta, so alpha = (omega_f^2 - omega_i^2) / (2 theta)
Substitution: alpha = (0 - (41.9)^2) / (2 x 314)
alpha = -1755 / 628
Magnitude of angular acceleration = 2.79 rad/s^2 (retardation)
Formula: omega_f = omega_i + alpha t, so t = omega_i / |alpha|
Substitution: t = 41.9 / 2.79
Answer: Angular acceleration = 2.79 rad/s^2, stopping time = 15.0 s

Q: Q3. A string 1m long is used to whirl a 100g stone in a horizontal circle at a speed of 2 m s^-1. Find the tension in the string.

Ans: Given: Length of string (radius), r = 1 m
Mass of stone, m = 100 g = 0.1 kg
Speed, v = 2 m/s
Formula: Tension provides the centripetal force, T = m v^2 / r
Substitution: T = 0.1 x (2)^2 / 1
T = 0.1 x 4
Answer: T = 0.4 N

Q: Q4. The moon revolves around the earth in almost a circle of radius 382400km in 27.3 days. What is the centripetal acceleration?

Ans: Given: Radius of orbit, r = 382400 km = 3.824 x 10^8 m
Time period, T = 27.3 days = 27.3 x 24 x 3600 s = 2.36 x 10^6 s
Formula: Orbital speed, v = 2 pi r / T
Substitution: v = 2 x 3.14 x 3.824 x 10^8 / 2.36 x 10^6
v = 1.02 x 10^3 m/s
Formula: Centripetal acceleration, a_c = v^2 / r
Substitution: a_c = (1.02 x 10^3)^2 / 3.824 x 10^8
a_c = 1.04 x 10^6 / 3.824 x 10^8
Answer: a_c = 0.00271 m/s^2

Q: Q5. A modern F1 car can accelerate from 0 to 62 mile/h (100km/h) in 2.50 s. What is the angular acceleration of its 170 mm-radius wheels?

Ans: Given: Initial speed, v_i = 0
Final speed, v_f = 100 km/h = 27.7 m/s
Time, t = 2.50 s
Radius of wheels, r = 170 mm = 0.170 m
Formula: Linear acceleration, a = (v_f - v_i) / t
Substitution: a = 27.7 / 2.50 = 11.1 m/s^2
Formula: Angular acceleration, alpha = a / r
Substitution: alpha = 11.1 / 0.170
Answer: alpha = 65.17 rad/s^2 (approx.)

Q: Q6. An electric motor is running at 1800 rev min^-1. It comes to rest in 20 s. If the angular acceleration is uniform find the number of revolutions it made before stopping.

Ans: Given: Initial rotation rate = 1800 rev/min = 30 rev/s
Final angular velocity, omega_f = 0
Time to stop, t = 20 s
Formula: For uniform angular acceleration, average angular velocity = (omega_i + omega_f) / 2
Average rate = (30 + 0) / 2 = 15 rev/s
Formula: Number of revolutions = average rate x time
Substitution: Revolutions = 15 x 20
Answer: 300 rev

Q: Q7. What is the moment of inertia of a 100 kg sphere whose radius is 50 cm?

Ans: Given: Mass of sphere, M = 100 kg
Radius, R = 50 cm = 0.50 m
Formula: Moment of inertia of a solid sphere, I = (2/5) M R^2
Substitution: I = (2/5) x 100 x (0.50)^2
I = 0.4 x 100 x 0.25
Answer: I = 10 kg m^2

Q: Q8. A rope is wrapped several times around a cylinder of radius 0.2 m and mass 30 kg. What is the angular acceleration of the cylinder if the tension in the rope is 40 N and it turns without friction?

Ans: Given: Radius of cylinder, R = 0.2 m
Mass, M = 30 kg
Tension in rope, T = 40 N
Formula: Moment of inertia of the cylinder, I = (1/2) M R^2
Substitution: I = (1/2) x 30 x (0.2)^2 = 0.6 kg m^2
Formula: Torque, tau = T x R
Substitution: tau = 40 x 0.2 = 8 N m
Formula: alpha = tau / I
Substitution: alpha = 8 / 0.6
Answer: alpha = 13.3 rad/s^2

Q: Q9. What is the kinetic energy of a 5.0 kg solid ball whose diameter is 15 m if it rolls across a level surface with a speed of 2 m s^-1?

Ans: Given: Mass of ball, M = 5.0 kg
Speed, v = 2 m/s
The ball rolls without slipping, so it has both translational and rotational kinetic energy.
Formula: Total K.E = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2, with I = (2/5) M R^2 and omega = v / R
Substitution: Rotational K.E = (1/2) x (2/5) M R^2 x (v / R)^2 = (1/5) M v^2
Total K.E = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/5) M v^2 = (7/10) M v^2
Total K.E = (7/10) x 5.0 x (2)^2
Total K.E = 0.7 x 5.0 x 4
Answer: 14 J

Q: Q10. A cylinder of 50cm diameter at the top of an incline 29.4cm high and 10m long is released and rolls down the incline. Find its linear and angular speeds at the bottom. Neglect friction.

Ans: Given: Diameter of cylinder = 50 cm, so radius R = 0.25 m
Height of incline, h = 29.4 cm = 0.294 m
g = 9.8 m/s^2
The cylinder rolls without slipping, so loss of potential energy = gain of translational + rotational kinetic energy.
Formula: M g h = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2, with I = (1/2) M R^2 and omega = v / R
Working: M g h = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/4) M v^2 = (3/4) M v^2
So v = sqrt(4 g h / 3)
Substitution: v = sqrt(4 x 9.8 x 0.294 / 3)
v = sqrt(3.84)
v = 1.96 m/s
Formula: omega = v / R
Substitution: omega = 1.96 / 0.25
Answer: Linear speed = 1.96 m/s, angular speed = 7.84 rad/s

Q: Q11. A disc without slipping rolls down a hill of vertical height 1000cm. If the disc starts from rest at the top of the hill, what is its magnitude of velocity at the bottom?

Ans: Given: Vertical height, h = 1000 cm = 10 m
Initial velocity = 0
g = 9.8 m/s^2
The disc rolls without slipping, so loss of potential energy = gain of translational + rotational kinetic energy.
Formula: M g h = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/2) I omega^2, with I = (1/2) M R^2 for a disc and omega = v / R
Working: M g h = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/4) M v^2 = (3/4) M v^2
So v = sqrt(4 g h / 3)
Substitution: v = sqrt(4 x 9.8 x 10 / 3)
v = sqrt(130.7)
Answer: v = 11.4 m/s

Q: Q12. A motor car is traveling at a speed of 30 m s^-1. If its wheel has a diameter of 1.5m, find its angular speed in rad s^-1 and rev s^-1.

Ans: Given: Speed of car, v = 30 m/s
Diameter of wheel = 1.5 m, so radius r = 0.75 m
Formula: Angular speed, omega = v / r
Substitution: omega = 30 / 0.75
omega = 40 rad/s
Formula: Angular speed in rev/s = omega / 2 pi
Substitution: 40 / (2 x 3.14) = 6.36 rev/s
Answer: 40 rad/s, 6.36 rev/s

mcqs.q: A rotating pulley completes 12 rev in 4 s. Determine the average angular velocity in rad/s.
mcqs.why: Formula: omega = total angular displacement / time, with 1 rev = 2 pi rad. Substitution: omega = 12 rev / 4 s = 3.00 rev/s, then 3.00 x 2 pi. Step: 3.00 x 6.28 = 18.8. Result: 18.8 rad/s.

mcqs.q: An airplane dives along a curved path of radius R and velocity v. The centripetal acceleration is 10 m/s^2. If both the velocity and the radius are doubled, what will be the new acceleration?
mcqs.why: Formula: a_c = v^2 / R. Substitution: a_new = (2v)^2 / (2R) = 4v^2 / 2R. Step: a_new = 2 x (v^2 / R) = 2 x 10. Result: 20 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: At what speed (in m/s) is a bank angle of 45 degrees required for an aeroplane to turn on a radius of 60 m?
mcqs.why: Formula: tan theta = v^2 / (R g), so v = sqrt(R g tan theta). Substitution: v = sqrt(60 x 9.8 x tan 45 degrees) = sqrt(588). Step: tan 45 degrees = 1, sqrt(588) = 24.2. Result: 24.2 m/s, equal to 87.3 km/h.

mcqs.q: A cord is wrapped around the rim of a cylinder that has a mass of 10 kg and a radius of 30 cm. If the rope is pulled with a force of 60 N, what is the angular acceleration of the cylinder?
mcqs.why: Formula: I = (1/2) M R^2, tau = F R, alpha = tau / I. Substitution: I = 0.5 x 10 x 0.30^2 = 0.45 kg m^2, tau = 60 x 0.30 = 18 N m. Step: alpha = 18 / 0.45. Result: 40 rad/s^2.

mcqs.q: A belt is wrapped around the edge of a pulley that is 40 cm in diameter. The pulley rotates with a constant angular acceleration of 3.50 rad/s^2. At t = 0, the rotational speed is 2 rad/s. What is the angular displacement of the pulley 2 s later?
mcqs.why: Formula: theta = omega_i t + (1/2) alpha t^2. Substitution: theta = 2 x 2 + 0.5 x 3.50 x 2^2 = 4 + 7. Step: the two terms add to 11. Result: 11 rad. Note: the book's printed 238 rad is wrong because the substitution gives 4 + 7 = 11 rad.

mcqs.q: A DVD disc has a radius of 0.0600 m, and a mass of 0.0200 kg. When a DVD in a certain machine starts playing, it has an angular velocity of 160.0 rad/s. What is the angular momentum of this disc?
mcqs.why: Formula: I = (1/2) M R^2 and L = I omega. Substitution: I = 0.5 x 0.0200 x 0.0600^2 = 3.6 x 10^-5 kg m^2, L = 3.6 x 10^-5 x 160.0. Step: multiply to get 5.76 x 10^-3. Result: 0.00576 kg m^2/s.

mcqs.q: A spring balance is attached to the ceiling of a lift. A man hangs his bag on the spring and the spring reads 49 N, when the lift is stationary. If the lift moves downward with an acceleration of 5 m/s^2, what will be the reading of the spring balance?
mcqs.why: Formula: m = W / g and apparent weight = m(g - a). Substitution: m = 49 / 9.8 = 5.0 kg, apparent weight = 5.0 x (9.8 - 5) = 5.0 x 4.8. Step: 5.0 x 4.8 = 24. Result: 24 N. The book's alternative 784 N does not follow from m(g - a).

mcqs.q: If the plate microwave oven has a radius of 0.15 m and rotates at 6.0 rev/min, calculate the total distance traveled by the fly during a 2.0 min cooking period.
mcqs.why: Formula: distance per revolution = 2 pi r, total distance = revolutions x distance per revolution. Substitution: 2 x 3.14 x 0.15 = 0.942 m, revolutions = 6.0 x 2.0 = 12. Step: total = 12 x 0.942. Result: 11.3 m.

mcqs.q: A circular drum is initially rotating at 400 revolution/min. It is brought to stop after making 50 revolutions. What is the magnitude of the angular acceleration?
mcqs.why: Formula: omega_i = 400 x 2 pi / 60 and alpha = (omega_f^2 - omega_i^2) / (2 theta). Substitution: omega_i = 41.9 rad/s, theta = 50 x 2 pi = 314 rad, alpha = (0 - 41.9^2) / (2 x 314). Step: -1755 / 628 = -2.79. Result: magnitude 2.79 rad/s^2.

mcqs.q: A string 1m long is used to whirl a 100g stone in a horizontal circle at a speed of 2 m/s. Find the tension in the string.
mcqs.why: Formula: tension provides centripetal force, T = m v^2 / r. Substitution: T = 0.1 x 2^2 / 1 = 0.1 x 4. Step: 0.1 multiplied by 4 gives 0.4. Result: T = 0.4 N.

mcqs.q: The moon revolves around the earth in almost a circle of radius 382400km in 27.3 days. What is the centripetal acceleration?
A modern F1 car can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 2.50 s. What is the angular acceleration of its 170 mm-radius wheels?
mcqs.why: Formula: a = (v_f - v_i) / t and alpha = a / r. Substitution: v_f = 27.7 m/s, a = 27.7 / 2.50 = 11.1 m/s^2, alpha = 11.1 / 0.170. Step: 11.1 divided by 0.170 is about 65.17. Result: 65.17 rad/s^2 approximately.

mcqs.q: What is the moment of inertia of a 100 kg sphere whose radius is 50 cm?
mcqs.why: Formula: for a solid sphere I = (2/5) M R^2. Substitution: I = 0.4 x 100 x 0.50^2 = 0.4 x 100 x 0.25. Step: 100 x 0.25 = 25, times 0.4 gives 10. Result: I = 10 kg m^2.

mcqs.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 5.0 kg solid ball if it rolls across a level surface with a speed of 2 m/s?
mcqs.why: Formula: total K.E = (1/2) M v^2 + (1/5) M v^2 = (7/10) M v^2 for a rolling solid sphere. Substitution: total = 0.7 x 5.0 x 2^2 = 0.7 x 5.0 x 4. Step: 0.7 x 20 = 14. Result: 14 J.

mcqs.q: A motor car is traveling at a speed of 30 m/s. If its wheel has a diameter of 1.5m, find its angular speed in rad/s.
mcqs.why: Formula: omega = v / r, with r = diameter / 2. Substitution: r = 1.5 / 2 = 0.75 m, omega = 30 / 0.75. Step: 30 divided by 0.75 equals 40. Result: 40 rad/s, equal to 6.36 rev/s.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Substances that do not flow easily, like honey, have a high coefficient of viscosity.
  • One centipoise equals 10^-3 N s/m^2, and Stokes law applies only to a small spherical body moving slowly.
  • At terminal velocity the resultant force and the acceleration of a falling body are both zero.
  • In the equation of continuity A v = constant, the constant is the volume flow rate.
  • At a constriction the fluid speed is greater and its pressure is lower, by continuity and Bernoulli's principle.
  • The speed of efflux from a hole grows with its depth below the surface, as v = sqrt(2 g h).
  • A Venturi meter measures the speed of fluid flow from the pressure difference between pipe and throat.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: Q1. For substances that do not flow easily (like honey) have the ______ value for the coefficient of viscosity

Options: (a) low (b) high (c) zero (d) negative

Correct answer: high

Q: Q2. A unit for viscosity, the centipoise, is equal to which of the following?

Options: (a) 10^-3 N s/m^2 (b) 10^-2 N s/m^2 (c) 10^2 N s/m^2 (d) 10^3 N s/m^2

Correct answer: 10^-3 N s/m^2

Q: Q3. Stokes law is applicable only if a body is moving through a liquid with slow speed and has __________ shape.

Options: (a) a cubical (b) a spherical (c) a rough (d) any

Correct answer: a spherical

Q: Q4. The net force that acts on a 10-N falling object, when it encounters 4 N of air resistance is

Options: (a) 0 N (b) 4 N (c) 6 N (d) 10 N

Correct answer: 6 N

Q: Q5. A skydiver jumps from a high-flying helicopter. Before reaching terminal velocity, her acceleration

Options: (a) increase (b) decrease (c) remain the same (d) is zero

Correct answer: decrease

Q: Q6. At terminal velocity the acceleration of a falling object is

Options: (a) 0 m s^-2 (b) 1 m s^-2 (c) - 9.8 m s^-2 (d) + 9.8 m s^-2

Correct answer: 0 m s^-2

Q: Q7. According to equation of continuity Av = constant. This constant is equal to

Options: (a) volume of fluid (b) mass of fluid (c) density of fluid (d) volume flow rate

Correct answer: volume flow rate

Q: Q8. At the constriction in the cross-section for ideal flow, from equation of continuity it follows that, the speed of fluid is

Options: (a) greater (b) less (c) same (d) zero

Correct answer: greater

Q: Q9. As water in a level pipe passes from a narrow cross section of pipe to a wider cross section, the pressure against the wall

Options: (a) increases (b) decreases (c) remains the same (d) is zero

Correct answer: increases

Q: Q10. A 4 m high tank filled with water is drilled with four identical small holes at 1 m, 1.5 m, 2 m and 2.5 m from the bottom of tank, the speed of efflux will be greatest from the hole at

Options: (a) 1 m (b) 1.5 m (c) 2 m (d) 2.5 m

Correct answer: 1 m

Q: Q11. Venturi meter is a device used to measure the

Options: (a) mass of fluid (b) viscosity of fluid (c) speed of fluid (d) density of fluid

Correct answer: speed of fluid

Q: Q12. A certain pipe has a cross-sectional area of 0.0001 m^2 in which water is flowing at 10 m/s. The volume flow rate is

Options: (a) 0.00001 m^3/s (b) 0.001 m^3/s (c) 1 m^3/s (d) 10.0001 m^3/s

Correct answer: 0.001 m^3/s

Q: Q13. At sufficiently high speeds the flow of viscous fluid becomes

Options: (a) unexpected (b) stream line (c) non-viscous (d) turbulent

Correct answer: turbulent

Q: Q14. The water in the tank is 10 m above the leak point. The speed with which the water emerge from the leak is

Options: (a) 10 m/s (b) 14 m/s (c) 194 m/s (d) 0.1 m/s

Correct answer: 14 m/s

Q: Q15. When the radius of the artery is reduced, the blood pressure

Options: (a) increased (b) decreased (c) remains the same (d) is zero

Correct answer: decreased

mcqs.q: For substances that do not flow easily (like honey) have the ______ value for the coefficient of viscosity
mcqs.why: Honey flows with difficulty because of its internal friction, so substances that do not flow easily have a high coefficient of viscosity.

mcqs.q: A unit for viscosity, the centipoise, is equal to which of the following?
mcqs.why: One centipoise equals one-thousandth of a pascal-second, that is 10 to the power minus 3 newton-seconds per square metre, as keyed in the book.

mcqs.q: Stokes law is applicable only if a body is moving through a liquid with slow speed and has __________ shape.
mcqs.why: Stokes law F equals 6 pi eta r v is derived for a small spherical body moving slowly, so it applies only to a spherical shape at slow speed.

mcqs.q: The net force that acts on a 10-N falling object, when it encounters 4 N of air resistance is
mcqs.why: Weight acts downward at 10 N and air resistance acts upward at 4 N, so the net force is 10 minus 4, which equals 6 N downward.

mcqs.q: A skydiver jumps from a high-flying helicopter. Before reaching terminal velocity, her acceleration
mcqs.why: As speed grows the drag grows towards the weight, so the resultant force and therefore the acceleration steadily decrease before terminal velocity.

mcqs.q: At terminal velocity the acceleration of a falling object is
mcqs.why: At terminal velocity drag plus upthrust exactly balance the weight, the resultant force is zero, and so the acceleration is 0 metres per second squared.

mcqs.q: According to equation of continuity Av = constant. This constant is equal to
mcqs.why: In Av equals constant, A times v is the volume passing a section each second, so the constant is the volume flow rate of the fluid.

mcqs.q: At the constriction in the cross-section for ideal flow, from equation of continuity it follows that, the speed of fluid is
mcqs.why: By continuity Av stays constant, so where the cross-section is constricted the area is smaller and the speed of the fluid must be greater.

mcqs.q: As water in a level pipe passes from a narrow cross section of pipe to a wider cross section, the pressure against the wall
mcqs.why: In a wider section the fluid slows down, and by Bernoulli's principle slower flow means higher pressure against the wall, so the pressure increases.

mcqs.q: A 4 m high tank filled with water is drilled with four identical small holes at 1 m, 1.5 m, 2 m and 2.5 m from the bottom of tank, the speed of efflux will be greatest from the hole at
mcqs.why: Efflux speed grows with depth below the surface; the hole 1 m from the bottom of a 4 m tank is 3 m deep, the greatest depth, so its speed is greatest.

mcqs.q: Venturi meter is a device used to measure the
mcqs.why: A Venturi meter uses the pressure difference between the pipe and its narrow throat, with continuity and Bernoulli, to measure the speed of fluid flow.

mcqs.q: A certain pipe has a cross-sectional area of 0.0001 m^2 in which water is flowing at 10 m/s. The volume flow rate is
mcqs.why: Volume flow rate equals area times speed, so 0.0001 square metres times 10 metres per second gives 0.001 cubic metres per second.

mcqs.q: At sufficiently high speeds the flow of viscous fluid becomes
mcqs.why: At sufficiently high speeds streamline flow breaks down and the flow of a viscous fluid becomes irregular and turbulent, as keyed in the book.

mcqs.q: The water in the tank is 10 m above the leak point. The speed with which the water emerge from the leak is
mcqs.why: By Torricelli's theorem v equals the square root of 2 g h, so root of 2 times 9.8 times 10 is root 196, which equals 14 metres per second.

mcqs.q: When the radius of the artery is reduced, the blood pressure
mcqs.why: Where an artery narrows the blood speeds up, and by Bernoulli's principle the pressure in the narrowed part decreases, matching the keyed answer.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The light air-filled ball reaches terminal velocity first because a small drag at low speed balances its small weight.
  • A squirrel survives a fall because its large area compared with its mass gives it a low terminal velocity.
  • Opening a parachute greatly increases area, so drag balances weight at a much lower terminal speed.
  • By continuity A v = constant, partly covering a hose end reduces A and so increases the exit speed of the water.
  • Fast wind over a chimney top lowers the pressure there by Bernoulli's principle and draws the smoke up faster.
  • Water between two side-by-side boats flows faster and is at lower pressure, pushing the boats towards each other.
  • Dimples on a golf ball keep the boundary layer attached longer, narrowing the wake and greatly reducing drag.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: Q1. From the top of a tall building, you drop two table-tennis balls, one filled with air and the other with water. Which ball reaches terminal velocity first and why?

Ans: The air-filled ball reaches terminal velocity first. Terminal velocity is reached when the viscous drag plus upthrust balances the weight, so the acceleration becomes zero. The air-filled ball is very light, so only a small drag is needed to balance its small weight; since drag grows with speed, this balance is reached at a low speed, after falling only a short distance. The water-filled ball is much heavier; a far greater drag, and therefore a far greater speed, is needed to balance its weight, so it keeps accelerating for much longer and reaches its (much higher) terminal velocity later.

Q: Q2. Why can a squirrel jump from a tree branch to the ground and run away undamaged, while a human could break a bone in such a fall?

Ans: Terminal velocity depends on the balance between weight, which grows with volume (size cubed), and air drag, which grows with surface area (size squared). A small animal like a squirrel has a large surface area compared with its mass, and its bushy tail and spread body increase the drag further. Its terminal velocity is therefore low, only a few metres per second, and it can survive the fall and run away. A human has a much larger mass for the area presented to the air, so a human's terminal velocity is very high (about 55 m/s); striking the ground at such a speed produces forces large enough to break bones.

Q: Q3. How does the terminal speed of a parachutist before opening a parachute compare to the terminal speed afterward? Why is there a difference?

Ans: Before the parachute opens, the parachutist presents a small area to the air, so a large speed is needed before the drag grows enough to equal the weight; the terminal speed is therefore high, about 50 to 60 m/s. After the parachute opens, the area facing the air becomes very large, so the drag equals the weight at a much smaller speed; the terminal speed falls to about 5 m/s. The difference is entirely due to the greatly increased cross-sectional area, which produces the same drag force at a much lower speed.

Q: Q4. You can squirt water over a greater distance by placing your thumb over the end of a garden hose, than by leaving it completely uncovered. Explain how this works.

Ans: The same volume of water must pass through every part of the hose each second, so by the equation of continuity A v = constant. Placing your thumb over the end reduces the area A of the opening. To keep A v constant, the speed v of the water leaving the hose must increase in proportion. The faster jet travels a greater horizontal distance before falling to the ground, just as a projectile launched faster has a longer range. That is why the partly covered hose squirts water much farther.

Q: Q5. Why does smoke rise faster in a chimney on a windy day?

Ans: On a windy day the wind blows fast across the top opening of the chimney. By Bernoulli's principle, the fast-moving air at the top has a lower pressure than the still air at the base of the chimney and inside the house. Smoke and hot gases in the chimney are therefore pushed up by the higher pressure below and drawn out by the low pressure at the top. The greater the wind speed, the lower the pressure at the top and the faster the smoke rises; on a calm day this suction effect is missing and the smoke rises only slowly by its own buoyancy.

Q: Q6. Two boats moving in parallel paths close to one another risk colliding. Why?

Ans: When two boats travel side by side in the same direction, the water between them is forced through a narrow gap and flows faster than the water on their outer sides. By Bernoulli's principle, the faster water between the boats is at a lower pressure, while the slower water outside is at higher pressure. This pressure difference pushes both boats inwards, towards each other. If the boats are close, the sideways push can overcome the steering and the boats risk colliding; ships therefore keep a wide separation when passing.

Q: Q7. A cricket ball moves past an observer from left to right, spinning counter clockwise. In which direction will the ball tend to deflect?

Ans: The ball is moving from left to right and spinning counter-clockwise as seen by the observer, so the top surface of the ball is moving towards the left, in the same direction as the air streaming past it, while the bottom surface moves against the air stream. The air therefore passes over the top of the ball faster than under the bottom. By Bernoulli's principle the pressure above the ball is lower and the pressure below it is higher. This pressure difference (the Magnus effect) pushes the ball upward, so the ball tends to deflect upward, opposite to the side where the surface moves against the flow.

Q: Q8. If aero-foil lift the aero-plane in upright position, how do the pilots make the aero-planes fly upside down?

Ans: Lift does not depend on the wing being the 'right way up' but on the angle at which the wing meets the air, the angle of attack. When flying upside down, the pilot pushes the controls so that the inverted wing is tilted to give a suitable angle of attack relative to the oncoming air. Air is then still deflected and the streamlines and pressure difference are arranged so that the resultant aerodynamic force points towards the ground side of the wing, which, with the plane inverted, is towards the sky. Many aerobatic aeroplanes also use nearly symmetrical aerofoils, which can produce lift in either orientation when given the proper angle of attack.

Q: Q9. Why do the golf balls have dimples?

Ans: The dimples make the thin layer of air next to the ball (the boundary layer) turbulent. A turbulent boundary layer has more energy and clings to the ball's surface longer, separating later at the back of the ball. The wake behind the ball is therefore much narrower, and the pressure drag is greatly reduced. With less drag the ball keeps its speed longer and travels much farther than a smooth ball hit with the same force. The dimples also help the spinning ball grip the air and generate lift, keeping it in the air longer.

Q: Q10. How by using wind deflectors on the top truck cabs reduce fuel consumption?

Ans: Without a deflector, air striking the tall front face of the trailer (container) behind the cab is forced around sharp corners, forming a turbulent, low-pressure wake that drags the truck backwards and wastes engine power. The wind deflector on top of the cab is an inclined aerofoil-shaped panel that turns the air smoothly upward and over the trailer. The flow stays streamlined, turbulence and drag are reduced, and the engine needs less force to maintain speed. Less force at the same speed means less work done and therefore less fuel consumed.

mcqs.q: Two table-tennis balls are dropped, one air-filled and one water-filled. Which reaches terminal velocity first?
options: The water-filled ball, because it is heavier
The air-filled ball, because only a small drag at low speed is needed to balance its small weight
Both reach it at the same time
mcqs.why: Terminal velocity is reached when drag balances weight; the light air-filled ball needs only a small drag, reached at a low speed after a short fall, unlike the heavy water-filled ball.

mcqs.q: Why can a squirrel survive a fall from a tree while a human may break a bone?
options: The squirrel has a low terminal velocity because its surface area is large compared with its mass
The squirrel weighs nothing in the air
Humans fall faster because of gravity differences
The squirrel's fall is slowed by its colour
mcqs.why: Drag grows with area while weight grows with volume; the squirrel's large area-to-mass ratio gives a low terminal velocity, while a human's terminal velocity is about 55 m/s.

mcqs.q: Why is a parachutist's terminal speed much lower after the parachute opens?
options: The parachute reduces the parachutist's weight
The open parachute greatly increases area, so drag balances weight at a much lower speed of about 5 m/s
mcqs.why: Before opening, a small area needs 50 to 60 m/s for drag to equal weight; the opened parachute's large area produces the same drag at only about 5 m/s.

mcqs.q: Why does placing a thumb over a hose end make water squirt farther?
options: It increases the water pressure in the tank
Continuity A v = constant means the reduced area forces the exit speed to increase
It increases the area of the opening
mcqs.why: The same volume must pass each second, so with A reduced at the opening, v must increase in proportion, and the faster jet travels farther before falling.

mcqs.q: Why does smoke rise faster in a chimney on a windy day?
options: Wind pushes the smoke down the chimney
Fast wind over the top lowers the pressure there, drawing smoke up from the higher pressure below
Smoke becomes lighter on windy days
mcqs.why: By Bernoulli's principle the fast air across the chimney top is at lower pressure, so higher pressure below pushes the smoke and hot gases up and out.

mcqs.q: Why do two boats travelling side by side risk colliding?
options: Water between them flows faster and is at lower pressure, so higher outside pressure pushes them together
mcqs.why: Water forced through the narrow gap between the boats flows faster, its pressure drops by Bernoulli's principle, and the higher pressure outside pushes both boats inwards.

mcqs.q: A ball moving left to right spins counter-clockwise. Which way does it tend to deflect?
options: Upward, because air is faster over the top and pressure is lower there
mcqs.why: With counter-clockwise spin the air passes faster over the top of the ball, so pressure is lower above and higher below; this Magnus effect pushes the ball upward.

mcqs.q: How can an aeroplane fly upside down?
options: The pilot gives the inverted wing a suitable angle of attack so the aerodynamic force still points skyward
The wings stop producing any force
mcqs.why: Lift depends on the angle of attack, not on being the right way up; with the proper tilt the inverted wing deflects air so the resultant force points towards the sky.

mcqs.q: Why do golf balls have dimples?
options: Dimples make the boundary layer turbulent so it clings longer, narrowing the wake and reducing drag
To make the ball spin slower
mcqs.why: A turbulent boundary layer stays attached longer and separates later, giving a much narrower wake and greatly reduced pressure drag, so the ball travels farther.

mcqs.q: How does a wind deflector on a truck cab save fuel?
options: It turns air smoothly over the trailer, reducing turbulence and drag so the engine does less work
It increases the truck's speed automatically
It blocks all air from the truck
mcqs.why: The inclined deflector guides air smoothly over the tall trailer instead of forming a turbulent low-pressure wake, cutting drag and therefore the fuel needed at the same speed.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Stokes law gives the viscous drag on a small slow sphere as F = 6 pi eta r v.
  • Terminal velocity is v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / (9 eta), from balancing weight against upthrust plus drag.
  • The equation of continuity A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 expresses conservation of mass in steady flow.
  • Bernoulli's equation P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant expresses conservation of energy along a streamline.
  • Torricelli's theorem gives the speed of efflux as v = sqrt(2 g h) for a leak at depth h.
  • A Venturi meter finds fluid speed from the pressure difference between the pipe and its narrow throat.
  • Aerofoil lift arises because faster air over the wing's top surface is at lower pressure than the slower air below.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Q1. What is viscous drag? State and explain Stokes Law.

Ans: Viscous drag is the resistive force experienced by a body moving through a fluid, caused by the internal friction (viscosity) of the fluid. Layers of fluid stick to the body and slide over neighbouring layers, and the friction between layers opposes the motion, just as friction opposes sliding between solids.
Stokes law states that for a small spherical body of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of coefficient of viscosity eta, the viscous drag is F = 6 pi eta r v.
The law holds only for a spherical body, moving at low speed, in a fluid of effectively unlimited extent, with streamline (laminar) flow around the body.
The drag is directly proportional to the radius of the sphere, to its speed, and to the coefficient of viscosity of the fluid. This law is the basis for finding terminal velocity and for measuring viscosity.

Q: Q2. What is terminal velocity? Derive mathematical relation for terminal velocity by using Stokes law.

Ans: Terminal velocity is the constant maximum velocity with which a body falls through a fluid, reached when the resultant force on it becomes zero.
Derivation: Let a sphere of radius r and density rho fall through a fluid of density sigma and viscosity eta.
Weight of the sphere, W = (4/3) pi r^3 rho g (downward).
Upthrust, U = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g (upward).
Viscous drag by Stokes law, F = 6 pi eta r v (upward), which grows as v grows.
At terminal velocity v_t the forces balance: W = U + F.
(4/3) pi r^3 rho g = (4/3) pi r^3 sigma g + 6 pi eta r v_t.
(4/3) pi r^3 (rho - sigma) g = 6 pi eta r v_t.
Solving: v_t = (2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g) / (9 eta).
Thus terminal velocity is proportional to r^2 and to the difference of densities, and inversely proportional to the viscosity.

Q: Q3. Derive mathematically the equation of continuity, and relate it to the time rate of volume flow. How equation of continuity is based on conservation of mass?

Ans: Consider a steady, incompressible flow through a pipe of varying cross-section. Let the fluid enter a wide section of area A_1 with speed v_1 and leave a narrow section of area A_2 with speed v_2 in time Delta t.
Volume entering in time Delta t = A_1 v_1 Delta t, so mass entering = rho A_1 v_1 Delta t.
Volume leaving in time Delta t = A_2 v_2 Delta t, so mass leaving = rho A_2 v_2 Delta t.
In steady flow no fluid accumulates in the pipe, so mass entering = mass leaving.
rho A_1 v_1 Delta t = rho A_2 v_2 Delta t, hence A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = constant.
This is the equation of continuity. The constant A v is the volume flow rate, Delta V / Delta t = A v, the volume of fluid passing a cross-section per second.
The derivation is based on conservation of mass: because rho cancels for an incompressible fluid, equal volumes (and hence equal masses) must pass every section each second; the fluid speeds up where the pipe narrows and slows where it widens.

Q: Q4. Derive mathematical expression for the Bernoulli's equation. How Bernoulli's equation is based on conservation of energy?

Ans: Consider steady flow of an ideal incompressible fluid through a pipe. Take a fluid element that moves from point 1 (pressure P_1, speed v_1, height h_1) to point 2 (pressure P_2, speed v_2, height h_2), carrying a small volume Delta V of mass Delta m = rho Delta V.
Work done by pressure forces = P_1 Delta V - P_2 Delta V = (P_1 - P_2) Delta V.
Change in kinetic energy = (1/2) Delta m v_2^2 - (1/2) Delta m v_1^2.
Change in potential energy = Delta m g h_2 - Delta m g h_1.
By the work-energy principle, work done = change in K.E + change in P.E.
(P_1 - P_2) Delta V = (1/2) rho Delta V (v_2^2 - v_1^2) + rho Delta V g (h_2 - h_1).
Dividing by Delta V and rearranging: P_1 + (1/2) rho v_1^2 + rho g h_1 = P_2 + (1/2) rho v_2^2 + rho g h_2.
Hence along any streamline P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant. This is Bernoulli's equation.
It is based on conservation of energy: each term is an energy per unit volume (pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy), and their sum stays constant because the work done by pressure is converted into kinetic and potential energy with no loss in an ideal fluid.

Q: Q5. Using Bernoulli's equation, what is the speed of efflux from a leak at the bottom of large storage tank?

Ans: Apply Bernoulli's equation between the top surface of the water in the tank (point 1) and the leak at the bottom (point 2).
Both points are open to the air, so P_1 = P_2 = atmospheric pressure.
The tank is large, so the top surface sinks very slowly and v_1 is nearly zero.
Let the leak be at a depth h below the surface: h_1 - h_2 = h.
Bernoulli: P_1 + (1/2) rho v_1^2 + rho g h_1 = P_2 + (1/2) rho v_2^2 + rho g h_2.
Cancelling the pressures and putting v_1 = 0: rho g (h_1 - h_2) = (1/2) rho v_2^2.
rho g h = (1/2) rho v^2, so v = sqrt(2 g h).
This is Torricelli's result: the speed of efflux equals the speed a body would gain falling freely through the height h.

Q: Q6. By Bernoulli's equation, how we can determine the speed of the fluid in a pipe?

Ans: The speed of a fluid in a pipe is measured with a Venturi meter, a section of pipe with a narrow throat, fitted with pressure gauges (or a manometer) at the wide part and at the throat.
Let A_1, v_1, P_1 be the area, speed and pressure in the main pipe and A_2, v_2, P_2 those at the throat.
From the equation of continuity: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2, so v_2 = v_1 A_1 / A_2.
From Bernoulli's equation for a level pipe: P_1 + (1/2) rho v_1^2 = P_2 + (1/2) rho v_2^2, so P_1 - P_2 = (1/2) rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2).
Substituting v_2 from continuity and solving for v_1: v_1 = A_2 sqrt( 2 (P_1 - P_2) / (rho (A_1^2 - A_2^2)) ).
Thus, measuring the pressure difference between the pipe and the throat gives the speed of the fluid in the pipe, and A_1 v_1 then gives the volume flow rate.

Q: Q7. What is aero-foil? Explain aero-foil lift on the wing of an aero-plane.

Ans: An aerofoil is a body shaped so that the relative motion between it and a fluid produces a force perpendicular to the flow; an aeroplane wing is the standard example. Its upper surface is more curved than the lower surface.
As the wing moves forward, the streamlines of air are crowded together above the wing and spread out below it.
By the equation of continuity, the air must move faster where the streamlines are crowded, so the air speed over the top surface is greater than under the bottom surface.
By Bernoulli's principle, the faster air above the wing is at lower pressure and the slower air below is at higher pressure.
The pressure difference, acting over the area of the wing, produces a net upward force: F = (P_bottom - P_top) x A. This upward component of the aerodynamic force is the lift that supports the aeroplane.

Q: Q8. Use Bernoulli's equation to explain the working of engine carburetor and perfume bottle spray.

Ans: Both devices work on the pressure drop produced where a fluid speeds up at a constriction, as given by Bernoulli's equation.
Engine carburetor: Air is drawn through a narrow throat (venturi) in the carburetor on its way to the engine. At the throat the air speed is high, so its pressure falls below atmospheric pressure. The petrol in the float chamber is at atmospheric pressure, so petrol is pushed through a fine jet into the throat, where it mixes with the fast air stream as a fine spray and passes into the engine.
Perfume bottle spray: Squeezing the rubber bulb forces air rapidly across the top of a vertical tube whose lower end dips in the perfume. The fast air lowers the pressure at the top of the tube, so atmospheric pressure on the perfume surface pushes the liquid up the tube. The rising perfume meets the air blast and is blown away as a fine spray of droplets.

mcqs.q: What is the viscous drag on a small sphere of radius r moving slowly with speed v through a fluid of viscosity eta, by Stokes law?
options: F = 6 pi eta r squared v
F = eta r v divided by 6 pi
F = 6 pi eta v divided by r
mcqs.why: Stokes law gives the drag as 6 pi eta r v for a small sphere at low speed in streamline flow, proportional to radius, speed and coefficient of viscosity.

mcqs.q: What is the terminal velocity of a sphere of radius r and density rho falling in a fluid of density sigma?
options: v_t = 9 eta divided by 2 r squared (rho - sigma) g
v_t = 2 r (rho - sigma) g divided by eta
v_t = r^2 eta g divided by (rho - sigma)
mcqs.why: Balancing weight against upthrust plus Stokes drag gives v_t equals 2 r squared times rho minus sigma times g, divided by 9 eta.

mcqs.q: What does the equation of continuity state for steady incompressible flow?
options: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 = constant, expressing conservation of mass
Pressure is the same at all sections
Speed is the same at all sections
mcqs.why: Equal masses must pass every section each second, so for constant density A v is the same everywhere; A v is the volume flow rate.

mcqs.q: What is Bernoulli's equation along a streamline?
options: P v + rho g h = constant
P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant, expressing conservation of energy
(1/2) rho v^2 = rho g h always
mcqs.why: Bernoulli's equation sums pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume to a constant, following from the work-energy principle for an ideal fluid.

mcqs.q: What is the speed of efflux from a leak at depth h below the surface of a large tank?
options: v = square root of g h divided by 2
v = square root of 2 g h, by Torricelli's theorem
mcqs.why: Applying Bernoulli between the surface and the leak, with both at atmospheric pressure and the surface nearly at rest, gives rho g h equals one-half rho v squared, so v equals root 2 g h.

mcqs.q: How does a Venturi meter measure the speed of fluid in a pipe?
options: From the pressure difference between the wide pipe and the narrow throat, using continuity and Bernoulli's equation
mcqs.why: Continuity gives the throat speed in terms of the pipe speed, and Bernoulli converts the measured pressure drop into the pipe speed v_1 and hence the flow rate.

mcqs.q: Why does an aerofoil wing produce lift?
options: Air moves faster over the curved top, so pressure is lower above than below and the difference lifts the wing
Air moves slower over the top, raising pressure above
The wing is lighter than air
Gravity acts upward on the wing
mcqs.why: Streamlines crowd above the wing, so by continuity the air is faster there and by Bernoulli its pressure is lower; the pressure difference over the wing area is the lift.

mcqs.q: How does an engine carburetor draw petrol into the air stream?
options: A pump injects petrol at high pressure
Air speeding through the narrow throat drops in pressure, so atmospheric pressure pushes petrol through the jet as a spray
The engine sucks petrol by heating it
mcqs.why: At the venturi throat the air is fast and its pressure falls below atmospheric, so petrol at atmospheric pressure in the float chamber is pushed into the throat and mixes as a fine spray.

mcqs.q: How does a perfume spray work?
options: Fast air over the tube top lowers pressure there, so atmospheric pressure pushes perfume up the tube into the air blast
Squeezing heats the perfume until it evaporates
Perfume is pumped by a motor
mcqs.why: Air forced rapidly across the top of the dip tube lowers the pressure there; atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface then pushes perfume up to be blown away as droplets.

mcqs.q: In the terminal velocity formula, how does v_t depend on the sphere's radius and the fluid's viscosity?
options: v_t is proportional to r and inversely proportional to root eta
v_t is proportional to r squared and inversely proportional to eta
v_t is proportional to eta and inversely proportional to r squared
mcqs.why: From v_t equals 2 r squared (rho - sigma) g over 9 eta, terminal velocity grows with the square of the radius and falls as viscosity increases.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Terminal velocity proportional to r squared lets combined drops and Stokes-law particle sizes be found directly.
  • Bernoulli's equation links pressure, speed and height changes between two points in a flowing fluid.
  • Torricelli's speed v = sqrt(2 g h) gives both efflux speed and, with the hole area, the discharge rate.
  • In a Venturi meter the throat speed exceeds the pipe speed by the area ratio A_1 / A_2.
  • Volume flow rate equals volume divided by time, and flow speed equals flow rate divided by tube area.
  • Lift on a small wing equals the Bernoulli pressure difference multiplied by the wing area.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 6.1

Q: Q1. A certain globular protein particle has a density of 1246 kg m^-3. It falls through water (having coefficient of viscosity 8.91 x 10^-4 Pa s) with a terminal speed of 8.33 x 10^-6 m s^-1. Find the radius of the particle.

Ans: Given: Density of particle, rho = 1246 kg/m^3
Coefficient of viscosity of water, eta = 8.91 x 10^-4 Pa s
Terminal speed, v_t = 8.33 x 10^-6 m/s
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: By Stokes law, terminal velocity v_t = 2 r^2 rho g / (9 eta)
Rearranging for r: r = sqrt(9 eta v_t / (2 rho g))
Substitution: r = sqrt(9 x 8.91 x 10^-4 x 8.33 x 10^-6 / (2 x 1246 x 9.8))
r = sqrt(6.68 x 10^-8 / 24422)
r = sqrt(2.74 x 10^-12)
Answer: r = 1.6 x 10^-6 m

Assignment 6.2

Q: Q1. The heart pumps blood into the aorta, which has an inner radius of 1.0 cm. The aorta feeds 32 major arteries (each have an inner radius of 0.21 cm). If blood in the aorta travels at a speed of 25 cm/s, at approximately what average speed does it travel in the arteries? Assume that blood can be treated as an ideal fluid.

Ans: Given: Radius of aorta, r_1 = 1.0 cm
Speed of blood in aorta, v_1 = 25 cm/s
Number of arteries, n = 32
Radius of each artery, r_2 = 0.21 cm
Formula: Equation of continuity: A_1 v_1 = n A_2 v_2, so v_2 = A_1 v_1 / (n A_2) = r_1^2 v_1 / (n r_2^2)
Substitution: v_2 = (1.0)^2 x 25 / (32 x (0.21)^2)
v_2 = 25 / (32 x 0.0441)
v_2 = 25 / 1.41
v_2 = 17.7 cm/s
Answer: 0.18 m/s (approx.)

Assignment 6.3

Q: Q1. Water is flowing smoothly through a closed pipe system. At one point the speed of water is 3 m s^-1, while at another point 3 m higher, the speed is 4 m s^-1. At lower point the pressure is 80 kPa. Find the pressure at the upper point.

Ans: Given: At the lower point: speed v_1 = 3 m/s, pressure P_1 = 80 kPa = 80000 Pa, height h_1 = 0
At the upper point: speed v_2 = 4 m/s, height h_2 = 3 m
Density of water, rho = 1000 kg/m^3
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: Bernoulli equation: P_1 + (1/2) rho v_1^2 + rho g h_1 = P_2 + (1/2) rho v_2^2 + rho g h_2
Rearranging: P_2 = P_1 + (1/2) rho (v_1^2 - v_2^2) - rho g (h_2 - h_1)
Substitution: P_2 = 80000 + (1/2) x 1000 x (9 - 16) - 1000 x 9.8 x 3
P_2 = 80000 - 3500 - 29400
P_2 = 47100 Pa
Answer: 47.1 kPa

Extension Exercise

Q: Q1. If the opening from spigot points upward, how high does the resulting 'fountain' go?

Ans: This question refers to Example 6.4: the spigot is at a depth h = 1.2 m below the water surface, and the water leaves the spigot with the Torricelli speed v = 4.85 m/s.
Given: Speed of the upward jet, v = 4.85 m/s
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: At the top of the fountain the speed becomes zero, so by v_f^2 = v^2 - 2 g H, H = v^2 / (2 g)
Substitution: H = (4.85)^2 / (2 x 9.8)
H = 23.5 / 19.6
Answer: H = 1.2 m above the spigot, that is, the fountain rises just up to the level of the water surface in the tank.

Assignment 6.4

Q: Q1. A tank full of water has a (small) hole near its bottom at a depth of 2.0 m from the top surface, which is open to air. What is the speed of the stream of water emerging from the hole?

Ans: Given: Depth of hole below the top surface, h = 2.0 m
g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: Torricelli theorem: speed of efflux, v = sqrt(2 g h)
Substitution: v = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 2.0)
v = sqrt(39.2)
Answer: v = 6.3 m/s

Assignment 6.5

Q: Q1. A venturi meter is measuring the flow of water in a pipe having cross-sectional area of 0.0038 m^2, a throat with cross-sectional area of 0.00031 m^2 is connected to it. If the pressure difference is measured to be 2.4 kPa, what is the speed of the water in the pipe?

Ans: Given: Cross-sectional area of pipe, A_1 = 0.0038 m^2
Cross-sectional area of throat, A_2 = 0.00031 m^2
Pressure difference, P_1 - P_2 = 2.4 kPa = 2400 Pa
Density of water, rho = 1000 kg/m^3
Formula: Continuity: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2, so v_2 = v_1 A_1 / A_2 = v_1 x 0.0038 / 0.00031 = 12.26 v_1
Formula: Bernoulli (level pipe): P_1 - P_2 = (1/2) rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2)
Substitution: 2400 = (1/2) x 1000 x ((12.26 v_1)^2 - v_1^2)
2400 = 500 x 149.3 x v_1^2
v_1^2 = 2400 / 74650 = 0.0322
Answer: v_1 = 0.18 m/s
Note: The book's printed answer (2.2 m/s) is incorrect because 2.2 m/s is the speed at the narrow throat, v_2 = 12.26 x 0.18; the speed of the water in the pipe itself is 0.18 m/s.

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: Q1. Eight equal drops of oil are falling through air with steady velocity of 0.1 m s^-1. the drops recombine to form a single drop, what should be the new terminal velocity?

Ans: Given: Terminal velocity of each small drop, v = 0.1 m/s
Number of drops combining = 8
Formula: Volume of the big drop = 8 x volume of one small drop, so (4/3) pi R^3 = 8 x (4/3) pi r^3
Working: R^3 = 8 r^3, so R = 2 r
Formula: Terminal velocity is proportional to radius squared, v_t proportional to r^2 (from v_t = 2 r^2 (rho - sigma) g / 9 eta)
Working: New terminal velocity = v x (R / r)^2 = 0.1 x (2)^2
New terminal velocity = 0.1 x 4
Answer: 0.4 m/s

Q: Q2. Water travels through a 9.6 cm diameter fire hose with a speed of 1.3 m/s. At the end of the hose, the water flows out through a nozzle whose diameter is 2.5 cm. (a) What is the speed of the water coming out of the nozzle? (b) What diameter nozzle is required to give water speed of 21 m/s?

Ans: Given: Diameter of hose, d_1 = 9.6 cm; speed in hose, v_1 = 1.3 m/s
Diameter of nozzle, d_2 = 2.5 cm
(a) Formula: Equation of continuity: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2, so v_2 = v_1 (d_1 / d_2)^2
Substitution: v_2 = 1.3 x (9.6 / 2.5)^2
v_2 = 1.3 x 14.75
v_2 = 19 m/s
(b) Required nozzle speed, v_2 = 21 m/s
Formula: d_2 = d_1 sqrt(v_1 / v_2)
Substitution: d_2 = 9.6 x sqrt(1.3 / 21)
d_2 = 9.6 x 0.249
Answer: (a) 19 m/s, (b) 2.4 cm

Q: Q3. A fish tank has dimensions 0.30 m wide by 1.0 m long by 0.60 m high. If the filter should process all the water in the tank once every 3.0 h, what should the flow speed be in the 3.0 cm diameter input tube for the filter?

Ans: Given: Tank dimensions: 0.30 m wide, 1.0 m long, 0.60 m high
Time to process all the water, t = 3.0 h = 10800 s
Diameter of input tube = 3.0 cm, so radius r = 0.015 m
Formula: Volume of water, V = 0.30 x 1.0 x 0.60 = 0.18 m^3
Formula: Volume flow rate = V / t
Substitution: Flow rate = 0.18 / 10800 = 1.67 x 10^-5 m^3/s
Formula: Area of tube, A = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (0.015)^2 = 7.07 x 10^-4 m^2
Formula: Flow speed, v = flow rate / A
Substitution: v = 1.67 x 10^-5 / 7.07 x 10^-4 = 0.0236 m/s
Answer: 2.4 cm/s
Note: The book's printed answer (2.8 cm/s) is incorrect because dividing the required flow rate 1.67 x 10^-5 m^3/s by the tube area 7.07 x 10^-4 m^2 gives 0.0236 m/s = 2.4 cm/s.

Q: Q4. A venturi meter is measuring the flow of water; it has a main diameter of 3.5 cm tapering down to a throat diameter of 1.0 cm. If the pressure difference is measured to be 18 mm-Hg, what is the speed of the water entering the venturi throat?

Ans: Given: Main diameter, d_1 = 3.5 cm; throat diameter, d_2 = 1.0 cm
Pressure difference = 18 mm-Hg
Convert pressure: Delta P = 0.018 m x 13600 kg/m^3 x 9.8 m/s^2 = 2400 Pa (approx.)
Density of water, rho = 1000 kg/m^3
Formula: Continuity: v_2 = v_1 (A_1 / A_2) = v_1 (d_1 / d_2)^2 = v_1 x (3.5 / 1.0)^2 = 12.25 v_1
Formula: Bernoulli (level pipe): Delta P = (1/2) rho (v_2^2 - v_1^2)
Substitution: 2400 = (1/2) x 1000 x ((12.25 v_1)^2 - v_1^2)
2400 = 500 x 149.1 x v_1^2
v_1^2 = 0.0322
v_1 = 0.18 m/s
The speed at the throat is v_2 = 12.25 x 0.18 = 2.2 m/s
Answer: The speed of the water entering the venturi (in the main pipe) is 0.18 m/s, rising to 2.2 m/s at the throat.
