Q: Q9. The spacing of one set of crystal planes in NaCl (table salt) is d = 0.282 nm. A monochromatic beam of X-rays produces a Bragg maximum when its glancing angle with these planes is theta = 7 degrees. Assuming that this is a first order maximum (n = 1), find the wavelength of the X-rays.

Ans: Given: plane spacing d = 0.282 nm = 2.82 x 10^-10 m, glancing angle theta = 7 degrees, order n = 1
Formula: Bragg's law, 2 d sin theta = n lambda, so lambda = 2 d sin theta / n
Substitution: lambda = 2 x 0.282 nm x sin 7 degrees / 1 = 0.564 x 0.1219 nm = 0.0687 nm
Answer: lambda = 0.069 nm

mcqs.q: The 3rd bright fringe in a double slit experiment makes a 2.4 degrees angle with respect to the central line. The wavelength of the monochromatic light used is 480nm. Find the distance d between the two sources.
mcqs.why: Formula: for a bright fringe, d sin theta = m lambda, so d = m lambda / sin theta. Substitution: d = (3 x 480 x 10^-9 m) / sin 2.4 degrees = 1.44 x 10^-6 / 0.0419. Step: dividing gives d = 3.44 x 10^-5 m. Result: d = 3.44 x 10^-5 m = 0.0344 mm.

mcqs.q: A beam of X-rays of wavelength 0.3 nm is incident on a crystal, and gives a first-order maximum when the glancing angle is 9.0 degrees. Find the atomic spacing.
mcqs.why: Formula: Bragg's law, 2 d sin theta = m lambda, so d = m lambda / (2 sin theta). Substitution: d = (1 x 3.0 x 10^-10 m) / (2 x sin 9.0 degrees) = 3.0 x 10^-10 / (2 x 0.1564). Step: the denominator is 0.3129, so d = 3.0 x 10^-10 / 0.3129 = 9.59 x 10^-10 m. Result: d = 9.6 x 10^-10 m (0.96 nm).

mcqs.q: In a young double slit experiment the separation of the slits is 1 mm and red light of wavelength 620 nm is falling on it. Determine the distance between the central bright band and the fifth bright fringe on the screen which is 3m away from the slit.
mcqs.why: Formula: fringe width beta = lambda L / d, and the distance of the mth bright fringe is y = m beta = m lambda L / d. Substitution: beta = (620 x 10^-9 x 3) / (1 x 10^-3) = 1.86 x 10^-3 m. Step: y = 5 x 1.86 x 10^-3 m = 9.3 x 10^-3 m. Result: y = 9.3 mm.

mcqs.q: Two parallel slits are illuminated by light of two wavelengths, one of which is 5.8 x 10^-7 m. On the screen the fourth dark line of the known wavelength coincides with the fifth bright line of the light of unknown wavelength. Find the unknown wavelength.
mcqs.why: Formula: the 4th dark fringe lies at y = (7/2) lambda1 L / d because dark fringes sit at lambda/2, 3 lambda/2, 5 lambda/2 and 7 lambda/2 times L/d, while the 5th bright fringe is at y = 5 lambda2 L / d. Substitution: 5 lambda2 = (7/2) x 5.8 x 10^-7, so lambda2 = (7 x 5.8 x 10^-7) / 10. Step: lambda2 = 40.6 x 10^-7 / 10 = 4.06 x 10^-7 m. Result: lambda2 = 4.06 x 10^-7 m. The book's printed 5.2 x 10^-7 m wrongly places the fourth dark fringe at (9/2) lambda L / d.

mcqs.q: When the movable mirror of a Michelson interferometer is moved 0.1 mm. How may dark fringes pass through the reference point, if light of wavelength 580 nm is used?
mcqs.why: Formula: moving the mirror by Delta x changes the path difference by 2 Delta x, and one fringe passes per wavelength of path change, so N = 2 Delta x / lambda. Substitution: N = (2 x 1.0 x 10^-4 m) / (580 x 10^-9 m) = 2.0 x 10^-4 / 5.80 x 10^-7. Step: the quotient is 344.8. Result: about 345 fringes pass the reference point.

mcqs.q: A soap film has a refractive index of 1.40. How thick must the film be, if it appears black, when mercury light of wavelength 546.1 nm falls on it normally?
mcqs.why: Formula: in reflected light one ray suffers a phase change of pi, so the film appears black when 2 mu t = m lambda; the smallest non-zero thickness, m = 1, gives t = lambda / (2 mu). Substitution: t = 546.1 x 10^-9 / (2 x 1.40) = 546.1 x 10^-9 / 2.80. Step: dividing gives 195 x 10^-9 m. Result: t = 1.95 x 10^-7 m.

mcqs.q: A diffraction grating has 5000 lines per centimeter. At what angle does the second order spectrum of the sodium yellow light of wavelength 589 nm occur?
mcqs.why: Formula: grating element d = 1 / N and d sin theta = m lambda, so sin theta = m lambda / d. Substitution: d = 1 / (5.00 x 10^5 per m) = 2.00 x 10^-6 m, and sin theta = (2 x 589 x 10^-9) / (2.00 x 10^-6) = 0.589. Step: theta = sin^-1 (0.589) = 36.1 degrees. Result: theta = 36 degrees approx. The book's printed 0.36 degrees is a decimal misprint, 100 times too small.

mcqs.q: Light is incident normally on a grating which has 250 lines / mm. Find the wavelength of spectral line for which the deviation in second order is 12 degrees.
mcqs.why: Formula: grating element d = 1 / N and d sin theta = m lambda, so lambda = d sin theta / m. Substitution: d = 1 / (2.50 x 10^5 per m) = 4.00 x 10^-6 m, and lambda = (4.00 x 10^-6 x sin 12 degrees) / 2 = (4.00 x 10^-6 x 0.2079) / 2. Step: the numerator is 8.316 x 10^-7, halved to 4.158 x 10^-7 m. Result: lambda = 4158 x 10^-10 m.

mcqs.q: In a certain X-rays diffraction experiment the first order image is observed at an angle of 5 degrees for a crystal plane spacing of 2.8 x 10^-10 m. What is the wavelength of X-rays used?
mcqs.why: Formula: Bragg's law, 2 d sin theta = m lambda, so lambda = 2 d sin theta / m. Substitution: lambda = 2 x 2.8 x 10^-10 x sin 5 degrees / 1 = 5.6 x 10^-10 x 0.0872. Step: multiplying gives 4.88 x 10^-11 m. Result: lambda = 0.49 x 10^-10 m.

mcqs.q: The spacing of one set of crystal planes in NaCl (table salt) is d = 0.282 nm. A monochromatic beam of X-rays produces a Bragg maximum when its glancing angle with these planes is theta = 7 degrees. Assuming that this is a first order maximum (n = 1), find the wavelength of the X-rays.
mcqs.why: Formula: Bragg's law, 2 d sin theta = n lambda, so lambda = 2 d sin theta / n. Substitution: lambda = 2 x 0.282 nm x sin 7 degrees / 1 = 0.564 x 0.1219 nm. Step: multiplying gives 0.0687 nm. Result: lambda = 0.069 nm.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Internal energy and temperature are state functions, so Delta U and Delta T depend only on the initial and final states, while heat and work depend on the path.
  • In an isothermal change of an ideal gas the internal energy remains constant, because internal energy depends only on temperature.
  • Work done on a system, such as shaking a thermos of coffee, is converted into internal energy and raises its temperature.
  • The actual efficiency of a heat engine is eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1, always less than the Carnot efficiency between the same temperatures.
  • Raising the source temperature or lowering the sink temperature increases the efficiency of a Carnot engine, eta = 1 - T2 / T1.
  • A real gas behaves most like an ideal gas at low density, where its molecules are far apart and intermolecular forces are negligible.
  • Entropy measures disorder: cooling a gas decreases its entropy, while shattering, scrambling and diffusion increase entropy.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Multiple Choice Questions

Q: Q1. Assume we can change the equilibrium state of a system via two different processes. Assume that the initial and the final state are the same. Which of the quantities Delta U, Delta Q, Delta W, and Delta T must be the same for the two processes?

Options: (a) only Delta Q and Delta W (b) only Delta U and Delta T (c) only Delta Q and Delta T (d) only Delta U and Delta W

Correct answer: only Delta U and Delta T

Q: Q2. In any process the maximum amount of mechanical energy that can be converted to heat

Options: (a) Depends upon the amount of friction (b) Depends upon the intake and exhaust temperature (c) Depends upon whether kinetic or potential energy is involved (d) Is 100 %

Correct answer: Is 100 %

Q: Q3. In an isothermal change, internal energy

Options: (a) Decreases (b) Increases (c) Becomes zero (d) Remains constant

Correct answer: Remains constant

Q: Q4. A thermos bottle containing hot coffee is vigorously shaken. Consider coffee as the system, then its temperature

Options: (a) Increases (b) Decreases below 0 degrees C (c) Remains the same (d) Decreases

Correct answer: Increases

Q: Q5. Maximum work can be obtained in the process called

Options: (a) Cyclic (b) Isothermal (c) Adiabatic (d) Isochoric

Correct answer: Isothermal

Q: Q6. A heat engine takes in 800 J of heat at 1000 K and exhausts 600 J of heat at 400 K. What is the actual efficiency of this engine?

Options: (a) 25% (b) 40% (c) 50% (d) 75%

Correct answer: 25%

Q: Q7. If the temperature of the heat source is increased, the efficiency of a Carnot's engine

Options: (a) Increases (b) Decreases (c) Remains constant (d) First increases and then becomes constant

Correct answer: Increases

Q: Q8. Triple point of water is

Options: (a) 273.16 degrees F (b) 372.16 K (c) 273.16 degrees F (d) 273.16 K

Correct answer: 273.16 K

Q: Q9. A real gas can be approximated to an ideal gas at

Options: (a) Low density (b) High pressure (c) High density (d) Low temperature

Correct answer: Low density

Q: Q10. If the volume of the gas is to be increased by 4 times, then

Options: (a) Temperature and pressure must be double (b) At constant P the temperature must be increased by four times (c) At constant T the pressure must be increased by four times (d) It cannot be increased

Correct answer: At constant P the temperature must be increased by four times

Q: Q11. In which of the systems listed below is the entropy decreasing?

Options: (a) A gas is cooled. (b) A plate is shattered. (c) An egg is scrambled. (d) A drop of dye diffuses in a cup of water.

Correct answer: A gas is cooled.

Q: Q12. If the temperature of source and sink of a carnot engine having efficiency eta are each decreased by 100K, then the efficiency eta'

Options: (a) remain constant (b) become 1. (c) increases. (d) decreases

Correct answer: increases.

mcqs.q: Assume we can change the equilibrium state of a system via two different processes. Assume that the initial and the final state are the same. Which of the quantities Delta U, Delta Q, Delta W, and Delta T must be the same for the two processes?
options: only Delta Q and Delta W
only Delta U and Delta T
only Delta Q and Delta T
only Delta U and Delta W
mcqs.why: Internal energy and temperature are state functions fixed by the initial and final states, so Delta U and Delta T are the same for both processes, while heat and work depend on the path taken.

mcqs.q: In any process the maximum amount of mechanical energy that can be converted to heat
options: Depends upon the amount of friction
Depends upon the intake and exhaust temperature
Depends upon whether kinetic or potential energy is involved
mcqs.why: Mechanical energy such as kinetic or potential energy can be dissipated completely, for example by friction, so up to 100 percent of it can be converted into heat; the reverse conversion is the one that is limited.

mcqs.q: In an isothermal change, internal energy
mcqs.why: For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on temperature, so in an isothermal change, where the temperature does not change, the internal energy remains constant and all the heat supplied becomes work.

mcqs.q: A thermos bottle containing hot coffee is vigorously shaken. Consider coffee as the system, then its temperature
mcqs.why: Shaking does work on the coffee, and this work is converted into internal energy of the coffee as its molecules move faster, so the temperature of the coffee increases.

mcqs.q: A heat engine takes in 800 J of heat at 1000 K and exhausts 600 J of heat at 400 K. What is the actual efficiency of this engine?
mcqs.why: Formula: efficiency eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1. Substitution: eta = (800 - 600) / 800 = 200 / 800. Step: the quotient is 0.25. Result: the actual efficiency is 25 percent, well below the Carnot value for these temperatures.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of the heat source is increased, the efficiency of a Carnot's engine
options: First increases and then becomes constant
mcqs.why: Formula: Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1. Substitution: raising the source temperature T1 makes the ratio T2 / T1 smaller. Step: one minus a smaller ratio is a larger number. Result: the efficiency of a Carnot engine increases when the source temperature is increased.

mcqs.q: A real gas can be approximated to an ideal gas at
mcqs.why: An ideal gas is a model in which the molecules exert no forces on each other except in collisions; a real gas approaches this behaviour when its density is low, so the molecules are far apart and their interactions are negligible.

mcqs.q: If the volume of the gas is to be increased by 4 times, then
options: Temperature and pressure must be double
At constant P the temperature must be increased by four times
At constant T the pressure must be increased by four times
mcqs.why: Formula: at constant pressure the ideal gas law gives V proportional to T. Substitution: to make the volume four times, V2 / V1 = 4 = T2 / T1. Step: the absolute temperature must also become four times. Result: at constant pressure the temperature must be increased by four times.

mcqs.q: In which of the systems listed below is the entropy decreasing?
options: A drop of dye diffuses in a cup of water.
mcqs.why: Cooling a gas reduces the random motion and disorder of its molecules, so its entropy decreases; shattering, scrambling and diffusion all increase disorder and therefore increase entropy.

mcqs.q: If the temperature of source and sink of a carnot engine having efficiency eta are each decreased by 100K, then the efficiency eta'
mcqs.why: Formula: eta = 1 - T2 / T1 and eta' = 1 - (T2 - 100) / (T1 - 100). Substitution: subtracting the same 100 K from both temperatures makes the ratio of sink to source temperature smaller than T2 / T1. Step: one minus a smaller ratio is larger. Result: the efficiency increases when both temperatures are decreased by 100 K.

lessons.title: Conceptual Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Thermal equilibrium requires equal temperatures and no net heat flow, so the earth at about 300 K is not in equilibrium with the sun at about 6000 K.
  • On heating, a hole in a block expands by the same fraction as every other length, exactly like a photographic enlargement of the block.
  • At the same temperature lighter molecules move faster, with rms speed proportional to 1 / sqrt(molar mass), so hydrogen leaks from a cylinder about four times faster than oxygen.
  • An air conditioner inside a closed room warms the room, because it rejects Q2 + W of heat into the room while removing only Q2 from it.
  • Air escaping rapidly from a tube cools because the near-adiabatic expansion does external work at the expense of the air's internal energy.
  • The first law only conserves energy; it cannot state the direction of a process or how much heat can be converted into work, which is the role of the second law.
  • The specific heat of a gas depends on the process: zero for an adiabatic change, infinite for an isothermal change, and possibly negative.
  • No engine between 500 K and 300 K can exceed the Carnot efficiency of 40 percent, so a claimed 45 percent efficiency violates the second law.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Conceptual Questions

Q: Q1. Why is the earth not in thermal equilibrium with the sun?

Ans: Thermal equilibrium requires two bodies to be at the same temperature with no net flow of heat between them. The surface of the sun is at about 6000 K while the earth is at about 300 K, so the temperatures are very different. The earth continuously receives a large amount of radiant energy from the sun and re-radiates energy into cold space, so there is a one-way net flow of heat from the sun to the earth. Because the temperatures differ greatly and heat keeps flowing, the earth and the sun are not in thermal equilibrium.

Q: Q2. When a block with a hole in it is heated, why does not the material around the hole expand into the hole and make it small?

Ans: On heating, every linear dimension of a body increases in the same proportion, exactly as in a photographic enlargement of the block. The material around the hole expands, but it expands outwards in all directions, so the circumference and diameter of the hole increase by the same fraction as any other length in the block. Another way to see it: imagine the hole filled with a plug of the same material; on heating, the plug would expand, and the hole must grow to exactly the size of the expanded plug. Hence the hole becomes bigger, not smaller.

Q: Q3. A thermometer is placed in direct sunlight. Will it read the temperature of the air, or of the sun, or of some thing else?

Ans: It reads neither the air temperature nor the temperature of the sun. It reads its own temperature. The bulb absorbs radiant energy from the sun and warms up, while at the same time it loses heat to the surrounding air. It settles at the temperature where the absorbed radiation balances the heat lost, which is higher than the true air temperature. That is why, for measuring air temperature, a thermometer is always kept in the shade. It certainly cannot read the sun's temperature of about 6000 K, since it is not in contact or equilibrium with the sun.

Q: Q4. The pressure in a gas cylinder containing hydrogen will leak more quickly than if it is containing oxygen. Why?

Ans: At the same temperature, the average kinetic energy of all gas molecules is the same, so the lighter hydrogen molecules (molar mass 2) move much faster than the heavier oxygen molecules (molar mass 32); the rms speed varies as 1 / sqrt(molar mass), making hydrogen molecules about four times faster. The faster, smaller hydrogen molecules therefore escape (effuse) through any tiny leak, valve gap or pore in the cylinder walls much more rapidly than oxygen molecules, so the pressure of the hydrogen cylinder falls more quickly.

Q: Q5. What happens to the temperature of a room in which an air conditioner is left running on a table in the middle of the room?

Ans: The room slowly becomes warmer, not cooler. An air conditioner takes heat Q2 from its front side but rejects a larger amount of heat Q1 = Q2 + W to its back side, where W is the electrical work consumed by its motor and compressor. When the unit sits inside the room, both the cooled air and the rejected heat remain in the same room, so the net effect is that all the electrical energy consumed is added to the room as heat. The temperature of the room therefore rises gradually.

Q: Q6. Why does the pressure of the air in automobile tyre increases if the automobile is driven for a while?

Ans: While the automobile is driven, the tyre is repeatedly compressed and flexed at the point of contact with the road, and there is friction between the tyre and the road. This work done on the tyre is converted into heat, which warms the air enclosed in the tyre. The volume of the tyre remains almost constant, so by the pressure law (P proportional to T at constant volume) the rise in temperature of the enclosed air produces a rise in its pressure.

Q: Q7. On removing the valve, the air escaping from a cycle tube cool. Why?

Ans: The air inside the tube is at high pressure. When the valve is removed, this air expands rapidly into the atmosphere. The expansion is so quick that there is no time for heat to flow in from outside, so it is nearly adiabatic. In expanding, the air does external work in pushing back the surrounding atmosphere, and this work is done at the expense of its own internal energy. A fall in internal energy means a fall in temperature, so the escaping air feels cool.

Q: Q8. Write the limitations of first law of thermodynamics.

Ans: The first law is only a statement of conservation of energy, and it has several limitations: (1) it does not tell us the direction in which a process can take place; for example, it allows heat to flow from a cold body to a hot body as long as energy is conserved, which never happens by itself. (2) It does not tell us how much of the heat supplied can be converted into work; it permits a perfectly efficient engine, which is impossible in practice. (3) It does not tell us whether a process is feasible at all, or the conditions (temperature, pressure) under which it will occur. These questions are answered by the second law of thermodynamics.

Q: Q9. Is it possible, according to the second law of thermodynamics, to construct an heat engine that is free from thermal pollution?

Ans: No. According to the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law, no cyclic heat engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work; a part of the heat Q2 must always be rejected to the cold sink. This rejected heat, discharged into rivers, lakes or the atmosphere, is exactly what causes thermal pollution. The efficiency eta = 1 - Q2/Q1 can approach 1 only if Q2 approaches zero, which the second law forbids. Thermal pollution can be reduced by building more efficient engines, but it can never be eliminated completely.

Q: Q10. Can specific heat of a gas be zero or infinity? Can specific heat be negative?

Ans: Yes, all three are possible, because the specific heat of a gas depends on the process, not only on the gas. Specific heat c = Delta Q / (m Delta T). In an adiabatic change Delta Q = 0 while Delta T is not zero, so c = 0. In an isothermal change Delta T = 0 while heat is absorbed or given out, so c becomes infinite. The specific heat is negative when the gas gives out heat (Delta Q negative) yet its temperature rises (Delta T positive), or absorbs heat while its temperature falls; this happens, for example, when a gas is compressed strongly while losing a smaller amount of heat, so that work done on it raises its temperature. Thus a gas can have any specific heat value between minus infinity and plus infinity depending on the process.

Q: Q11. An inventor claims to have developed an heat engine, working between 27 degrees C and 227 degrees C having an efficiency of 45 %. Is the claim valid? Why?

Ans: Given: source temperature T1 = 227 degrees C = 500 K, sink temperature T2 = 27 degrees C = 300 K
Formula: maximum possible efficiency is the Carnot efficiency, eta(max) = 1 - T2 / T1
Substitution: eta(max) = 1 - 300 / 500 = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 = 40%
Answer: No, the claim is not valid. No engine working between these two temperatures can exceed the Carnot efficiency of 40%, and a real engine always has an even lower efficiency because of friction and other losses. A claimed efficiency of 45% would violate the second law of thermodynamics (Carnot's theorem).

mcqs.q: The earth is not in thermal equilibrium with the sun because:
options: The earth does not receive any heat from the sun
Their temperatures are very different, about 300 K and 6000 K, and heat flows continuously one way from the sun to the earth
The earth rotates too fast for equilibrium
There is no material medium between them
mcqs.why: Thermal equilibrium needs equal temperatures and no net heat flow. The sun's surface is about 6000 K and the earth about 300 K, and the earth continually receives radiant energy from the sun and re-radiates it into cold space, so a one-way net flow persists.

mcqs.q: When a block with a hole in it is heated, the hole becomes larger because:
options: The material melts and flows away from the hole
The hole shrinks but the block grows faster
Every linear dimension grows in the same proportion, like a photographic enlargement, so the hole's diameter grows by the same fraction as any other length
Air pressure inside the hole increases
mcqs.why: On heating, all lengths in the block increase by the same fraction. Imagining the hole filled with a plug of the same material, the plug would expand on heating, and the hole must grow to exactly the size of the expanded plug.

mcqs.q: Hydrogen leaks from a gas cylinder faster than oxygen at the same temperature because:
options: Hydrogen molecules are larger than oxygen molecules
Hydrogen is stored at a higher pressure
Oxygen molecules move faster than hydrogen molecules
The lighter hydrogen molecules move about four times faster, since rms speed varies as 1 / sqrt(molar mass), and escape through tiny leaks more rapidly
mcqs.why: At the same temperature all molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so speed varies inversely with the square root of molar mass. With molar masses 2 and 32, hydrogen molecules move about four times faster than oxygen molecules and effuse through leaks much more quickly.

mcqs.q: An air conditioner running on a table in the middle of a closed room makes the room:
options: Cooler, because it blows out cold air
Warmer, because it rejects Q2 + W of heat into the same room while removing only Q2, so all its electrical energy ends up as heat in the room
Neither warmer nor cooler, because the effects cancel exactly
Cooler at first and then steady
mcqs.why: The unit takes heat Q2 from its front but rejects the larger amount Q1 = Q2 + W at its back, where W is the electrical work consumed. With both sides inside one room, the net effect is that all the electrical energy consumed is added to the room as heat.

mcqs.q: The pressure of air in a car tyre rises after driving for a while because:
options: More air is pumped into the tyre by the motion
The tyre expands and squeezes the air
Flexing of the tyre and friction with the road do work that heats the enclosed air, and at almost constant volume pressure rises in proportion to temperature
The road heats the air directly through the valve
mcqs.why: While driving, the tyre is repeatedly compressed and flexed and rubs against the road; this work becomes heat that warms the enclosed air. The volume stays almost constant, so by the pressure law, P proportional to T, the pressure rises with the temperature.

mcqs.q: Air escaping from a cycle tube feels cool because:
options: The air was stored in the shade
It expands rapidly and almost adiabatically, doing external work at the expense of its own internal energy, so its temperature falls
It loses its moisture while escaping
Friction with the valve heats the tube instead
mcqs.why: The expansion on removing the valve is so quick that no heat can flow in, making it nearly adiabatic. The air does work pushing back the atmosphere, paid for from its internal energy, and a fall in internal energy means a fall in temperature.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a limitation of the first law of thermodynamics?
options: It applies only to ideal gases
It says nothing about the direction of a process or about how much of the heat supplied can be converted into work
It cannot be used for cyclic processes
mcqs.why: The first law is only energy conservation: it would allow heat to flow from cold to hot and would permit a perfectly efficient engine, as long as energy balanced. The direction of processes, their feasibility and the fraction of heat convertible into work are settled by the second law.

mcqs.q: A heat engine completely free of thermal pollution is impossible because:
options: Engines are always built with some friction
The second law requires part of the absorbed heat Q2 to be rejected to the cold sink, and this rejected heat is the thermal pollution
The sink temperature is too high
mcqs.why: By the Kelvin-Planck statement no cyclic engine can convert all the absorbed heat into work; some heat Q2 must always be rejected to the sink, and that discharged heat causes thermal pollution. Better efficiency can reduce it but never eliminate it.

mcqs.q: The specific heat of a gas can be zero, infinite or even negative because:
options: The mass of the gas keeps changing
Specific heat depends on the process: it is zero in an adiabatic change, infinite in an isothermal change, and negative when the gas loses heat yet its temperature rises
Thermometers cannot measure gas temperatures exactly
Gases have no definite specific heat at any time
mcqs.why: With c = Delta Q / (m Delta T), an adiabatic change has Delta Q = 0 with a temperature change, giving c = 0, while an isothermal change has Delta T = 0 with heat exchanged, giving infinite c. If a strongly compressed gas loses a smaller amount of heat, it gives out heat while its temperature rises, making c negative.

mcqs.q: An inventor claims an engine working between 27 degrees C and 227 degrees C with 45 percent efficiency. The claim is:
options: Valid, because modern materials reduce friction enough
Valid, because 45 percent is less than 100 percent
Invalid, because the Carnot limit for these temperatures is 40 percent and no engine between them can exceed it
Invalid, because engines cannot work above 200 degrees C
mcqs.why: Formula: Carnot efficiency eta(max) = 1 - T2 / T1 with T1 = 500 K and T2 = 300 K. Substitution: eta(max) = 1 - 300 / 500 = 0.40. Step: the maximum possible efficiency is 40 percent, and a real engine is lower still. Result: a claim of 45 percent violates the second law and is not valid.

lessons.title: Comprehensive Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A system may be open, closed or isolated; state variables such as P, V, T and U depend only on the state, while heat and work depend on the path.
  • The first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, is energy conservation applied to thermal processes and rules out a perpetual motion machine of the first kind.
  • For one mole of an ideal gas Cp - Cv = R, because at constant pressure part of the heat does expansion work P Delta V = R Delta T.
  • A reversible process is retraced through the same states with system and surroundings restored; all natural processes, such as free expansion and friction, are irreversible.
  • A heat engine absorbs Q1 from a hot source, does work W = Q1 - Q2 and rejects Q2 to a cold sink, with efficiency eta = 1 - Q2 / Q1; the Kelvin-Planck statement forbids converting all the heat from one reservoir into work in a cycle, and the Clausius statement forbids heat flowing by itself from cold to hot.
  • Carnot's theorem: no engine between two temperatures beats a reversible engine between them, and all reversible engines there have efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1.
  • A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse, with coefficient of performance COP = Q2 / W, which for a Carnot refrigerator equals T2 / (T1 - T2).
  • Entropy is a state function measuring disorder, Delta S = Delta Q / T for reversible heating, and the total entropy of the universe never decreases.

Solved Exercises

Exercise - Comprehensive Questions

Q: Q1. Explain, briefly, the following terms used in thermodynamics: System, Surroundings, Boundary and State variables.

Ans: System: the part of the universe chosen for study, for example the gas enclosed in a cylinder. A system may be open (exchanges matter and energy), closed (exchanges energy only) or isolated (exchanges neither). Surroundings: everything outside the system that can exchange energy or matter with it, for example the air and the cylinder walls around the gas. Boundary: the real or imaginary surface that separates the system from its surroundings; it may be fixed or movable (like a piston), and conducting (diathermic) or insulating (adiabatic). State variables: the measurable quantities that describe the equilibrium state of the system, such as pressure P, volume V, temperature T and internal energy U. Their values depend only on the present state of the system, not on the path by which that state was reached; heat and work are not state variables because they depend on the path.

Q: Q2. Distinguish among the three forms of energy: work; heat and internal energy.

Ans: Internal energy is the energy stored inside a system: the sum of the kinetic energies of the random motion of its molecules and the potential energies due to the forces between them. It is a property of the system and a state function; for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature. Heat and work are not stored in a system; they are forms of energy in transit across the boundary. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference between the system and its surroundings, and it is associated with the disordered random motion of molecules. Work is energy transferred by a macroscopic force acting through a displacement, for example the work P Delta V done by an expanding gas on a piston, and it is associated with ordered motion. Once transferred, both heat and work become part of the internal energy of the receiving system, and the three are linked by the first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W.

Q: Q3. State and explain the first law of thermodynamics.

Ans: Statement: when a quantity of heat Delta Q is supplied to a system, a part of it increases the internal energy of the system by Delta U and the remaining part is used in doing external work Delta W by the system. That is, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W. Explanation: this law is the principle of conservation of energy applied to thermal processes: energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only converted from one form to another. Sign convention: heat supplied to the system is positive, heat given out is negative; work done by the system is positive, work done on the system is negative; an increase in internal energy is positive. Special cases: in an isothermal change of an ideal gas Delta U = 0, so Delta Q = Delta W; in an adiabatic change Delta Q = 0, so Delta W = -Delta U, meaning work is done at the expense of internal energy; in an isochoric change Delta W = 0, so all the heat goes into internal energy. The law also shows that a perpetual motion machine of the first kind (which produces work without energy input) is impossible.

Q: Q4. Define the molar heat capacities Cp and Cv for a gas. Show that, for a mole of an ideal gas, Cp - Cv = R

Ans: Molar heat capacity at constant volume, Cv, is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a gas by 1 K while its volume is kept constant. Molar heat capacity at constant pressure, Cp, is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of one mole of a gas by 1 K while its pressure is kept constant. Cp is greater than Cv because at constant pressure part of the heat is used in doing expansion work. Proof for one mole: at constant volume no work is done, so all the heat increases internal energy: Cv = Delta U / Delta T, that is, Delta U = Cv Delta T. At constant pressure, Delta Q = Delta U + P Delta V, so Cp Delta T = Cv Delta T + P Delta V. For one mole of an ideal gas, P V = R T, so for a temperature rise Delta T at constant pressure, P Delta V = R Delta T. Substituting: Cp Delta T = Cv Delta T + R Delta T. Dividing by Delta T gives Cp - Cv = R, where R = 8.314 J mole^-1 K^-1 is the universal gas constant.

Q: Q5. Explain with examples reversible and irreversible processes.

Ans: A reversible process is one that can be retraced in the opposite direction by an infinitesimal change in the conditions, passing back through exactly the same states, so that both the system and the surroundings are restored to their original state with no other change. It must be carried out extremely slowly (quasi-statically) and without friction or heat loss. Examples: the very slow isothermal expansion or compression of a gas in a cylinder with a frictionless piston, the Carnot cycle, and the slow melting or freezing of ice at 0 degrees C. An irreversible process cannot be retraced in this way; reversing the conditions does not restore the system and surroundings exactly. All natural processes are irreversible. Examples: free expansion of a gas into a vacuum, conduction of heat from a hot body to a cold body, work done against friction, burning of fuel, and Joule heating of a resistor. Irreversibility is caused by friction, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, and similar dissipative effects, and in every irreversible process the entropy of the universe increases.

Q: Q6. What is meant by a heat engine? What is its main purpose? How is its efficiency defined?

Ans: A heat engine is a device that converts heat energy into mechanical work by operating in a cycle. Diagram (in words): at the top is a box labelled hot reservoir (source) at temperature T1; an arrow labelled Q1 (heat absorbed) points from it down into a circle in the centre labelled engine. From the circle, an arrow to the right is labelled W (work output). A second arrow points from the circle down into a box labelled cold reservoir (sink) at temperature T2, and this arrow is labelled Q2 (heat rejected). Main purpose: to obtain useful mechanical work from heat, as in steam engines, petrol and diesel engines. Working: in each cycle the working substance absorbs heat Q1 from the source, converts a part of it into work W, and rejects the remaining heat Q2 to the sink, returning to its initial state. Efficiency: the thermal efficiency is defined as the ratio of the useful work obtained to the heat taken from the source, eta = W / Q1 = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1 = 1 - Q2 / Q1. It is always less than 1 (100%) because Q2 can never be zero.

Q: Q7. State the second law of thermodynamics in its alternative forms. Discuss the assertions of the first and second laws about heat and work energies.

Ans: Kelvin-Planck statement: it is impossible to construct an engine working in a cycle whose sole effect is to take heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work; some heat must always be rejected to a cold sink. Clausius statement: it is impossible for heat to flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body without the performance of external work; this is why a refrigerator needs a motor. The two statements are equivalent: violating one would violate the other. Discussion: the first law asserts that heat and work are mutually convertible forms of energy and that the total energy remains constant; it treats heat and work as equivalent and puts no limit on conversion either way. The second law asserts that the two conversions are not equally easy: work can be converted completely into heat (for example by friction), but heat cannot be converted completely into work in a cycle. Heat is a lower, more disordered form of energy, and every conversion of heat into work involves a degradation of energy. The first law speaks of the quantity of energy, the second law of its quality and of the direction in which processes can occur.

Q: Q8. What were the basic questions that led Carnot to invent Carnot engine?

Ans: In Carnot's time the steam engine was being widely used, but its efficiency was very low and nobody knew how it could be improved or what its limit was. The basic questions Carnot asked were: (1) Can the efficiency of a heat engine be increased without limit by improving its design and materials? (2) What is the maximum fraction of the heat supplied that can possibly be converted into work? (3) Does the maximum efficiency depend on the working substance used (steam, air or any other), or only on the temperatures between which the engine works? (4) What conditions must an engine satisfy to reach this maximum? To answer these questions he imagined an ideal, perfectly reversible engine working in a cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, the Carnot engine. He showed that its efficiency, eta = 1 - T2 / T1, depends only on the temperatures of the source and the sink, and that no real engine working between the same temperatures can exceed it.

Q: Q9. State Carnot Theorem about the characteristics of a Carnot engine.

Ans: Carnot's theorem has two parts. (1) No heat engine working between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a reversible (Carnot) engine working between the same two temperatures. (2) All reversible engines working between the same two temperatures have exactly the same efficiency, whatever the working substance and whatever the details of their construction. Characteristics that follow: the efficiency of a Carnot engine is eta = 1 - T2 / T1, where T1 is the source temperature and T2 the sink temperature on the Kelvin scale. It depends only on these two temperatures: it increases if T1 is raised or T2 is lowered, and it would become 100% only if T2 were 0 K, which is unattainable. The Carnot engine is an ideal standard, not a practical machine, because its processes must be infinitely slow and completely free of friction; it sets the upper limit against which all real engines (steam, petrol, diesel) are judged.

Q: Q10. What do you mean by a refrigerator? How does it function? Derive an expression for the Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator.

Ans: A refrigerator is a device that transfers heat from a cold body to a hot body by doing external work on the working substance; it is a heat engine run in reverse, and it keeps the inside of a cabinet cold. Functioning: a volatile liquid (refrigerant) evaporates in coils inside the cabinet and absorbs its latent heat Q2 from the contents, cooling them. The vapour is then compressed by an electrically driven compressor, which does work W on it and raises its temperature above that of the room. The hot vapour passes through condenser coils outside the cabinet, where it rejects heat Q1 = Q2 + W to the surroundings and liquefies. The liquid then passes through an expansion valve, cools sharply, and returns to the evaporator coils to repeat the cycle. Coefficient of performance: the COP measures the effect obtained per unit work input, COP = (heat removed from the cold space) / (work input) = Q2 / W. Since W = Q1 - Q2, COP = Q2 / (Q1 - Q2). For a reversible (Carnot) refrigerator, Q1 / Q2 = T1 / T2, so COP = T2 / (T1 - T2), where T2 is the temperature of the cold space and T1 that of the surroundings. Unlike efficiency, COP is greater than 1, typically between 2 and 5.

Q: Q11. Explain the concept of entropy. Mention its major properties. How is the second law of thermodynamics expressed in terms of entropy?

Ans: Entropy is a state function that measures the disorder (randomness) of a system and the unavailability of its energy for doing useful work. When a system absorbs a small quantity of heat Delta Q reversibly at absolute temperature T, its entropy changes by Delta S = Delta Q / T, measured in J K^-1. Melting, evaporation and expansion increase entropy because the molecules become more disordered; cooling and compression decrease it. Major properties: (1) entropy is a state function, depending only on the initial and final states, not on the path; (2) it is an extensive quantity, proportional to the amount of matter; (3) in a reversible adiabatic process the entropy of the system stays constant; (4) in any irreversible process the entropy of the system plus surroundings increases; (5) the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0 K is zero. Second law in terms of entropy: for every process taking place in the universe, the total entropy either increases (irreversible process) or, in the ideal reversible limit, remains constant; it never decreases. In symbols, Delta S(universe) is greater than or equal to 0. This is why heat flows from hot to cold and why energy continually becomes less available for work, a process called degradation of energy.

mcqs.q: A closed thermodynamic system is one that:
options: Exchanges both matter and energy with its surroundings
Exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings
mcqs.why: A system is the part of the universe chosen for study. An open system exchanges matter and energy, a closed system exchanges energy only, and an isolated system exchanges neither; the boundary separating system from surroundings may be fixed or movable, conducting or insulating.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a state variable of a gas?
mcqs.why: State variables such as pressure, volume, temperature and internal energy depend only on the present equilibrium state, not on the path used to reach it. Heat and work are path-dependent quantities of energy in transit, so they are not state variables.

mcqs.q: Internal energy differs from heat and work in that internal energy:
options: Is energy in transit across a boundary
Is stored in the system as molecular kinetic and potential energy and is a state function
Exists only while a process is taking place
Is always equal to the work done
mcqs.why: Internal energy is the sum of the kinetic energies of random molecular motion and the potential energies of intermolecular forces, stored inside the system; for an ideal gas it depends only on temperature. Heat and work are not stored; they are forms of energy crossing the boundary, heat due to a temperature difference and work due to a macroscopic force.

mcqs.q: In an adiabatic change of a system, the first law gives:
options: Delta W = -Delta U, so work is done at the expense of internal energy
mcqs.why: The first law is Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W. In an adiabatic change Delta Q = 0, so Delta W = -Delta U: expansion work is paid for by a fall in internal energy. In an isothermal change of an ideal gas Delta U = 0 and Delta Q = Delta W, and in an isochoric change Delta W = 0.

mcqs.q: Cp is greater than Cv for a gas because at constant pressure:
options: No work is done by the gas
Part of the heat supplied is used in doing expansion work in addition to raising the internal energy
The gas loses heat to the surroundings
The temperature rise is smaller for the same heat
mcqs.why: At constant volume all the heat raises internal energy, giving Cv. At constant pressure the gas expands and does work P Delta V as well, so more heat is needed for the same temperature rise, which is why Cp exceeds Cv and why Cp - Cv = R for one mole of an ideal gas.

mcqs.q: For one mole of an ideal gas heated at constant pressure through Delta T, the expansion work P Delta V equals:
mcqs.why: From P V = R T for one mole, a temperature rise Delta T at constant pressure gives P Delta V = R Delta T. Substituting this in Cp Delta T = Cv Delta T + P Delta V and dividing by Delta T yields the relation Cp - Cv = R, with R = 8.314 J per mole per kelvin.

mcqs.q: A reversible process must be carried out:
options: Very quickly, before heat can escape
Extremely slowly and without friction, so it can be retraced through exactly the same states, restoring both system and surroundings
mcqs.why: A reversible process can be reversed by an infinitesimal change of conditions, passing back through the same states with system and surroundings fully restored. Examples are the very slow isothermal compression of a gas with a frictionless piston and the slow melting of ice at 0 degrees C; all natural processes are irreversible.

mcqs.q: Which of the following processes is irreversible?
options: The infinitely slow expansion of a gas with a frictionless piston
Free expansion of a gas into a vacuum
Slow freezing of water at 0 degrees C
mcqs.why: Free expansion cannot be retraced by reversing the conditions so as to restore system and surroundings exactly; the same holds for heat conduction across a finite temperature difference, friction and burning of fuel. Every irreversible process increases the entropy of the universe.

mcqs.q: The efficiency of a heat engine is defined as:
mcqs.why: In each cycle the engine absorbs Q1 from the hot source, does work W = Q1 - Q2 and rejects Q2 to the cold sink. Efficiency is the useful work obtained divided by the heat taken from the source, eta = W / Q1 = 1 - Q2 / Q1, and it is always less than 1 because Q2 can never be zero.

mcqs.q: The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law says it is impossible to build a cyclic engine whose sole effect is to:
options: Take heat from a single reservoir and convert it completely into work
Reject any heat to a cold sink
Work between two reservoirs at different temperatures
mcqs.why: Kelvin-Planck: no engine working in a cycle can convert all the heat from one reservoir into work; some heat must always be rejected to a cold sink. Work, by contrast, can be converted completely into heat, for example by friction, which shows the two conversions are not equally easy.

mcqs.q: The Clausius statement of the second law implies that a refrigerator:
options: Can move heat from cold to hot without any work input
Needs external work, supplied by a motor, to transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter one
Violates the first law of thermodynamics
Must reject heat to a colder body
mcqs.why: Clausius: heat cannot flow by itself from a colder body to a hotter body without the performance of external work. That is exactly why a refrigerator needs a motor-driven compressor, and the Kelvin-Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent forms of the same law.

mcqs.q: Carnot designed his ideal engine mainly to answer the question:
options: Which fuel gives the most heat
Whether the maximum efficiency of a heat engine depends on the working substance or only on the temperatures of source and sink
How to build a faster steam engine
mcqs.why: Steam engine efficiency in Carnot's time was very low and its limit was unknown. Carnot asked whether efficiency could rise without limit, what maximum fraction of heat could become work, and whether that maximum depended on the working substance; his reversible engine showed it depends only on the two temperatures.

mcqs.q: According to Carnot's theorem, all reversible engines working between the same two temperatures:
options: Have efficiencies that depend on their working substance
Are less efficient than any real engine between those temperatures
Have exactly the same efficiency, eta = 1 - T2 / T1, whatever the working substance
mcqs.why: Carnot's theorem states that no engine between two given temperatures can beat a reversible engine between them, and that all reversible engines between the same temperatures share the one efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1. It would reach 100 percent only at a sink temperature of 0 K, which is unattainable.

mcqs.q: The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator is defined as:
options: The heat removed from the cold space divided by the work input, Q2 / W
The efficiency of the same machine run as an engine
mcqs.why: A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: the refrigerant absorbs Q2 inside the cabinet, the compressor does work W on it, and it rejects Q1 = Q2 + W outside. The COP measures the effect per unit work, COP = Q2 / W = Q2 / (Q1 - Q2), and for a Carnot refrigerator COP = T2 / (T1 - T2); unlike efficiency it is greater than 1, typically 2 to 5.

mcqs.q: Expressed in terms of entropy, the second law of thermodynamics states that:
options: The entropy of the universe decreases in every natural process
The total entropy of the universe never decreases: it increases in irreversible processes and stays constant only in the reversible limit
Entropy is constant in all processes
Entropy depends on the path taken between two states
mcqs.why: Entropy, defined by Delta S = Delta Q / T for a reversible absorption of heat, is a state function measuring disorder. In any irreversible process the entropy of system plus surroundings increases, and it can at best stay constant in a reversible process, which is why heat flows from hot to cold and energy is continually degraded.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems and Assignments
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The first law in the form Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W gives the change in internal energy from the heat supplied and the work done by the system.
  • Engine efficiency is eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1, and the work per cycle is W = Q1 - Q2.
  • For melting at a fixed temperature the entropy change is Delta S = m L / T, with the temperature taken in kelvin.
  • Gravitational potential energy lost by falling water can appear as heat, m g h = m c Delta T, giving Delta T = g h / c.
  • The Carnot efficiency between the steam point (373 K) and the ice point (273 K) is 26.8 percent.
  • The least work to freeze water with a refrigerator is set by the Carnot refrigerator, W = Q2 (T1 - T2) / T2.
  • When temperature changes during heating, the entropy change is Delta S = m c ln (T2 / T1), not m c Delta T / T.
  • The number of moles in a gas sample follows from the ideal gas equation, n = P V / (R T), with the volume converted to cubic metres.

Solved Exercises

Assignment 1

Q: Q1. An ideal gas absorbs 5.00 x 10^3 J of energy while doing 2.00 x 10^3 J of work on the environment during a constant pressure process. (a) Compute the change in the internal energy of the gas. (b) If the internal energy now drops by 4.50 x 10^3 J and 7.50 x 10^3 J is expelled from the system, find the change in volume, assuming a constant pressure process at 1.01x10^5 Pa.

Ans: Given: (a) heat absorbed Delta Q = +5.00 x 10^3 J, work done by the gas Delta W = +2.00 x 10^3 J
Formula: first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, so Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W
Substitution: Delta U = 5.00 x 10^3 J - 2.00 x 10^3 J = 3.00 x 10^3 J
Answer (a): Delta U = 3.00 x 10^3 J
Given: (b) Delta U = -4.50 x 10^3 J (internal energy drops), Delta Q = -7.50 x 10^3 J (heat expelled), pressure P = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa
Formula: Delta W = Delta Q - Delta U, and at constant pressure Delta W = P Delta V, so Delta V = Delta W / P
Substitution: Delta W = -7.50 x 10^3 - (-4.50 x 10^3) = -3.00 x 10^3 J (the negative sign means work is done on the gas)
Delta V = -3.00 x 10^3 / 1.01 x 10^5 = -2.97 x 10^-2 m^3
Answer (b): Delta V = -2.97 x 10^-2 m^3 (the volume decreases)
Note: The book's printed answer (3.00 x 10^5 J) is incorrect because 5.00 x 10^3 J - 2.00 x 10^3 J = 3.00 x 10^3 J; the printed exponent 5 should be 3.

Assignment 2

Q: Q1. During one cycle, an engine extracts 2.00 x 10^3 J of energy from a hot reservoir and transfers 1.50 x 10^3 J to a cold reservoir. (a) Find the thermal efficiency of the engine. (b) How much work does this engine do in one cycle? (c) What average power does the engine generate if it goes through four cycles in 2.50 s?

Ans: Given: heat taken from hot reservoir Q1 = 2.00 x 10^3 J, heat rejected to cold reservoir Q2 = 1.50 x 10^3 J
Formula: (a) efficiency eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1
Substitution: eta = (2.00 x 10^3 - 1.50 x 10^3) / 2.00 x 10^3 = 500 / 2000 = 0.250
Answer (a): eta = 0.250, or 25.0%
Formula: (b) work per cycle W = Q1 - Q2
Substitution: W = 2.00 x 10^3 - 1.50 x 10^3 = 5.00 x 10^2 J
Answer (b): W = 5.00 x 10^2 J
Formula: (c) average power = total work / time = (4 x W) / t
Substitution: total work in 4 cycles = 4 x 500 J = 2000 J, so P = 2000 J / 2.50 s = 800 W
Answer (c): P = 8.00 x 10^2 W

Assignment 3

Q: Q1. (a) Find the change in entropy of 3.00 x 10^2 g of lead when it melts at 327 degrees C. Lead has a latent heat of fusion of 2.45 x 10^4 J/kg. (b) Suppose the same amount of energy is used to melt part of a piece of silver, which is already at its melting point of 961 degrees C. Find the change in the entropy of the silver.

Ans: Given: (a) mass of lead m = 3.00 x 10^2 g = 0.300 kg, latent heat of fusion L = 2.45 x 10^4 J/kg, melting temperature T = 327 degrees C = 600 K
Formula: heat absorbed in melting Delta Q = m L, and change in entropy Delta S = Delta Q / T
Substitution: Delta Q = 0.300 x 2.45 x 10^4 = 7350 J
Delta S = 7350 / 600 = 12.25 J/K
Answer (a): Delta S = 12.3 J/K
Given: (b) same energy Delta Q = 7350 J, melting point of silver T = 961 degrees C = 1234 K
Formula: Delta S = Delta Q / T
Substitution: Delta S = 7350 / 1234 = 5.96 J/K
Answer (b): Delta S = 5.96 J/K (smaller than for lead because the same heat is absorbed at a higher temperature)

Exercise - Numerical Questions

Q: Q1. Water at 20 degrees C falls from a height of 854 meters. If the whole energy is used in increasing the temperature, find out the final temperature. Specific heat of water is 4200 J K^-1 kg^-1

Ans: Given: height h = 854 m, initial temperature = 20 degrees C, specific heat of water c = 4200 J K^-1 kg^-1, g = 9.8 m/s^2
Formula: loss of potential energy = gain of heat energy, m g h = m c Delta T, so Delta T = g h / c
Substitution: Delta T = (9.8 x 854) / 4200 = 8369 / 4200 = 1.99 degrees C, about 2 degrees C
Final temperature = 20 degrees C + 2 degrees C = 22 degrees C
Answer: 22 degrees C

Q: Q2. 25200 J of heat is supplied to the system while the system does 6000 J of work. Calculate the change in internal energy of the system.

Ans: Given: heat supplied Delta Q = 25200 J, work done by the system Delta W = 6000 J
Formula: first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, so Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W
Substitution: Delta U = 25200 J - 6000 J = 19200 J
Answer: Delta U = 19200 J (the internal energy increases by 19200 J)

Q: Q3. A sample of ideal gas is uniformly heated at constant pressure. If the amount of 180 J of heat is supplied to the gas, calculate the Change in internal energy of the gas and Work done by the gas. Take gamma = 1.41

Ans: Given: heat supplied at constant pressure Delta Q = 180 J, gamma = Cp / Cv = 1.41
Formula: at constant pressure, Delta U / Delta Q = Cv / Cp = 1 / gamma, so Delta U = Delta Q / gamma, and Delta W = Delta Q - Delta U
Substitution: Delta U = 180 / 1.41 = 127.66 J
Delta W = 180 - 127.66 = 52.34 J
Answer: Delta U = 127.66 J, Delta W = 52.34 J

Q: Q4. Find the efficiency of a Carnot's heat engine working between the steam and ice points?

Ans: Given: source temperature (steam point) T1 = 100 degrees C = 373 K, sink temperature (ice point) T2 = 0 degrees C = 273 K
Formula: Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1
Substitution: eta = 1 - 273 / 373 = 1 - 0.732 = 0.268
Answer: eta = 26.8 %

Q: Q5. A Carnot heat engine absorbs 2000 J of heat from the source of heat engine at 227 degrees C and rejects 1200 J of heat during each cycle to sink. Calculate efficiency of engine temperature of sink and amount of work done during each cycle.

Ans: Given: heat absorbed Q1 = 2000 J, heat rejected Q2 = 1200 J, source temperature T1 = 227 degrees C = 500 K
Formula: efficiency eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1, work W = Q1 - Q2, and for a Carnot engine Q2 / Q1 = T2 / T1, so T2 = T1 x Q2 / Q1
Substitution: eta = (2000 - 1200) / 2000 = 800 / 2000 = 0.40 = 40%
W = 2000 - 1200 = 800 J
T2 = 500 x 1200 / 2000 = 300 K = 300 - 273 = 27 degrees C
Answer: eta = 40%, sink temperature = 27 degrees C, W = 800 J

Q: Q6. What is the least amount of work that must be performed to freeze one gram of water at 0 degrees C by means of a refrigerator? Take the temperature of the surrounding as 37 degrees C. How much heat is passed on to the surrounding during this process?

Ans: Given: mass m = 1 g = 1 x 10^-3 kg, cold temperature T2 = 0 degrees C = 273 K, surroundings T1 = 37 degrees C = 310 K, latent heat of fusion of ice L = 3.36 x 10^5 J/kg
Formula: heat to be removed Q2 = m L; least work corresponds to a Carnot refrigerator, W = Q2 (T1 - T2) / T2; heat passed to surroundings Q1 = Q2 + W
Substitution: Q2 = 1 x 10^-3 x 3.36 x 10^5 = 336 J
W = 336 x (310 - 273) / 273 = 336 x 37 / 273 = 45.54 J
Q1 = 336 + 45.54 = 381.54 J
Answer: W = 45.54 J, heat passed to the surroundings = 381.54 J

Q: Q7. Calculate the change in entropy when 10 kg of water is heated from 90 degrees C to 100 degrees C? (Specific heat of water is 4180 J mole^-1 K^-1.

Ans: Given: mass m = 10 kg, specific heat of water c = 4180 J kg^-1 K^-1 (the unit is printed as J mole^-1 K^-1 in the book), initial temperature T1 = 90 degrees C = 363 K, final temperature T2 = 100 degrees C = 373 K
Formula: since the temperature changes, Delta S = m c ln (T2 / T1)
Substitution: Delta S = 10 x 4180 x ln (373 / 363) = 41800 x ln (1.0275) = 41800 x 0.02717 = 1135.8 J K^-1
Answer: Delta S = 1135.8 J K^-1

Q: Q8. A system absorbs 1176 J of heat and at the same time does 352.8 J of external work. Find the change in internal energy of the system? Find the change in internal energy in the system when it absorbs 1050 J of heat while 84 J of work is done? What will be the change in internal energy of the gas if 210 J of heat is removed at constant volume?

Ans: Given: first case Delta Q = 1176 J, Delta W = 352.8 J; second case Delta Q = 1050 J, Delta W = 84 J; third case Delta Q = -210 J at constant volume, so Delta W = 0
Formula: first law, Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W
Substitution: first case Delta U = 1176 - 352.8 = 823.2 J
Second case Delta U = 1050 - 84 = 966 J
Third case Delta U = -210 - 0 = -210 J
Answer: 823.2 J, 966 J, and -210 J (in the third case the internal energy decreases by 210 J; the book's bracket lists only the first two values)

Q: Q9. An ideal gas at 20.0 degrees C and a pressure of 1.50 x 10^5 Pa is in a container having a volume of 1.00 L. (a) Determine the number of moles of gas in the container. (b) The gas pushes against a piston, expanding to twice its original volume, while the pressure falls to atmospheric pressure. Find the final temperature.

Ans: Given: temperature T1 = 20.0 degrees C = 293 K, pressure P1 = 1.50 x 10^5 Pa, volume V1 = 1.00 L = 1.00 x 10^-3 m^3, R = 8.314 J mole^-1 K^-1
Formula: (a) ideal gas equation P V = n R T, so n = P1 V1 / (R T1)
Substitution: n = (1.50 x 10^5 x 1.00 x 10^-3) / (8.314 x 293) = 150 / 2436 = 0.0616 mole
Answer (a): n = 6.16 x 10^-2 mol
Given: (b) final volume V2 = 2.00 L = 2.00 x 10^-3 m^3, final pressure P2 = atmospheric pressure = 1.01 x 10^5 Pa
Formula: T2 = P2 V2 / (n R)
Substitution: T2 = (1.01 x 10^5 x 2.00 x 10^-3) / (0.0616 x 8.314) = 202 / 0.512 = 395 K
Answer (b): T2 = 395 K

Q: Q10. A block of ice at 273 K is put in thermal contact with a container of steam at 373 K, converting 25.0 g of ice to water at 273 K while condensing some of the steam to water at 373 K. (a) Find the change in entropy of the ice. (b) Find the change in entropy of the steam. (c) Find the change in entropy of the Universe.

Ans: Given: mass of ice melted m = 25.0 g = 0.0250 kg, latent heat of fusion of ice L = 3.33 x 10^5 J/kg, ice temperature = 273 K, steam temperature = 373 K
Formula: heat absorbed by ice Delta Q = m L; entropy change at constant temperature Delta S = Delta Q / T
Substitution: Delta Q = 0.0250 x 3.33 x 10^5 = 8325 J
(a) Delta S(ice) = +8325 / 273 = +30.5 J/K (entropy increases as the ice melts)
(b) The steam loses the same 8325 J in condensing, so Delta S(steam) = -8325 / 373 = -22.3 J/K
(c) Delta S(Universe) = 30.5 - 22.3 = +8.2 J/K
Answer: (a) 30.5 J/K, (b) -22.3 J/K, (c) +8.2 J/K (the total entropy increases, as the second law requires for this irreversible transfer of heat)

mcqs.q: An ideal gas absorbs 5.00 x 10^3 J of energy while doing 2.00 x 10^3 J of work on the environment during a constant pressure process. Compute the change in the internal energy of the gas.
mcqs.why: Formula: first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, so Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W. Substitution: Delta U = 5.00 x 10^3 J - 2.00 x 10^3 J. Step: subtracting gives 3.00 x 10^3 J. Result: Delta U = 3.00 x 10^3 J. The book's printed 3.00 x 10^5 J has the wrong exponent; the subtraction gives an exponent of 3, not 5.

mcqs.q: During one cycle, an engine extracts 2.00 x 10^3 J of energy from a hot reservoir and transfers 1.50 x 10^3 J to a cold reservoir. Find the thermal efficiency of the engine.
mcqs.why: Formula: efficiency eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1, where the work per cycle is W = Q1 - Q2. Substitution: eta = (2.00 x 10^3 - 1.50 x 10^3) / 2.00 x 10^3 = 500 / 2000. Step: the quotient is 0.250. Result: eta = 0.250, or 25.0 percent, with 5.00 x 10^2 J of work done per cycle.

mcqs.q: Find the change in entropy of 3.00 x 10^2 g of lead when it melts at 327 degrees C. Lead has a latent heat of fusion of 2.45 x 10^4 J/kg.
mcqs.why: Formula: heat absorbed in melting Delta Q = m L, and change in entropy Delta S = Delta Q / T, with T in kelvin. Substitution: m = 0.300 kg and T = 327 + 273 = 600 K, so Delta Q = 0.300 x 2.45 x 10^4 = 7350 J. Step: Delta S = 7350 / 600 = 12.25 J/K. Result: Delta S = 12.3 J/K.

mcqs.q: Water at 20 degrees C falls from a height of 854 meters. If the whole energy is used in increasing the temperature, find out the final temperature. Specific heat of water is 4200 J K^-1 kg^-1
mcqs.why: Formula: loss of potential energy equals gain of heat energy, m g h = m c Delta T, so Delta T = g h / c. Substitution: Delta T = (9.8 x 854) / 4200 = 8369 / 4200. Step: the temperature rise is 1.99 degrees C, about 2 degrees C. Result: final temperature = 20 + 2 = 22 degrees C.

mcqs.q: 25200 J of heat is supplied to the system while the system does 6000 J of work. Calculate the change in internal energy of the system.
mcqs.why: Formula: first law, Delta Q = Delta U + Delta W, so Delta U = Delta Q - Delta W. Substitution: Delta U = 25200 J - 6000 J. Step: subtracting gives 19200 J. Result: Delta U = 19200 J, so the internal energy of the system increases by 19200 J.

mcqs.q: Find the efficiency of a Carnot's heat engine working between the steam and ice points?
mcqs.why: Formula: Carnot efficiency eta = 1 - T2 / T1, with temperatures in kelvin. Substitution: steam point T1 = 373 K and ice point T2 = 273 K, so eta = 1 - 273 / 373 = 1 - 0.732. Step: the difference is 0.268. Result: eta = 26.8 percent.

mcqs.q: A Carnot heat engine absorbs 2000 J of heat from the source of heat engine at 227 degrees C and rejects 1200 J of heat during each cycle to sink. Calculate efficiency of engine temperature of sink and amount of work done during each cycle.
options: Efficiency 60%, sink 27 degrees C, work 1200 J
Efficiency 40%, sink 27 degrees C, work 800 J
Efficiency 40%, sink 300 degrees C, work 800 J
Efficiency 25%, sink 27 degrees C, work 500 J
mcqs.why: Formula: efficiency eta = (Q1 - Q2) / Q1, work W = Q1 - Q2, and for a Carnot engine T2 = T1 x Q2 / Q1. Substitution: eta = (2000 - 1200) / 2000 = 800 / 2000 = 0.40, W = 800 J, and T2 = 500 K x 1200 / 2000 = 300 K. Step: 300 K is 300 - 273 = 27 degrees C. Result: efficiency 40 percent, sink temperature 27 degrees C, work 800 J per cycle.

mcqs.q: What is the least amount of work that must be performed to freeze one gram of water at 0 degrees C by means of a refrigerator? Take the temperature of the surrounding as 37 degrees C.
mcqs.why: Formula: heat to be removed Q2 = m L, and the least work, for a Carnot refrigerator, is W = Q2 (T1 - T2) / T2. Substitution: Q2 = 1 x 10^-3 kg x 3.36 x 10^5 J/kg = 336 J, with T2 = 273 K and T1 = 310 K, so W = 336 x (310 - 273) / 273 = 336 x 37 / 273. Step: the quotient is 45.54 J, and the heat passed to the surroundings is Q1 = 336 + 45.54 = 381.54 J. Result: least work W = 45.54 J.

mcqs.q: Calculate the change in entropy when 10 kg of water is heated from 90 degrees C to 100 degrees C? (Specific heat of water is 4180 J kg^-1 K^-1.)
mcqs.why: Formula: when the temperature changes, Delta S = m c ln (T2 / T1). Substitution: T1 = 363 K and T2 = 373 K, so Delta S = 10 x 4180 x ln (373 / 363) = 41800 x ln (1.0275). Step: ln (1.0275) = 0.02717, and 41800 x 0.02717 = 1135.8. Result: Delta S = 1135.8 J/K.

mcqs.q: An ideal gas at 20.0 degrees C and a pressure of 1.50 x 10^5 Pa is in a container having a volume of 1.00 L. Determine the number of moles of gas in the container.
mcqs.why: Formula: ideal gas equation P V = n R T, so n = P1 V1 / (R T1). Substitution: V1 = 1.00 x 10^-3 m^3 and T1 = 293 K, so n = (1.50 x 10^5 x 1.00 x 10^-3) / (8.314 x 293) = 150 / 2436. Step: the quotient is 0.0616. Result: n = 6.16 x 10^-2 mol.
